items.stem: Iodine-131 ($^{131}\text{I}$) is used to check thyroid function. Its physical half-life is $T_{\text{P}} = 192\text{ h}$ and its biological half-life is $T_{\text{B}} = 96.0\text{ h}$. Calculate its effective half-life $T_{\text{E}}$.
items.workedSolution: Using $\frac{1}{T_{\text{E}}} = \frac{1}{T_{\text{B}}} + \frac{1}{T_{\text{P}}} = \frac{1}{96.0} + \frac{1}{192} = \frac{3}{192}$, we get $T_{\text{E}} = 64.0 h$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 64.0 h.

items.stem: Around 1900, two experiments broke classical wave physics. These were the black-body radiation spectrum and the photoelectric effect.
items.workedSolution: Classical black-body theory predicted infinite UV intensity (the ultraviolet catastrophe). Planck solved this with discrete quanta $E = hf$, suppressing high-frequency UV emission. Wave theory also failed for photoelectricity. Einstein explained threshold frequency, instant emission, and $E_{\text{k(max)}}$ using one-to-one photon absorption ($hf = \phi + E_{\text{k(max)}}$), proving light is quantised.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Describes the ultraviolet catastrophe: classical wave theory predicted black-body intensity rising toward infinity at short (UV) wavelengths, contradicting observed curves.
L1: States Planck's resolution: radiation energy is emitted/absorbed in discrete packets (quanta) of size $E = hf$.
L2: Explains why quanta stop UV divergence: at high frequencies $hf$ is much larger than thermal energy, so UV emission is rare.
L2: Gives two wave failures in photoelectricity: threshold frequency $f_0$, instant emission at low intensity, or intensity-independent $E_{\text{k(max)}}$.
L3: Explains Einstein's photon model: one photon of energy $hf$ hits one electron ($hf = \phi + E_{\text{k(max)}}$), freeing it instantly if $hf \ge \phi$.
L3: States significance: Einstein applied quantisation to light itself, establishing wave–particle duality.

parts.prompt: Explain the ultraviolet catastrophe and how Max Planck's quantum idea solved it. Then explain why classical wave theory failed for photoelectricity, and why Einstein's photon model mattered.
parts.expectedAnswer: Classical Rayleigh–Jeans theory treated thermal energy as continuous and predicted infinite intensity in the ultraviolet. Real black-body curves peak and drop to zero at short wavelengths. Planck solved this by quantising oscillator energy into discrete packets $E = hf$, making high-frequency UV emission rare. Classical wave theory also failed to explain photoelectric threshold frequency, instant emission, and intensity-independent maximum kinetic energy. Einstein extended quantisation to light itself as photons acting one-to-one on electrons ($hf = \phi + E_{\text{k(max)}}$). This established the quantum particle nature of light.
workingSteps: Define the ultraviolet catastrophe: classical continuous-energy equipartition predicted infinite spectral intensity at short UV wavelengths, contradicting experimental curves.
Explain Planck's resolution (1900): oscillators emit/absorb discrete energy quanta E = hf, suppressing high-frequency UV modes because hf >> kT.

State classical wave failures in photoelectricity: predicted any frequency should emit electrons if intense enough (no threshold frequency), expected a time delay at low intensity, and predicted $E_{\text{k(max)}}$ should rise with intensity.

State Einstein's photon model (1905): EM radiation travels as discrete quanta (photons) of energy $hf$ absorbed one-to-one by surface electrons ($hf = \phi + E_{\text{k(max)}}$), explaining threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi / h$, instant emission, and intensity affecting current only.
State significance: electromagnetic waves show particle-like quantised behaviour alongside wave interference (wave–particle duality).

items.stem: A CT X-ray tube runs at an accelerating p.d. of $120\text{ kV}$. Filters then form a narrow monochromatic beam. Calculate the minimum X-ray wavelength emitted by the tube in picometres.
items.workedSolution: $E_{\max} = eV = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.20 \times 10^5 = 1.92 \times 10^{-14}\text{ J}$. Then $\lambda_{\min} = \frac{hc}{E_{\max}} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^8}{1.92 \times 10^{-14}} = 10.4 pm$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 10.4 pm.

items.stem: A single-electron O⁷⁺ ion (Z = 8) has energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The ion starts in level n = 2. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest photon wavelength that can ionize the ion from n = 2?
items.workedSolution: Initial level energy Eₙ = −13.6 × 8² / 2² = −218 eV. Ionization requires ΔE = 218 eV = 3.48 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Maximum ionizing wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = 5.71 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV and λ = hc / ΔE = 5.71 nm (A).

items.stem: A deuterium nucleus has nucleon number A = 2 and proton number Z = 1. Its nuclear mass is 2.013553 u. Take mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this deuterium nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 2 − 1 = 1. Mass defect Δm = 1(1.007276) + 1(1.008665) − 2.013553 = 2.39 × 10⁻³ u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 2.22 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 2.22 / 2 = 1.11 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 2.39 × 10⁻³ u, B = 2.22 MeV, and B / A = 1.11 MeV (C).

items.stem: A beam of thermal neutrons moves through a vacuum tube at a steady speed of 3100 m s⁻¹. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₙ = 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the thermal neutrons?
items.workedSolution: Momentum p = mv = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)(3100) = 5.19 × 10⁻²⁴ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (5.19 × 10⁻²⁴) = 0.128 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 0.128 nm (C).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: An X-ray tube emission spectrum has a smooth continuous curve with a sharp short-wavelength cutoff. Narrow discrete spikes sit on top of this curve.
items.workedSolution: Level 3: Decelerating electrons produce the continuous bremsstrahlung curve, with cutoff $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$. Inner-shell jumps in tungsten emit sharp K-line peaks. A rotating tungsten-copper anode removes heat. Higher filament current raises intensity only, while higher anode voltage raises intensity and shortens $\lambda_{\min}$ with fixed K-lines.

markScheme.criterion: Explains continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum arises from electrons decelerating by varying amounts near target nuclei.
Explains sharp cutoff $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$ occurs when all kinetic energy of an electron becomes a single photon.
Explains characteristic spikes come from inner-shell vacancies filled by outer-shell electrons emitting fixed energy differences.
Explains ~99% of energy becomes heat, managed by a rotating high-melting-point tungsten anode in copper/oil cooling.
Correctly states increasing filament current increases intensity across the spectrum without altering $\lambda_{\min}$.
Correctly states increasing anode voltage shortens $\lambda_{\min}$ and increases intensity while keeping K-line wavelengths fixed.

parts.prompt: Explain how both the continuous spectrum (including its sharp cutoff) and the discrete peaks form. Describe how anode heat is removed. Compare raising filament current with raising anode p.d.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons accelerate onto a tungsten target. Most decelerate by varying amounts near tungsten nuclei, emitting continuous bremsstrahlung radiation. The cutoff $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$ happens when an electron converts 100% of its kinetic energy $eV$ into one photon. Discrete $K_\alpha$ and $K_\beta$ spikes happen when electrons knock out inner K-shell electrons. Outer L- or M-shell electrons drop into the gap, emitting photons of fixed energy. About 99% of electron energy becomes heat, so high-melting-point tungsten spins on a disc in copper and cooling oil. Higher filament current sends more electrons per second, raising intensity without changing $\lambda_{\min}$. Higher anode voltage raises intensity and shortens $\lambda_{\min}$, while K-line wavelengths stay fixed.
workingSteps: Explain bremsstrahlung continuum from variable electron deceleration near tungsten nuclei.
Derive sharp short-wavelength limit $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$ from complete conversion of electron KE.
Explain characteristic K-lines from inner-shell vacancy ionisation and outer-to-inner atomic transitions.
Explain thermal management (~99% heat): rotating tungsten anode in thermally conducting copper block.
State effect of higher filament current: greater electron flux raises intensity with unchanged $\lambda_{\min}$.
State effect of higher anode voltage: shorter $\lambda_{\min}$, higher intensity, fixed K-line wavelengths.

items.stem: Mo-99 decays by beta-minus emission to form excited technetium-99 in the metastable 0.14 MeV state (Tc-99m). It drops to the 0 MeV ground state with a 6.0-hour half-life. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) 3.38 × 10¹⁹ Hz. (b) 8.88 pm. (c) Tc-99m has a six-hour metastable half-life and emits pure gamma rays, without damaging alpha or beta particles.

markScheme.criterion: Converts 0.14 MeV into 2.24 × 10⁻¹⁴ J and divides by h.
Obtains f = 3.38 × 10¹⁹ Hz.
Applies λ = c / f and converts to picometres.
Obtains λ = 8.88 pm.
States pure gamma emission escapes the patient for external detection without tissue-damaging α/β.
States 6 h metastable half-life is long enough to image yet short enough to limit patient dose.

items.stem: A nuclear fusion reaction is: 2 deuterons (each of mass 2.013553 u) → triton (3.015501 u) + proton (1.007276 u). Use u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 4.33 × 10⁻³ u. Final answer: 4.33 × 10⁻³ u. (b) Q = 4.33 × 10⁻³ × 931.5 = 4.03 MeV. Final answer: 4.03 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 4. Final answer: 4.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Correct answer: 4.33 × 10⁻³ u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.

items.stem: A student slowly raises the p.d. across a forward-biased LED. It just begins to glow at threshold voltage $V_0$. Which energy relation holds at this point?
items.workedSolution: At switch-on, electrical work eV₀ (eV0) done by one electron equals the photon energy hf = hc/λ. Thus electrical work eV0 equals hc divided by lambda.

markScheme.criterion: States electrical work eV0 per electron equals emitted photon energy hc divided by lambda.

items.stem: A beam of light of frequency 2.06 × 10¹⁵ Hz hits a clean zinc plate in a vacuum. The zinc surface has work function Φ = 4.33 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the threshold frequency f₀ of the zinc surface?
items.workedSolution: Work function Φ = 4.33 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f₀ = Φ / h = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Finds f₀ = Φ / h = 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz (D).

items.stem: Cosmic-ray muons travel at constant speed v = 0.96c through Earth's atmosphere over a proper distance L₀ = 4800 m. The mean lifetime of a muon in its rest frame is Δt₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ s. What dilated time interval Δt is measured in the stationary frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.96²) = 3.57. Dilated time interval Δt = γ Δt₀ = 3.57 × 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ = 7.86 × 10⁻⁶ s.

markScheme.criterion: Finds γ = 3.57 and Δt = γ Δt₀ = 7.86 × 10⁻⁶ s (A).

items.stem: A 1:1 Minkowski diagram shows frame S′ moving at v = 0.80c relative to frame S. It also shows calibration hyperbolae (ct)² − x² = ±s₀² with s₀ = 2.0 ls.
items.workedSolution: (a) γ = 1.67. (b) ct = 3.33 ls. (c) x = 2.67 ls. (d) Stretch ratio = 2.13. (e) Unit ticks on the tilted ct′ and x′ axes are wider on paper than on perpendicular ct and x axes. The hyperbolae mark equal invariant intervals on the primed axes.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.67.
Applies x = βct into (ct)² − x² = s₀² (or inverse Lorentz transform ct = γct′).
Obtains ct = 3.33 ls.
Applies x = βct = γβs₀.
Obtains x = 2.67 ls.
Computes Euclidean paper distance √(x² + (ct)²) divided by s₀.
Obtains stretch factor = 2.13.
States unit ticks on tilted ct′ and x′ are spaced further apart on paper than on ct and x.
Explains the invariant hyperbolae (ct)² − x² = ±s₀² define equal proper intervals across frames.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Lorentz factor γ for v = 0.80c.
Determine the unprimed coordinate ct where the timelike hyperbola (ct)² − x² = +(2.0 ls)² intersects the ct′ axis (at ct′ = 2.0 ls, x′ = 0).
workingSteps: Along x′ = 0, ct = γ s₀ = 1.67 × 2.0 = 3.33 ls

parts.prompt: Determine the corresponding unprimed position coordinate x of that calibration intersection point.
Calculate the geometric stretch ratio √(x² + (ct)²) / s₀ comparing paper tick spacing on ct′ to that on ct.
Explain why invariant calibration hyperbolae are needed to read primed coordinates on a Minkowski diagram.
parts.expectedAnswer: Unit ticks on the tilted ct′ and x′ axes are further apart on paper than on the perpendicular ct and x axes. The invariant hyperbolae ct² − x² = ±s² mark where those unit ticks sit on the primed axes.
workingSteps: Unit ticks on tilted ct′ and x′ are wider than on perpendicular ct and x, set by where hyperbolae intersect them.

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, 112 nm UV light strikes a zinc surface. The surface has work function Φ = 4.33 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁸ J; work function Φ = 4.33 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 1.08 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.54 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.54 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (A).

options.distractorRationale: Adds the work function Φ to hc/λ instead of subtracting Φ before solving ½mₑv² = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ.

options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 in vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ), evaluating √(Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Equates ½mₑv² directly to the incident photon energy hc/λ without subtracting the work function.

items.stem: A low-pressure gas emits sharp, separate coloured lines in its spectrum. What does this show about atomic structure?
items.workedSolution: Since $E = hf$, isolated frequencies mean atoms only absorb and emit fixed photon energies. This shows electrons occupy discrete atomic energy levels.

markScheme.criterion: States sharp spectral lines show atoms absorb and emit only specific quantized photon energies.

options.label: A
options.text: Electrons can spiral continuously at any radius and radiate a smooth unbroken rainbow of energies.
options.distractorRationale: Continuous radiation would produce a continuous spectrum, not isolated sharp lines.

options.label: B
options.text: Atomic nuclei have zero positive charge until struck by ultraviolet photons.
options.distractorRationale: Rutherford scattering showed nuclei carry permanent positive charge independent of illumination.

options.label: C
options.text: The sharp discrete spectral lines show atoms only absorb and emit specific quantized photon energies, corresponding to electrons transitioning between discrete atomic energy levels.

options.label: D
options.text: All chemical elements share identical atomic energy levels and identical spectral wavelengths.
options.distractorRationale: Each element has its own unique set of energy levels and spectral fingerprint.

items.stem: A $1.54\text{ MeV}$ gamma photon interacts near a tungsten nucleus to produce an electron and its antiparticle. Rest energy of an electron $= 0.511\text{ MeV}$, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Antiparticle: positron; $E_{\min} = 2E_0 = 1.02 MeV$. (b) $E_{\text{k,tot}} = 0.518 MeV$; $f_{\min} = (2E_0 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-13})/6.63 \times 10^{-34} = 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Name positron (reject 'antielectron').
Minimum energy $2E_0 = 1.02 MeV$.
Total kinetic energy $= 0.518 MeV$.
Convert $2E_0$ to joules using $1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J MeV}^{-1}$ and divide by $h$.
Threshold frequency $= 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$.

parts.prompt: Name the antiparticle produced and calculate the minimum photon energy in MeV needed for this pair production.
workingSteps: Name antiparticle: positron (do not accept 'antielectron' for positron).

parts.prompt: Calculate the total kinetic energy of the created pair in MeV and the threshold photon frequency in Hz.
parts.expectedAnswer: Total kinetic energy $= 0.518 MeV$; threshold frequency $= 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$
workingSteps: Convert $2E_0$ to joules and divide by $h$: $f_{\min} = 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$.

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student records 540 background counts in 20 minutes. They then mount a sealed gamma source opposite a GM tube. At ruler distances $x_1 = 150$ mm and $x_2 = 450$ mm, the raw count rates are 142.2 s⁻¹ and 18.71 s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.450 s⁻¹$. (b) Subtracting background gives $C_{\mathrm{corr},1} = 141.7$ s⁻¹ and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 18.26$ s⁻¹. The gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ is 0.500, so $k = 1/\mathrm{grad}^2 = 4.00 s⁻¹ m²$. (c) $x_0 = 18.0 mm$. (d) Handle the gamma source with long tongs, maximise distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal the systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.450 s⁻¹$.
Subtracts $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both raw rates and calculates $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$.
Finds gradient $\Delta(1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}})/\Delta x = 1/\sqrt{k}$.
Inverse-square constant $k = 4.00 s⁻¹ m²$.
Solves $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$ (or intercept/gradient) for $x_0$.
Systematic offset $x_0 = 18.0 mm$.
Long tongs + maximise distance + minimise time out of lead-lined box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Explains $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ remains linear despite unknown $x_0$ (whereas $C$ vs $1/x^2$ curves).
Identifies negative x-intercept $-x_0$ as the hidden offset inside source capsule and GM tube.

parts.prompt: Calculate the background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ in s⁻¹.
Subtract background radiation and find $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ at both positions. Use the gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ to find $k$.
Determine the hidden internal systematic offset $x_0$ in mm.
State the required radiological safety precautions and explain why plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ is preferred over $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs, keep maximum distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plotting one over square root corrected count rate against x gives a straight line that reveals the systematic offset.
workingSteps: Long tongs, maximum distance, point source away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box.
1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k stays linear and gives x₀ directly from the negative x-intercept.

items.stem: Calculate the magnitude of the specific charge of a bare $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$ nucleus. Take $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: Net charge magnitude $Q = 12 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁸ C$ and mass $m = 4.02 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, giving $Q/m = 4.78 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. Option D (4.78 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Correct specific charge $Q/m = 4.78 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$ (4.78 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹, option D).

items.stem: In a fusion plasma, deuterium (²H, BE/A = 1.11 MeV) and tritium (³H, BE/A = 2.83 MeV) fuse to produce helium-4 (⁴He, BE/A = 7.07 MeV) and a free neutron. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) 17.6 MeV. (b) 3.12 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. (c) 3.51 MeV. (d) The curve rises much more steeply on the low-A side than it falls on the high-A side. Fusion therefore releases more energy per nucleon and per kilogram.

markScheme.criterion: Computes total binding energies of reactants (10.71 MeV) and products (28.28 MeV).
Subtracts to obtain ΔE = 17.6 MeV.
Converts MeV to joules and applies Δm = ΔE / c².
Obtains mass decrease Δm = 3.12 × 10⁻²⁹ kg.
Divides by 5 nucleons to obtain 3.51 MeV.
Notes the curve rises much more steeply on the low-A fusion side than on the high-A fission side.
Links greater Δ(BE/A) per nucleon directly to larger energy release per kilogram of fuel.

parts.expectedAnswer: The curve rises much more steeply on the low-A fusion side than it falls on the high-A fission side. Fusion therefore releases more energy per nucleon and per kilogram than fission.

items.stem: Which statement compares the ionising power and range in air of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation?
items.workedSolution: Stronger ionisation means faster energy loss in air and a shorter range. Alpha is strongly ionising with a range of a few centimetres. Beta is moderately ionising with a range of around one metre. Gamma is weakly ionising with infinite range obeying an inverse-square law.

markScheme.criterion: Compares alpha (strongest, few cm), beta (moderate, ~one metre), and gamma (weakest, inverse-square infinite range).

options.label: A
options.text: Gamma photons are the most strongly ionising and stop within a few centimetres of air, whereas alpha particles travel several metres.
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the inverse link between ionising density and range in air.

options.label: B
options.text: Beta particles have the highest ionising power because their small mass lets them transfer energy rapidly in every collision.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles carry twice the charge (+2e) and move much more slowly, creating far denser ionisation tracks than beta particles.

options.label: C
options.text: All three emissions have identical range in air once corrected for background radiation because they travel at the speed of light.
options.distractorRationale: Only gamma photons travel at c; massive alpha and beta particles lose kinetic energy via frequent ionising collisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Across the three emissions, alpha particles have the greatest ionising power and shortest range in air of a few centimetres, beta particles are moderately ionising with a range of around one metre, and gamma photons are weakly ionising with infinite range obeying an inverse-square law.

items.stem: Sensors detect that more than one neutron per fission is causing another fission. How does the emergency shutdown system stop the chain reaction?
items.workedSolution: Boron or cadmium control rods drop fully into the core to absorb neutrons. This pushes k below 1, halting the critical chain reaction for safe shutdown.

markScheme.criterion: States fully inserting boron or cadmium control rods absorbs neutrons to shut down the chain reaction.

options.label: A
options.text: Fully inserting extra uranium fuel rods dilutes the neutron flux and stops fission immediately.
options.distractorRationale: Adding fissile fuel increases reactivity rather than shutting down the core.

options.label: B
options.text: Fully inserting boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a steady critical chain reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Fully inserting concrete blocks into the cooling water slows down the steam turbine directly.
options.distractorRationale: Concrete is the external biological shield; shutdown acts directly on core neutron population.

options.label: D
options.text: Fully inserting graphite rods speeds up thermal neutrons so they cannot escape the vessel.
options.distractorRationale: Graphite moderates (slows) neutrons to promote fission rather than absorbing them.

items.stem: An unstable isotope X lies directly above the stability belt at moderate Z. Which nuclear transition moves X closer to the line of stability?
items.workedSolution: Nuclei above the stability belt have too high an N/Z ratio. They decay by beta-minus emission, turning a neutron into a proton to lower N/Z.

markScheme.criterion: States beta-minus emission turns a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio.

options.label: A
options.text: It undergoes beta-plus emission converting a proton into a neutron to increase the N/Z ratio even further.
options.distractorRationale: Moving further above the belt pushes the nuclide away from stability.

options.label: B
options.text: It undergoes alpha emission even though its proton number is far below eighty-two.
options.distractorRationale: Nuclides above the belt at low/medium Z are neutron-rich and decay via β⁻ rather than α.

options.label: C
options.text: It undergoes electron capture to add another neutron and reduce proton number by one.
options.distractorRationale: Electron capture serves proton-rich nuclei below the belt, not neutron-rich nuclei above it.

options.label: D
options.text: It undergoes beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio

items.stem: High-energy 300 MeV electrons are scattered off a thin calcium-40 (A = 40) target to measure nuclear charge radius. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ = 4.14 fm. (b) R = 3.83 fm. (c) ρ = 2.82 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. (d) Electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force, so their diffraction minimum gives radius directly. Alpha closest approach gives only an energy-dependent upper bound.

markScheme.criterion: Converts MeV into joules and applies λ = hc / E.
Obtains λ = 4.14 fm.
Rearranges sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R for R.
Calculates R = 3.83 fm.
Computes nuclear density ρ = 2.82 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
States electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and give direct radius via diffraction minimum.
Contrasts with alpha closest approach, which gives only an energy-dependent upper bound.

parts.prompt: Assuming relativistic electrons obey λ ≈ hc / E, calculate the de Broglie wavelength λ of the incident electrons in femtometres.
The first non-zero diffraction minimum occurs at θ_min = 41.3°. Using sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R, calculate the nuclear radius R of calcium-40 in femtometres.
Taking nucleon mass u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, calculate the density of the calcium-40 nucleus.
Explain why high-energy electron diffraction determines nuclear radius more accurately than Rutherford alpha closest approach.
parts.expectedAnswer: High-energy electrons are leptons and do not feel the strong nuclear force. They diffract to a non-zero first minimum, giving nuclear radius directly. Alpha closest approach gives only an energy-dependent upper bound.
workingSteps: Electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong force, giving radius directly. Alpha closest approach gives only an upper bound.

items.stem: An X-ray photon of wavelength $\lambda_{\text{i}} = 25.0\text{ pm}$ is scattered directly backward ($\theta = 180^{\circ}$) by a stationary free electron. What kinetic energy is transferred to the recoil electron?
items.workedSolution: At $180^{\circ}$, $\Delta\lambda = 2\frac{h}{m_{\text{e}} c} = 4.85 pm$, so $\lambda_{\text{f}} = 29.9 pm$. By energy conservation, $E_{\text{k}} = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{i}}} - \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{f}}}\right) = 49.7 keV - 41.6 keV = 8.08 keV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 8.08 keV.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the electron absorbs the entire incident photon energy instead of the difference $E_{\text{i}} - E_{\text{f}}$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports the remaining energy of the scattered photon instead of the recoil electron kinetic energy.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses $(1 - \cos 90^{\circ}) = 1$ instead of $(1 - \cos 180^{\circ}) = 2$ for backscattering.

items.stem: Electrons ($m_0 = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$) in an accelerator reach a speed of $0.900c$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $E = 1.18 MeV$. (b) $E_k = 0.663 MeV$. (c) Classical $E_k = 0.208 MeV$, much smaller than relativistic KE.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates $\gamma = 1 / \sqrt{1 - 0.900^2} = 2.294$.
Computes $E = \gamma m_0 c^2$ and converts joules to MeV.
Correct total energy 1.18 MeV.
Subtracts rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$ from total energy.
Correct relativistic KE 0.663 MeV.
Computes $\frac{1}{2} m_0 (0.900c)^2$ and converts to MeV.
Correct classical KE 0.208 MeV noting severe underestimate.

items.stem: An alpha particle (charge +2e) with initial kinetic energy 3.9 MeV is fired head-on at a stationary silver nucleus (Z = 47, A = 107). It comes to rest at distance d before reversing. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 3.9 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 6.24 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(2e)(47e) / Eₖ = 3.47 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 34.7 fm. Final answer: 34.7 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (107)^(1/3) = 5.70 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 5.70 fm. (c) ρ = (107 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(5.70 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Eₖ to joules, equates Eₖ = k Q₁ Q₂ / d, and converts metres to femtometres.
Correct answer: 34.7 fm.
Applies R = 1.20 × A^(1/3) fm.
Correct answer: 5.70 fm.
Finds ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) in SI units.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Electrons accelerated from rest across 320 V strike a thin graphite (110) foil with atomic spacing d = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Diffraction rings appear on a fluorescent screen at distance L = 0.13 m behind the foil. Take sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = √(2mₑeV) = 9.66 × 10⁻²⁴ N s. λ = h / p = 6.86 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 68.6 pm. Final answer: 68.6 pm. (b) sin θ = λ / d = 6.86 × 10⁻¹¹ / (1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 0.558. θ = 33.9 °. Final answer: 33.9 °. (c) r = L tan θ = 0.13 × tan(33.9°) = 0.0874 m. Final answer: 0.0874 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = h / √(2mₑeV) with SI values and converts to picometres.
Correct answer: 68.6 pm.
Applies sin θ = λ / d and converts to degrees.
Correct answer: 33.9 °.
Finds r = L tan θ using the screen distance L.
Correct answer: 0.0874 m.

items.stem: Alpha particles (Z₁ = 2) of energy 7.2 MeV scatter from a spherical platinum-195 target nucleus (Z = 78, A = 195). The nuclear radius is given by R = R₀ A^(1/3). Use R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = 1.20 × (195)^(1/3) = 6.96 fm. Final answer: 6.96 fm. (b) R = 6.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Final answer: 6.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. (c) m = 195 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; V = (4/3)π(6.96 × 10⁻¹⁵)³. ρ = m / V = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes nucleon number A into R = R₀ A^(1/3).
Correct answer: 6.96 fm.
Multiplies R in fm by 10⁻¹⁵ m fm⁻¹ to obtain 6.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Divides nuclear mass A u by spherical volume (4/3)πR³.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Each induced fission of uranium-235 releases two or three neutrons. Why can a small sphere of pure fuel NOT sustain a chain reaction?
items.workedSolution: For a sphere, surface-area-to-volume ratio is S/V = 3/r, which grows as radius r shrinks. Below critical mass, S/V is too large, so too many neutrons escape through the surface before causing more fissions.

markScheme.criterion: States below critical mass the surface-area-to-volume ratio is too large, so too many neutrons escape.

options.label: A
options.text: Geometrically, below critical mass the surface-area-to-volume ratio is too large, causing too many fission neutrons to escape through the surface before inducing further fissions.

options.label: B
options.text: Small spheres of uranium-235 cannot undergo induced fission because their binding energy per nucleon exceeds iron-56.
options.distractorRationale: Binding energy per nucleon is an intrinsic nuclear property independent of sample size.

options.label: C
options.text: Small spheres have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, trapping neutrons inside so they decay before striking nuclei.
options.distractorRationale: Surface-area-to-volume ratio scales as 3/r, which is *larger* for smaller spheres.

options.label: D
options.text: Fission neutrons are attracted back to the centre by gravity only when the fuel mass exceeds critical mass.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity has negligible effect on fission neutrons. Neutron escape depends on sphere size versus mean free path.

items.stem: Atoms of potassium vapour have a first excited state at −2.73 eV and a nearby bound level at −4.34 eV. Ionization occurs at zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the lowest photon frequency needed to ionize the atom from the first excited state?
items.workedSolution: Energy needed to reach the continuum is ΔE = 2.73 eV = 4.37 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 4.37 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.59 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f = |E| e / h to obtain 6.59 × 10¹⁴ Hz (D).

items.stem: Electrons in an electron microscope accelerate from rest through an anode p.d. of 15.0 kV. Ignore relativistic effects. What is the speed of each electron leaving the anode? Take $m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$ and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: From $\frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 = eV$, $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 e V}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.50 \times 10^4}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 7.26 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 7.26 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The violet $\text{H}\gamma$ Balmer line comes from a hydrogen electron in a class A star. It jumps from $n = 2$ ($-3.40\text{ eV}$) to $n = 5$ ($-0.544\text{ eV}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta E = 2.86 eV$. (b) $\lambda = hc/\Delta E = 435 nm$. (c) In cool M stars, thermal energy is too low to excite electrons from n=1 to n=2.

Converts eV to J and applies $\lambda = hc/\Delta E$.
Correct wavelength 435 nm.
Notes Balmer absorption requires hydrogen atoms in the $n = 2$ state.
Explains that cool M stars lack thermal energy to excite electrons from n=1 to n=2.

parts.prompt: Explain why this absorption line is extremely weak in a cool red class M star ($< 3500\text{ K}$).
parts.expectedAnswer: Visible Balmer absorption needs electrons in the $n = 2$ state. In cool M stars, thermal energy is too low to excite electrons from n=1 to n=2. Almost all hydrogen stays in the ground state.
workingSteps: State Balmer absorption requires initial population of $n = 2$.
In cool M stars, thermal energy is too low to excite electrons from n=1 to n=2.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube measures a background count rate of 30 counts min⁻¹. An iodine-131 source with half-life 8 d is placed in front of the tube. The initial total count rate is 1054 counts min⁻¹. The detector is read again after 40 d. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 40 d?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 1054 − 30 = 1024 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 40 / 8 = 5. Remaining net count rate C = 1024 / 2^5 = 32 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 32 + 30 = 62.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (1024), divides by 2^5 (32), and adds 30 back to obtain 62.0 counts min⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides the net count rate by 2n instead of 2ⁿ.

items.stem: A sample of radium-223 starts with 7.4 × 10¹⁴ radioactive nuclei. Its half-life is T₁/₂ = 11.4 d. The sample is measured again after 13.5 d. What is the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Converting half-life to SI seconds: T₁/₂ = 11.4 × 86400 = 9.85 × 10⁵ s. Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 7.04 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 5.21 × 10⁸ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = ln 2 / (11.4 × 86400) and A₀ = λN₀ = 5.21 × 10⁸ Bq (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves T₁/₂ in d instead of converting to seconds when evaluating A₀ = (ln 2 / T₁/₂) N₀ in Bq.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor ln 2 ≈ 0.693 in λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Finds the decayed activity at elapsed time t instead of A₀ at t = 0.

items.stem: A doctor treats a small tumour with sealed beta-emitting implants placed inside it. A separate diagnostic tracer has $T_{\text{P}} = 64.0\text{ h}$ and $T_{\text{B}} = 192\text{ h}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Beta-emitting implants deliver short-range ionisation inside the tumour, sparing nearby healthy cells. (b) Alpha particles cannot leave the casing, while gamma rays expose distant healthy tissues. (c) $T_{\text{E}} = (64.0 \times 192)/(64.0 + 192) = 48.0 h$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains beta-emitting radioactive implants deliver short-range ionisation inside a tumour sparing surrounding healthy cells.
Notes millimetre range matches small tumour dimensions.
Notes alpha particles are stopped by capsule/very tiny range.
Notes gamma rays penetrate far beyond the tumour, increasing healthy-organ dose.
Substitutes into $1/T_{\text{E}} = 1/T_{\text{P}} + 1/T_{\text{B}}$.
Correct effective half-life 48.0 h.

items.stem: A nuclear fission power station delivers $900\text{ MW}$ of electrical power at overall thermal efficiency $36.0\%$. Each neutron-induced fission event has a mass defect of $0.215\text{ u}$ ($1\text{ u} = 931.5\text{ MeV }c^{-2}$). How many fission reactions occur per second in the reactor core?
items.workedSolution: Core thermal power $P_{\text{th}} = 900 / 0.360 = 2.50 × 10³ MW$. Energy per fission $Q = 0.215 \times 931.5 = 200 MeV = 3.20 × 10⁻¹¹ J$. Fission rate $= (2.50 \times 10^9) / (3.20 × 10⁻¹¹) = 7.80 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Computes $P_{\text{th}} = 2.50 × 10³ MW$, $Q = 3.20 × 10⁻¹¹ J$, and rate $7.80 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹$.

items.stem: The decay $\mu^- \to e^- + \gamma$ conserves charge, baryon number, and energy. Why has it never been observed?
items.workedSolution: Before: $L_\mu = +1, L_e = 0$. After: $L_\mu = 0, L_e = +1$. Electron and muon lepton numbers must each be conserved, so this decay breaks lepton number conservation. Option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: lepton number conservation.

items.stem: A bone-scan tracer has a physical half-life of 6.00 h and a biological half-life of 18.0 h. What percentage of the initial activity remains after 9.00 h?
items.workedSolution: $T_E = \frac{6.00 \times 18.0}{6.00 + 18.0} = 4.50\text{ h}$. Since $9.00\text{ h} = 2 T_E$, the remaining activity is $100 \times (1/2)^2 = 25.0\%$.

items.stem: Inside a fluorescent tube, a free electron has $7.50\text{ eV}$ of kinetic energy. It hits a ground-state mercury atom ($E_1 = -10.4\text{ eV}$) and excites an orbital electron to $E_2 = -4.9\text{ eV}$. Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Remaining KE $= 2.00\text{ eV}$; $\lambda = 226 nm$. (b) Colliding electrons need at least $\Delta E$ and keep spare energy, whereas a photon must match $\Delta E$. Excited mercury atoms emit UV photons. The phosphor coating absorbs them and drops in smaller steps to emit visible light.

markScheme.criterion: Remaining electron kinetic energy $= 2.00 eV$.
Convert $\Delta E = 5.50\text{ eV}$ to joules and apply $\lambda = hc/\Delta E$.
UV wavelength $= 226 nm$.
L1 (Area 1): Colliding electron needs KE >= ΔE and keeps any spare kinetic energy.
L1 (Area 1): Photon must have exact energy hf = ΔE to be absorbed.
L2 (Area 2): Excited mercury orbital electrons de-excite to lower discrete energy levels.
L2 (Area 2): Downward transitions emit discrete ultraviolet photons with hf = E₁ − E₂.
L3 (Area 3): Phosphor coating absorbs UV photons, exciting electrons in coating atoms.
L3 (Area 3): Phosphor electrons drop in smaller steps, emitting lower-energy visible photons.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy left with the free electron after the collision. Then find the wavelength in nm of the UV photon emitted when the atom drops back to the ground state.
parts.expectedAnswer: Remaining electron KE $= 2.00 eV$; UV photon wavelength $= 226 nm$
workingSteps: Excitation gap $\Delta E = (-4.9) - (-10.4) = 5.50\text{ eV}$, leaving $7.50 - 5.50 = 2.00 eV$ on the colliding electron.

parts.prompt: Compare excitation by a colliding electron with excitation by a photon. Explain how mercury vapour and the phosphor coating turn UV light into visible white light.
parts.expectedAnswer: A colliding electron can excite an atom if its kinetic energy is at least $\Delta E$. It keeps any leftover kinetic energy. A photon is absorbed only if its energy $hf$ equals $\Delta E$ exactly. In the tube, colliding electrons excite mercury electrons to higher levels. When they drop back, they emit UV photons ($hf = E_1 - E_2$). Phosphor atoms absorb these UV photons and drop down in several smaller steps. These smaller steps emit lower-energy, longer-wavelength visible photons.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Electron collision needs E_k >= ΔE and keeps extra KE. Photon absorption needs exact hf = ΔE.
Area 2 (L2): Explain mercury de-excitation emitting discrete UV photons.
Area 3 (L3): Phosphor absorbs UV photons and drops in smaller steps to emit visible light.

items.stem: For a one-electron N⁶⁺ ion (Z = 7), the bound energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. An electron is in state n = 5. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (7)² / (5)² = −26.7 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 26.7 eV. Final answer: 26.7 eV. (b) ΔE = 26.7 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.26 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. f = ΔE / h = 4.26 × 10⁻¹⁸ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.43 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Final answer: 6.43 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (6.43 × 10¹⁵) = 46.6 nm. Final answer: 46.6 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV for the specified Z and n.
Correct answer: 26.7 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Correct answer: 6.43 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f and expresses the wavelength in nm to obtain 46.6 nm.

items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = qV = 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. v = √(2Eₖ / m) = 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Final answer: 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (b) λ = h / (mv) = 4.82 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 0.0482 nm. Final answer: 0.0482 nm. (c) λ = 48.2 pm. Final answer: 48.2 pm.

Multiplies wavelength in nm by 1000 pm nm⁻¹ to obtain 48.2 pm.

items.stem: In a quantum practical, a group plots LED turn-on voltage $V_0$ against $1/\lambda$. They get a straight line through the origin of gradient $1.268 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V m}$. The blue LED has wavelength 460 nm. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ and $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 6.76, giving h = 6.76 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s). (b) V₀ = 2.76 V. (c) Viewing through a dark tube blocks room light, so the exact switch-on voltage is judged more accurately.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies gradient = hc/e and rearranges h = e × gradient / c.
Obtains A = 6.76 (h = 6.76 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
Converts wavelength from nm to m and evaluates V₀ = gradient / λ.
Obtains threshold voltage V₀ = 2.76 V.
States room light hides faint initial glow, causing V₀ to be overestimated.
Links the dark tube to lower systematic error when judging the exact switch-on voltage.

Using the best-fit line gradient, calculate the threshold voltage $V_0$ predicted for the 460 nm LED.

parts.expectedAnswer: An opaque dark tube blocks stray room light. This lets the student judge the exact switch-on voltage more accurately.
workingSteps: Viewing through a dark tube blocks room light, so the exact switch-on voltage is judged more accurately.

items.stem: Light of frequency 1.54 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a clean barium surface in a vacuum. The work function of barium is 2.52 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Φ = 2.52 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f₀ = Φ / h = 4.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.08 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 6.08 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (b) Photon energy E = hf / e = 6.38 eV. Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 6.38 − 2.52 = 3.86 eV. Final answer: 3.86 eV. (c) Vₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / e = 3.86 V. Final answer: 3.86 V.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Φ from eV to joules and applies f₀ = Φ / h.
Correct answer: 6.08 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Applies Einstein's photoelectric equation Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hf/e − Φ.
Correct answer: 3.86 eV.
Uses eVₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to obtain 3.86 V.

items.stem: The 1:1 Minkowski diagram shows perpendicular (x, ct) axes and tilted (x′, ct′) axes. Why are invariant hyperbolae drawn across both sets of axes?
items.workedSolution: In IB Physics (2025), ruler length on paper does not equal the spacetime interval. The invariant hyperbolae (ct)² − x² = ±s₀² cross the tilted ct′ and x′ axes further from the origin than on the perpendicular ct and x axes. This sets the wider unit tick spacing on the primed axes.

markScheme.criterion: States unit ticks on tilted ct′ and x′ axes are wider on paper than on perpendicular ct and x axes, set by invariant hyperbolae.

options.label: A
options.text: Because Euclidean ruler length on paper does not equal spacetime interval, circles centred on the origin calibrate the primed axes so unit ticks on ct′ lie closer together than on ct.
options.distractorRationale: Circular arcs would make unit ticks shorter; Minkowski geometry has a minus sign (ct)² − x² = ±s₀², producing hyperbolae whose ticks are spaced further apart.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Euclidean ruler length on paper does not equal spacetime interval, the unit tick marks on ct′ and x′ have the exact same paper spacing as on ct and x.
options.distractorRationale: Along the tilted axis, x² + (ct)² = s₀²(1+β²)/(1−β²) > s₀², so primed ticks are stretched on paper.

options.label: C
options.text: Because Euclidean ruler length on paper does not equal spacetime interval, hyperbolae represent the accelerating worldlines of photons bending inside the light cone.
options.distractorRationale: Photons follow straight 45° lines; hyperbolae represent loci of constant invariant spacetime interval ±s₀².

options.label: D
options.text: Because Euclidean ruler length on paper does not equal spacetime interval, the unit tick marks on the tilted ct prime and x prime axes are spaced further apart on the diagram than on the orthogonal ct and x axes, located where the invariant hyperbolae ct squared minus x squared equals plus or minus s squared intersect the primed axes.

items.stem: An electron and a positron with combined kinetic energy $0.36\text{ MeV}$ annihilate to produce two identical gamma photons. Each particle has rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$. What is the energy of each emitted photon?
items.workedSolution: Total energy is $2E_0 + E_{\text{k,tot}} = 1.022 + 0.36 = 1.382\text{ MeV}$, shared equally between two photons: $E_\gamma = 0.691 MeV$. Option D (0.691 MeV) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Each photon carries 0.691 MeV (0.691 MeV, option D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Gives the total energy of both photons rather than dividing by two for one photon.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds the full combined kinetic energy to each photon instead of sharing it equally.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the initial kinetic energy of the colliding particles.

items.stem: During Required Practical 12, plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against measured separation $x$ (in m) produces a straight line passing through $(0.11\text{ m}, 0.100)$ and $(0.39\text{ m}, 0.300)$. Determine the inverse-square constant $k$ in $C_{\mathrm{corr}} = k / (x + x_0)^2$.
items.workedSolution: Background rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 450/(15\times 60) = 0.500 s⁻¹$. From $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$, gradient $= 1/\sqrt{k} = 0.714$, so $k = 1.96 s⁻¹ m²$, $x_0 = \text{intercept}/\text{grad} = 30$ mm, and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 11.1 s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A calcium ion $^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ enters a mass spectrometer. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $N = 40 - 20 = 20$; electrons $= 18$. (b) $m = 6.698 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, $Q = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, so $Q/m = 4.78 × 10⁶ C kg⁻¹$. (c) Net charge comes from missing electrons, while neutrons still add to total mass.

markScheme.criterion: Correct neutron number $N = 20$.
Correct orbital electron count $= 18$.
Calculate total mass $m = 6.70 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$ including both protons and neutrons.
Substitute net charge $Q = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ into $Q/m$.
Obtain specific charge $= 4.78 × 10⁶ C kg⁻¹$.
State that ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

parts.prompt: State the number of neutrons in the Ca nucleus and the number of orbital electrons in this ion.
Calculate the total mass of the species in kilograms and hence determine the magnitude of its specific charge.
Explain why neutral neutrons affect the specific charge of a nucleus or ion.
parts.expectedAnswer: Neutrons have zero charge, so net ion charge depends only on excess or missing electrons. However, neutrons still add to total mass, lowering $Q/m$.
workingSteps: Link unchanged charge and larger denominator mass to smaller specific charge.

items.stem: In Rutherford scattering, the kinetic energy of alpha particles can be raised greatly. Why can Eₖ = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀rₘᵢₙ) still fail to give the exact nuclear radius?
items.workedSolution: At high alpha energies, the strong nuclear force alters scattering, so alpha closest approach gives only an energy-dependent upper bound. High-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum, giving radius directly.

markScheme.criterion: States alpha closest approach gives only an upper bound affected by the strong force, while electron diffraction gives radius directly.

options.label: A
options.text: At high alpha energies electrostatic repulsion turns attractive so rₘᵢₙ drops to zero.
options.distractorRationale: Electrostatic force between two positive nuclei always remains repulsive.

options.label: B
options.text: At high alpha energies the strong nuclear force alters scattering, whereas high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

options.label: C
options.text: At high alpha energies the de Broglie wavelength of the alpha particle grows larger than the gold atom.
options.distractorRationale: Higher energy shrinks de Broglie wavelength.

options.label: D
options.text: At high alpha energies Coulomb's constant changes value inside the foil.
options.distractorRationale: Fundamental constants do not change; strong-force onset and nuclear recoil invalidate pure Coulomb closest approach.

items.stem: In a shielding check with background 20 counts min⁻¹, a source gives 420 counts min⁻¹ behind 3 mm aluminium (stopping all beta) and 112 counts min⁻¹ behind 5 cm lead. What percentage of the corrected gamma count rate passes through the 5 cm lead block?
items.workedSolution: Corrected gamma before lead = 420 − 20 = 400 counts min⁻¹; behind lead = 112 − 20 = 92 counts min⁻¹; transmission = (92 / 400) × 100 = 23.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates gamma transmission through lead = 23.0%.

items.stem: Spent nuclear fuel rods contain hot, long-lived radioactive waste (high-level waste). Which sequence shows the safe handling and disposal of high-level waste?
items.workedSolution: High-level fission fragments are handled remotely and placed in cooling ponds first. They are then vitrified in glass inside steel canisters and placed in deep geologically stable underground storage.

markScheme.criterion: States remote handling in cooling ponds, vitrification in glass inside steel canisters, and deep stable storage.

items.stem: An artificially produced proton-rich medical isotope lies below the N–Z stability belt. Which decay transition moves it up and to the left toward stability?
items.workedSolution: Proton-rich nuclei below the belt decay by beta-plus emission or electron capture. This turns a proton into a neutron to raise the N/Z ratio.

markScheme.criterion: States beta-plus emission or electron capture turns a proton into a neutron to raise the N/Z ratio.

options.label: A
options.text: It undergoes beta-plus emission or electron capture converting a proton into a neutron to increase the N/Z ratio

options.label: B
options.text: It undergoes beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to decrease N/Z further.
options.distractorRationale: Beta-minus moves down-right away from stability for proton-rich nuclides.

options.label: C
options.text: It undergoes neutron emission to lower its neutron number while holding Z constant.
options.distractorRationale: Proton-rich nuclides already have too low an N/Z ratio.

options.label: D
options.text: It undergoes gamma emission which increases N by one and decreases Z by one.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma emission changes nuclear excitation energy only, never N or Z.

items.stem: Electrons accelerate from rest through $1600\text{ V}$ in a diffraction experiment. They pass through a thin target of effective width $b = 0.20\text{ nm}$ to form a pattern on a screen.
items.workedSolution: (a) $p = \sqrt{2(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(1600)} = 2.16 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹$, so $\lambda = h/p = 30.7 pm$. (b) $\theta_1 = \lambda / b = 0.153 rad = 8.79 °$. (c) Since $\lambda \propto V^{-1/2}$, higher p.d. shortens the de Broglie wavelength. The diffraction minimum shifts to a smaller angle.

Substitutes into $\lambda = h / p$.

Correct minimum angle 8.79 °.
Explains higher p.d. shortens de Broglie wavelength and moves the minimum to a smaller angle.
Notes $\theta_1$ decreases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

items.stem: An electron ($m_0 c^2 = 0.511\text{ MeV}$) is accelerated until its relativistic kinetic energy reaches 1.022 MeV (twice its rest energy). Express the electron's speed as a fraction of the speed of light ($v/c$).
items.workedSolution: Total energy is $E = E_k + m_0 c^2 = 3 m_0 c^2$, so $\gamma = 3.00$. From $1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2} = \frac{1}{\gamma^2} = \frac{1}{9}$, $\frac{v}{c} = \sqrt{\frac{8}{9}} = 0.943$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 0.943.

items.stem: In a decay chain, an oxygen-15 nucleus (A = 15, Z = 8) changes by beta-plus decay (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ). The product nucleus has A = 15 and Z = 7. How many u → d quark changes occur in this decay chain?
items.workedSolution: Each weak beta step flips exactly one quark inside a nucleon, changing Z by −1 while keeping A constant. Accounting for ΔA = 0 gives 1 weak quark transitions.

markScheme.criterion: Balances A and Z to identify 1 single-quark weak beta transitions (D).

items.stem: An alpha particle (charge +2e) carrying kinetic energy 6.5 MeV moves straight toward a fixed platinum nucleus (Z = 78, A = 195). It stops at closest approach distance d. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 6.5 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.04 × 10⁻¹² J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(2e)(78e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2)(78)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 1.04 × 10⁻¹² = 34.5 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 34.5 fm (B).

items.stem: A nucleus of Cf has nucleon number A = 252 and proton number Z = 98. It decays only by alpha and beta-minus emission. The final nucleus has A = 236 and Z = 92. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Parent neutron number N₀ = 252 − 98 = 154. Final neutron number N_f = 236 − 92 = 144. Therefore ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −10.

items.stem: The clean zinc plate on the gold-leaf electroscope is now positively charged. The same UV source (above threshold frequency) shines on it. What happens to the gold leaf?
items.workedSolution: Any electron freed from the surface is pulled straight back by the positive zinc plate. The gold leaf therefore stays deflected. Option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: gold leaf stays deflected because any freed electrons are attracted back to the positive zinc plate.

options.label: A
options.text: When the plate is positively charged, the gold leaf falls at the same rate because protons are emitted from the plate
options.distractorRationale: Ultraviolet photons have far too little energy to eject tightly bound nuclear protons.

options.label: B
options.text: When the plate is positively charged, the gold leaf falls faster because positive charge assists electron escape
options.distractorRationale: A positive plate attracts negative electrons back rather than repelling them away.

options.label: C
options.text: When the plate is positively charged, the gold leaf stays deflected because any freed electrons are attracted back to the positive zinc plate

options.label: D
options.text: When the plate is positively charged, the gold leaf collapses only if ultraviolet intensity is doubled
options.distractorRationale: Electrostatic attraction pulls freed electrons back onto the positive plate regardless of intensity.

items.stem: Electrons accelerated from rest across 320 V strike a thin silver foil with atomic spacing d = 2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Diffraction rings appear on a fluorescent screen at distance L = 0.17 m behind the foil. Take sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 6.86 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.291 yields θ = arcsin(0.291) = 16.9 °.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 16.9 ° (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves arcsin(λ / d) in radians while labelling the answer in degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inserts an extra factor of 2 in the denominator despite sin θ = λ / d being specified.

options.label: D

items.stem: A scattering test directs alpha particles (Z₁ = 2) of energy 6.3 MeV onto a nucleus of Zr-90 (Z = 40, A = 90). Assume a uniform spherical nucleus with R = R₀ A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Taking nuclear mass m ≈ A u, what is the nuclear density ρ of the Zr-90 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Since R = R₀ A^(1/3), V = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π R₀³ A. Thus ρ = (A u) / ((4/3)π R₀³ A) = 3u / (4π R₀³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ (A).

items.stem: The diagram compares a sub-critical sphere of uranium-235 against a sphere at or above critical mass.
items.workedSolution: (a) Critical mass is the minimum mass of uranium-235 so at least one neutron per fission causes another fission. (b) Below critical mass, surface-area-to-volume ratio is too large, so too many neutrons escape. (c) Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: every undecayed nucleus has constant probability lambda of decaying per second.

markScheme.criterion: Defines critical mass as minimum mass of fissile material for a self-sustaining chain reaction.
States on average at least one neutron per fission must trigger a further fission.
Notes smaller sphere has a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio (∝ 1/r).
Explains a larger proportion of neutrons escape through the surface without hitting U-235 nuclei.
Contrasts neutron-triggered fission with spontaneous random decay unaffected by environment.
Defines λ as constant probability of decay per nucleus per unit time.

parts.prompt: Define what is meant by the critical mass of a fissile material such as uranium-235.
parts.expectedAnswer: Critical mass is the minimum mass of uranium-235 needed to keep a chain reaction going. On average, at least one neutron per fission must trigger another fission instead of escaping.
workingSteps: Minimum mass of uranium-235 needed so at least one neutron per fission triggers another fission.

parts.prompt: Explain in terms of surface-area-to-volume ratio why a sphere below critical mass cannot sustain a chain reaction.
parts.expectedAnswer: Below critical mass, the surface-area-to-volume ratio is too large. Too many fission neutrons escape through the surface before hitting other nuclei.
workingSteps: Below critical mass, surface-area-to-volume ratio is too large, so too many neutrons escape.

parts.prompt: Distinguish between induced fission and spontaneous radioactive decay, stating the meaning of the decay constant λ.
parts.expectedAnswer: Induced fission is triggered by neutron absorption. Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random, unaffected by outside conditions. Every undecayed nucleus has the same constant probability lambda of decaying per second.
workingSteps: Decay is spontaneous and random: each undecayed nucleus has constant probability lambda of decaying per second.

items.stem: Atoms of potassium vapour have a first excited state at −2.69 eV and a nearby bound level at −4.25 eV. Ionization occurs at zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−2.69) = 2.69 eV. Final answer: 2.69 eV. (b) ΔE = 2.69 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 4.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.49 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 6.49 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (6.49 × 10¹⁴) = 4.62 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 462 nm. Final answer: 462 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 2.69 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Correct answer: 6.49 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Correct answer: 462 nm.

items.stem: An STM tip scans a gold crystal at constant height with an initial tunnelling current of 8.00 nA. The current obeys $I = I_0 e^{-k\Delta d}$ with $k = 16.0\text{ nm}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I/I_0 = 0.0907$, $I = 0.726 nA$. (b) Electrons cross the vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling. Current decays exponentially with gap width, giving high sensitivity.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies $8.00\text{ nA}$ by the exponential factor.
Correct new current 0.726 nA.
Explains electrons tunnel as waves across the narrow vacuum gap.
Links exponential dependence on gap width to extreme vertical sensitivity.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fractional factor $I / I_0$ and the new tunnelling current when the surface drops by $\Delta d = 0.150\text{ nm}$.
Explain why quantum tunnelling enables an STM to detect height variations far smaller than a single atomic diameter.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons cross the narrow vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling. The current decays exponentially as gap width grows. Even a tiny change in height therefore causes a large change in current.
workingSteps: Electron wavefunctions decay exponentially across the vacuum potential barrier.
Hence tiny vertical height steps cause dramatic, easily measurable shifts in tunnelling current.

items.stem: With no source present, a detector records a background count rate of 30 counts min⁻¹. When a source of Po-210 (half-life 138 d) is placed in front of it, the total reading is 158 counts min⁻¹. A second reading is taken after 276 d.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 158 − 30 = 128 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 128 counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 276 / 138 = 2 half-lives. C_net = 128 / 2^2 = 32.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 32.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 32 + 30 = 62.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 62.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 128 counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 2 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^2.
Correct answer: 32.0 counts min⁻¹.
Adds background count rate back to the remaining net count rate to obtain 62.0 counts min⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Determine the initial corrected count rate from the Po-210 source at t = 0.
Calculate the corrected count rate from the source alone at t = 276 d.
State the total count rate displayed by the detector at t = 276 d.

items.stem: A radioactive sample of sodium-24 contains 2.9 × 10¹⁴ undecayed nuclei. Its half-life is T₁/₂ = 15 h. The sample is left to decay for 42.5 h.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ from h to seconds and applies λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.
Correct answer: 1.28 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.
Multiplies λ in s⁻¹ by N₀ using A₀ = λN₀.
Correct answer: 3.72 × 10⁹ Bq.
Applies exponential decay law A = A₀ e^(−λt) with consistent time units.
Correct answer: 5.22 × 10⁸ Bq.

parts.prompt: Show the conversion of the half-life to seconds and calculate the decay constant λ in s⁻¹.
Calculate the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0.
Determine the activity A of the sample, in Bq, after t = 42.5 h.

items.stem: A photomultiplier tube (PMT) in a gamma camera has $10$ dynode stages. Each hitting electron frees an average of $4.00$ secondary electrons at every dynode. How many electrons reach the anode for one photoelectron from the photocathode?
items.workedSolution: Each dynode multiplies the electron pulse by $\delta = 4.00$, giving total gain $G = \delta^N = 4.00^{10} = 1.05 × 10⁶$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 1.05 × 10⁶.

items.stem: A nuclear power plant produces $1050\text{ MW}$ of electrical power at $35.0\%$ efficiency. Each fission has a mass defect of $0.220\text{ u}$ ($1\text{ u} = 931.5\text{ MeV }c^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $P_{\text{th}} = 3.00 × 10³ MW$. (b) Fission rate $= 9.15 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹$. (c) The heat exchanger moves thermal energy from radioactive primary coolant to a clean secondary steam loop. (d) The moderator slows fast neutrons, control rods absorb extra neutrons, and concrete shields radiation. Long-lived radioactive waste needs deep, secure storage.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P_th = P_el / η = 1050 / 0.350.
Obtains thermal power 3.00 × 10³ MW.
Computes energy per fission Q = 0.220 × 931.5 MeV in joules and divides P_th by Q.
Obtains fission rate 9.15 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹.
States heat exchanger transfers thermal energy from hot primary coolant to boil secondary water into steam.
States the heat exchanger keeps the radioactive primary loop separate from the steam turbines.
Correctly states role of moderator (slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds).
Correctly states roles of control rods (absorb neutrons) and biological shielding (absorbs radiation).
Identifies long half-lives / high radioactivity requiring secure long-term geological storage.

parts.prompt: Outline the roles of the moderator, control rods, and biological shielding, and state one major challenge in managing spent fission products.
parts.expectedAnswer: The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds to keep uranium-235 fission going. Control rods absorb extra neutrons to regulate the chain reaction. Thick concrete shielding absorbs escaping gamma rays and neutrons. Spent fission products stay strongly radioactive with long half-lives, needing deep geological storage.
workingSteps: Moderator slows fast neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons; concrete shielding attenuates radiation.
Spent fuel contains long-lived radioactive fission products needing cooling ponds and secure long-term storage.

items.stem: Newton's particle theory and Huygens' wave theory competed for over 150 years. Thomas Young then carried out his double-slit experiment.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's fringes come from wave superposition and path difference, impossible for corpuscles. Constructive interference gives bright fringes and destructive interference gives dark fringes. (b) Newton had great authority, and sharp shadows hid tiny-wavelength diffraction. (c) Acceptance followed transverse wave theory and Foucault's 1850 proof that $v_{\text{water}} < v_{\text{air}}$.

Notes inability at the time to measure light's speed inside glass or water.

parts.prompt: Explain in general terms how coherent light passing through Young's double slits produces alternating bright and dark fringes on a screen.
parts.expectedAnswer: Young's double-slit fringes come from wave superposition and path difference, impossible for corpuscles. Waves arriving in phase (whole-wavelength path difference) interfere constructively to form bright fringes. Waves arriving in antiphase (odd half-wavelength path difference) interfere destructively to form dark fringes.
workingSteps: State Young double-slit fringes arise from wave superposition and path difference impossible for corpuscles.
Link in-phase constructive superposition to bright fringes and antiphase destructive superposition to dark fringes.

parts.prompt: Give two reasons why Newton's corpuscular theory was widely preferred over Huygens' wave theory during the eighteenth century.
parts.expectedAnswer: Newton had great scientific authority. Also, sharp straight-line shadows hid tiny-wavelength diffraction, whereas waves were expected to bend clearly around objects.
workingSteps: State Newton had immense authority and sharp rectilinear shadows hid tiny-wavelength diffraction.
Note Newton's scientific prestige and straight-line shadow propagation.

parts.prompt: Explain why full acceptance of Huygens' wave theory was delayed until the mid-nineteenth century despite Young's 1801 fringes.
parts.expectedAnswer: Newton's authority stayed strong, and early longitudinal wave models could not explain polarisation. Acceptance came after Fresnel developed transverse waves and Foucault (1850) measured light moving slower in water than in air.
workingSteps: Note continuing reverence for Newton and scepticism of Young's apparatus/longitudinal wave assumptions.
Note decisive confirmation arrived only when Foucault measured $v_{\text{water}} < v_{\text{air}}$ (opposite to Newton's refraction prediction).

items.stem: In the electron diffraction tube shown, the anode p.d. $V$ is increased. The thin graphite target stays the same. What change is seen on the fluorescent screen?
items.workedSolution: Higher $V$ gives electrons more speed and momentum $p$. This decreases $\lambda = h/p$, so the diffraction rings move closer together. Option D is correct.

items.stem: In a hot gas, a Li²⁺ ion (Z = 3) has quantized energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The electron starts in level n = 3. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the lowest photon frequency needed to ionize the ion from n = 3?
items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from n = 3 is ΔE = 13.6 × 3² / 3² = 13.6 eV = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 3.28 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Finds f = (13.6 Z² / n²)(e / h) = 3.28 × 10¹⁵ Hz (D).

items.stem: A barium-141 nucleus has nucleon number A = 141 and proton number Z = 56. Its nuclear mass is 140.88354 u. Take mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this barium-141 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 141 − 56 = 85. Mass defect Δm = 56(1.007276) + 85(1.008665) − 140.88354 = 1.26 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 1.17 × 10³ MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 1.17 × 10³ / 141 = 8.33 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 1.26 u, B = 1.17 × 10³ MeV, and B / A = 8.33 MeV (C).

items.stem: A beam of alpha particles starts from rest in a vacuum and accelerates through 480 V. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mα = 6.644 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, and charge +2e with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the alpha particles?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 1.54 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 1.43 × 10⁻²¹ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 4.64 × 10⁻⁴ nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 4.64 × 10⁻⁴ nm (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wavelength by a wrong factor of 2.

items.stem: In the nuclear level chart, Co-60 (2.82 MeV above Ni-60 ground state) decays by beta-minus emission to the 2.50 MeV Ni-60 state. It then emits cascade gamma rays via the 1.33 MeV state. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) 0.320 MeV. (b) 1.17 MeV. (c) 2.82 × 10²⁰ Hz. (d) Nucleons occupy discrete nuclear energy levels, so gamma photons have fixed energies equal to level gaps.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains max β⁻ KE = 0.320 MeV.
Finds E(γ₁) = 1.17 MeV.
Converts MeV to joules and applies f = ΔE / h.
Computes f = 2.82 × 10²⁰ Hz.
States nuclear levels are discrete/quantised so γ photons have fixed ΔE.
Explains β⁻ energy is shared continuously with an electron antineutrino.

parts.prompt: State the maximum kinetic energy in MeV of a beta-minus particle emitted in the transition to the 2.50 MeV level.
Calculate the energy in MeV of photon γ₁ emitted between the 2.50 MeV and 1.33 MeV states.
Calculate the frequency of photon γ₁.
Explain why Ni-60 emits gamma rays only at discrete wavelengths whereas the beta-minus particles have a continuous range of energies.
parts.expectedAnswer: Nucleons occupy discrete nuclear energy levels, so gamma photons have only specific energies matching level gaps. In beta-minus decay, transition energy is shared at random with an electron antineutrino.
workingSteps: Nucleons sit in discrete energy levels, so gamma photons have fixed energies equal to level differences.

items.stem: Consider this nuclear fusion reaction: 2 deuterons (each of mass 2.013553 u) → helium-3 nucleus (3.014932 u) + neutron (1.008665 u). Take u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 3.51 × 10⁻³ u. Final answer: 3.51 × 10⁻³ u. (b) Q = 3.51 × 10⁻³ × 931.5 = 3.27 MeV. Final answer: 3.27 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 4. Final answer: 4.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Correct answer: 3.51 × 10⁻³ u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.
Correct answer: 3.27 MeV.
Sums nucleon numbers across reactants (or products) to obtain 4.

items.stem: In a photocell, light of frequency 1.66 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes an aluminium plate. The work function of aluminium is Φ = 4.08 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the maximum kinetic energy, in electron-volts (eV), of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.66 × 10¹⁵) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.88 eV. Subtracting Φ = 4.08 eV gives Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 2.80 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Converts hf to eV and subtracts Φ = 4.08 eV to obtain 2.80 eV (D).

items.stem: Relativistic kaons travel at speed v = 0.9c along a detector path of proper length L₀ = 27.8 m. In the kaon rest frame, the proper decay time is Δt₀ = 1.44 × 10⁻⁸ s. What dilated time interval Δt is measured in the stationary frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.9²) = 2.29. Dilated time interval Δt = γ Δt₀ = 2.29 × 1.44 × 10⁻⁸ = 3.30 × 10⁻⁸ s.

markScheme.criterion: Finds γ = 2.29 and Δt = γ Δt₀ = 3.30 × 10⁻⁸ s (C).

items.stem: In frame S, two beacons flash at the same time ct = 4.0 ls: Event A at x = 2.0 ls and Event B at x = 6.0 ls. Frame S′ moves along +x at v = 0.60c (γ = 1.25), with origins matching at t = t′ = 0.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ = 31.0°. (b) ct′_A = 3.50 ls, ct′_B = 0.500 ls. (c) Δ(ct′) = −3.00 ls. (d) Event B happens before Event A in frame S′ because its line parallel to x′ cuts ct′ lower than Event A. (e) (Δs)² = −16.0 ls².

markScheme.criterion: Applies tan θ = v/c = 0.60.
Obtains θ = 31.0°.
Substitutes into ct′ = γ(ct − βx) with γ = 1.25.
Obtains ct′_A = 3.50 ls.
Obtains ct′_B = 0.500 ls.
Calculates Δ(ct′) = −3.00 ls.
Constructs lines of simultaneity parallel to the tilted x′ axis through A and B.
Concludes Event B occurs first in S′ because its line cuts ct′ lower than Event A.
Applies (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)².
Obtains (Δs)² = −16.0 ls².

items.stem: UV light of wavelength 229 nm falls on a clean aluminium plate in a vacuum. The work function of aluminium is Φ = 4.08 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 8.69 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; work function Φ = 4.08 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 2.16 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 6.88 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 6.88 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A cosmic-ray gamma photon of energy $245\text{ MeV}$ creates a muon–antimuon pair near a nucleus. Take muon rest energy $= 105.659\text{ MeV}$, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, and $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Antiparticle: antimuon; $E_{\min} = 2E_0 = 211 MeV$. (b) $E_{\text{k,tot}} = 33.7 MeV$; $f_{\min} = (2E_0 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-13})/6.63 \times 10^{-34} = 5.10 × 10²² Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Name antimuon (reject 'antielectron').
Minimum energy $2E_0 = 211 MeV$.
Total kinetic energy $= 33.7 MeV$.
Convert $2E_0$ to joules using $1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J MeV}^{-1}$ and divide by $h$.
Threshold frequency $= 5.10 × 10²² Hz$.

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student records 360 background counts in 15 minutes. They then mount a sealed gamma source opposite a GM tube. At ruler distances $x_1 = 120$ mm and $x_2 = 360$ mm, the raw count rates are 108.9 s⁻¹ and 15.66 s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.400 s⁻¹$. (b) Subtracting background gives $C_{\mathrm{corr},1} = 108.5$ s⁻¹ and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 15.26$ s⁻¹. The gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ is 0.667, so $k = 1/\mathrm{grad}^2 = 2.25 s⁻¹ m²$. (c) $x_0 = 24.0 mm$. (d) Handle the gamma source with long tongs, maximise distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal the systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.400 s⁻¹$.
Subtracts $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both raw rates and calculates $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$.
Finds gradient $\Delta(1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}})/\Delta x = 1/\sqrt{k}$.
Inverse-square constant $k = 2.25 s⁻¹ m²$.
Solves $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$ (or intercept/gradient) for $x_0$.
Systematic offset $x_0 = 24.0 mm$.
Long tongs + maximise distance + minimise time out of lead-lined box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Explains $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ remains linear despite unknown $x_0$ (whereas $C$ vs $1/x^2$ curves).
Identifies negative x-intercept $-x_0$ as the hidden offset inside source capsule and GM tube.
