parts.prompt: Calculate the background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ in s⁻¹.
Subtract background radiation and find $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ at both positions. Use the gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ to find $k$.
Determine the hidden internal systematic offset $x_0$ in mm.
State the required radiological safety precautions and explain why plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ is preferred over $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs, keep maximum distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plotting one over square root corrected count rate against x gives a straight line that reveals the systematic offset.
workingSteps: Long tongs, maximum distance, point source away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box.
1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k stays linear and gives x₀ directly from the negative x-intercept.

items.stem: Adding 2 electrons forms an $^{16}_{8}\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ ion. Calculate the magnitude of its specific charge. Take $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: Net charge magnitude $Q = 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ and mass $m = 2.68 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, giving $Q/m = 1.19 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. Option C (1.19 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Correct specific charge $Q/m = 1.19 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$ (1.19 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹, option C).

items.stem: An absorber bench records an open-source count rate of 868 counts min⁻¹ when the steady laboratory background count rate is 28 counts min⁻¹. What is the background-corrected count rate of the source with no absorber?
items.workedSolution: Corrected count rate = 868 − 28 = 840 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background to obtain 840 counts min⁻¹.

items.stem: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons accelerate from rest through a p.d. of $2500\text{ V}$. Ignore relativistic effects. What is their de Broglie wavelength?
items.workedSolution: Momentum $p = \sqrt{2 m_{\text{e}} e V} = \sqrt{2(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(2500)} = 2.70 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹$. Thus $\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = 24.6 pm$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 24.6 pm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ of the electrons.
Calculate the relativistic kinetic energy of one electron in joules.
Explain why no finite accelerating potential difference can ever accelerate an electron to $v = c$.
parts.expectedAnswer: As $v \to c$, $\gamma \to \infty$, so infinite energy would be needed. Electron speed therefore approaches light speed asymptotically instead of following the classical straight line.
workingSteps: As $v \to c$, $\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \to 0$ so $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2 \to \infty$.
Hence $c$ is an unattainable upper speed limit for any particle with non-zero rest mass.

items.stem: A parent nucleus of Ge has nucleon number A = 68 and proton number Z = 32. It decays by beta-plus decay (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) to form a daughter nucleus with A = 68 and Z = 30.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 30 − 32 = −2. Final answer: −2. (b) N₀ = 68 − 32 = 36; N_f = 68 − 30 = 38. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2. Final answer: 2. (c) Accounting for ΔA = 0, charge conservation gives 2 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 2.

Correct answer: 2.
Links single-quark flavour conversion to ΔZ = ±1 per weak beta step.
Correct answer: 2.

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, a proton (charge +1e) of kinetic energy 5.1 MeV approaches a fixed lead nucleus (Z = 82, A = 208) head-on. Electrostatic repulsion stops it at a closest distance d. Neglect recoil and take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 5.1 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(1e)(82e) / Eₖ = 2.31 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 23.1 fm. Final answer: 23.1 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (208)^(1/3) = 7.11 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 7.11 fm. (c) ρ = (208 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Eₖ to joules, equates Eₖ = k Q₁ Q₂ / d, and converts metres to femtometres.
Correct answer: 23.1 fm.
Applies R = 1.20 × A^(1/3) fm.
Correct answer: 7.11 fm.
Finds ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) in SI units.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A negatively charged zinc plate on an electroscope discharges instantly under dim UV light. Yet it stays charged under bright visible light.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Wave theory fails because it predicts emission at any frequency after a delay and intensity-dependent KE. Einstein's photon model uses one-to-one absorption of photons ($E = hf \ge \phi$). Excess energy gives $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi = eV_{\text{s}}$. Higher intensity brings more photons per second, freeing more electrons from the zinc plate (never the gold leaf).

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Wave theory predicts emission at any frequency after a delay, contradicting threshold f₀ and instant emission.
L1 (Area 1): Wave theory predicts photoelectron kinetic energy should increase with intensity, contradicting observation that Ek(max) depends on frequency.
L2 (Area 2): Photon model states EM radiation consists of discrete packets (photons) of energy E = hf.
L2 (Area 2): One-to-one interaction: one electron absorbs one photon and escapes only if hf >= φ (work function).
L3 (Area 3): Applies Ek(max) = hf − φ = eVs, explicitly stating maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency and work function.
L3 (Area 3): Higher intensity (for f >= f₀) brings more photons per second, freeing more electrons from the zinc plate (reject 'gold leaf').

parts.prompt: Explain why the classical wave theory of light fails to explain these results. Explain how Einstein's photon model accounts for threshold frequency, maximum kinetic energy, and higher intensity above threshold.
parts.expectedAnswer: Wave theory says energy spreads smoothly over a wavefront, so electrons should store energy and escape at any frequency after a delay. It also predicts higher intensity should raise maximum kinetic energy. Both fail against experiment. In Einstein's model, light comes in photons of energy $E = hf$. One surface electron absorbs one photon instantly and escapes only if $hf \ge \phi$, giving threshold $f_0 = \phi/h$. Spare energy gives $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi = eV_{\text{s}}$, depending only on $f$ and $\phi$. Higher intensity (for $f \ge f_0$) delivers more photons per second, freeing more electrons per second from the zinc plate so the leaf falls faster.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Contrast wave predictions (any f after delay; KE rises with intensity) with observed f₀ and instant emission.
Area 2 (L2): State photon packets E = hf, one-to-one interaction, and surface work function threshold hf >= φ.
Area 3 (L3): Link Ek(max) = hf − φ = eVs (state 'maximum' KE). Higher intensity gives more photons/s and faster discharge from zinc.

items.stem: A beam of electrons is accelerated from rest through 2250 V onto a thin platinum foil (spacing d = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). A screen at distance L = 0.19 m shows bright diffraction rings. Use sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = √(2mₑeV) = 2.56 × 10⁻²³ N s. λ = h / p = 2.59 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 25.9 pm. Final answer: 25.9 pm. (b) sin θ = λ / d = 2.59 × 10⁻¹¹ / (2.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 0.114. θ = 6.55 °. Final answer: 6.55 °. (c) r = L tan θ = 0.19 × tan(6.55°) = 0.0218 m. Final answer: 0.0218 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = h / √(2mₑeV) with SI values and converts to picometres.
Correct answer: 25.9 pm.
Applies sin θ = λ / d and converts to degrees.
Correct answer: 6.55 °.
Finds r = L tan θ using the screen distance L.
Correct answer: 0.0218 m.

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, alpha particles (Z₁ = 2) of energy 6.9 MeV hit a tungsten-184 nucleus (Z = 74, A = 184). Model the nucleus as a uniform sphere with radius R = R₀ A^(1/3). Take R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = 1.20 × (184)^(1/3) = 6.83 fm. Final answer: 6.83 fm. (b) R = 6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Final answer: 6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. (c) m = 184 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; V = (4/3)π(6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵)³. ρ = m / V = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes nucleon number A into R = R₀ A^(1/3).
Correct answer: 6.83 fm.
Multiplies R in fm by 10⁻¹⁵ m fm⁻¹ to obtain 6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Divides nuclear mass A u by spherical volume (4/3)πR³.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: The diagram shows energy levels of argon gas. The ground level is at −15.7 eV, and a nearby bound level is at −4.18 eV. A free electron has zero energy. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest wavelength of light that can ionize an atom from the ground level?
items.workedSolution: Ionization from the ground level requires ΔE = 0 − (−15.7) = 15.7 eV = 2.51 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.51 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 79.2 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Converts ΔE = 15.7 eV to joules and applies λ = hc / ΔE to obtain 79.2 nm (C).

items.stem: Fast electrons collide with stationary protons. The Feynman diagram shows the weak interaction.
items.workedSolution: (a) W minus boson from electron to proton (weak nuclear interaction); charge conserved at electron and proton vertices. (b) up quark changes to down quark. (c) neutron, conserving $Q$ and $L_e$.

markScheme.criterion: Identify W minus boson from electron to proton (reject bare 'W' or 'W meson').
Confirm weak nuclear interaction / vertex charge conservation.
State up quark changes to down quark.
Identify outgoing particle as neutron.
Show explicit conservation of electron lepton number and electric charge.

items.stem: A TEM gives electrons a de Broglie wavelength much smaller than an atom. Why is its real image resolution still worse than the theoretical diffraction limit?
items.workedSolution: Thicker samples slow electrons down, increasing their wavelength. Magnetic lens aberrations and a spread of electron speeds also blur the image.

markScheme.criterion: States sample thickness slows electrons (longer wavelength), and lens aberrations and speed spread blur the image.

items.stem: A distant blue star has a surface temperature of $1.60 \times 10^4\text{ K}$. Take $\alpha = 2.90 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m K}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda_{\max} = 2.90 \times 10^{-3} / 16\,000 = 181 nm$. (b) $16\,000\text{ K}$ lies in spectral class B ($11\,000\text{–}25\,000\text{ K}$). (c) Prominent lines are He H.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into $\lambda_{\max} = 2.90 \times 10^{-3} / 16\,000$.
Correct peak wavelength 181 nm.
Identifies spectral class B.
States prominent lines He H.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak black-body wavelength $\lambda_{\max}$ of this star in nanometres.
workingSteps: Convert to nanometres to get 181 nm (ultraviolet).

parts.prompt: State which spectral class ($\text{O B A F G K M}$) this star belongs to.
parts.expectedAnswer: It belongs to spectral class B ($11\,000\text{–}25\,000\text{ K}$, intrinsic colour blue).
workingSteps: Match $16\,000\text{ K}$ to the $11\,000\text{–}25\,000\text{ K}$ band: spectral class B.

parts.prompt: State the prominent absorption lines seen in the spectrum of this class.
parts.expectedAnswer: Prominent neutral helium and hydrogen lines (He H).
workingSteps: Recall class B prominent lines: He H.

items.stem: A radiation detector operates in a steady background count rate of 38 counts min⁻¹. A fluorine-18 source of half-life 110 min gives an initial total count rate of 230 counts min⁻¹. The source decays for 220 min. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 220 min?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 230 − 38 = 192 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 220 / 110 = 2. Remaining net count rate C = 192 / 2^2 = 48 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 48 + 38 = 86.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (192), divides by 2^2 (48), and adds 38 back to obtain 86.0 counts min⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the uncorrected count rate first and subtracts the background count rate at the end.

items.stem: A radioactive sample of indium-111 contains 2.4 × 10¹³ undecayed nuclei. Its half-life is T₁/₂ = 2.8 d. The sample is left to decay for 6.1 d. What is the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Converting half-life to SI seconds: T₁/₂ = 2.8 × 86400 = 2.42 × 10⁵ s. Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 2.87 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 6.88 × 10⁷ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = ln 2 / (2.8 × 86400) and A₀ = λN₀ = 6.88 × 10⁷ Bq (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves T₁/₂ in d instead of converting to seconds when evaluating A₀ = (ln 2 / T₁/₂) N₀ in Bq.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor ln 2 ≈ 0.693 in λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Finds the decayed activity at elapsed time t instead of A₀ at t = 0.

items.stem: A patient has external radiotherapy with high-energy X-rays from a rotating linear accelerator. A total tumour dose of $66.0\text{ Gy}$ is split into $33$ equal daily sessions. The machine uses $10$ intersecting narrow beam directions.
items.workedSolution: (a) $66.0 / 33 = 2.00 Gy$. (b) $66.0 / 10 = 6.60 Gy$. (c) Healthy tissue is protected by rotating narrow beams that cross at the tumour. Tight lead collimators and daily fractionation also help normal cells recover.

markScheme.criterion: Correct dose per fraction 2.00 Gy.
Correct single-path healthy dose 6.60 Gy.
Explains rotating narrow high-energy X-ray beams cross at the tumour while limiting healthy tissue dose.
Mentions tight collimation / beam shaping and accurate patient alignment.
Mentions fractionation so healthy cells repair damage between sessions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tumour radiation dose delivered during each daily fraction.
workingSteps: Divide $66.0\text{ Gy}$ by $33$ fractions to obtain 2.00 Gy.

parts.prompt: The $10$ beam paths overlap only at the tumour. Calculate the total dose along one healthy entry path.
workingSteps: Divide $66.0\text{ Gy}$ by $10$ beams to obtain 6.60 Gy.

parts.prompt: Explain three methods used during high-energy X-ray radiotherapy to limit exposure and damage to surrounding healthy cells.
parts.expectedAnswer: Rotating narrow high-energy X-ray beams cross at the tumour, keeping dose low on healthy tissue. Lead collimators shape the beam tightly to the tumour outline. Splitting the total dose into daily fractions lets healthy cells repair DNA between sessions.
workingSteps: Use rotating or intersecting narrow beams so only the tumour gets the full summed dose.
Precision collimation & patient immobilisation to conform beam to tumour silhouette.
Fractionation over weeks allowing healthy tissue recovery between sessions.

items.stem: Engineers use a radioactive tracer to find a leak in a buried pipe. Doctors also use tracers to image organs. Which emission type and half-life work best?
items.workedSolution: Gamma rays pass through soil or tissue so outside detectors can pick them up. A short half-life limits radiation dose and avoids lasting contamination.

markScheme.criterion: Selects a gamma emitter (penetrates soil or tissue) with a short half-life (avoids lasting contamination).

options.label: A
options.text: An alpha emitter with a half-life of several thousand years so the radiation stays strongly ionizing inside the pipe forever.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles cannot penetrate soil or body tissue to reach an external detector, and a long half-life creates severe contamination.

options.label: B
options.text: A pure alpha emitter with a half-life of one millisecond so it decays before entering the pipe or patient.
options.distractorRationale: Both negligible penetration and an overly brief half-life prevent detection at the leak or target organ.

options.label: C
options.text: Underground pipe leak detection and medical imaging select a gamma emitter with a short half-life so radiation penetrates soil or tissue for external detection without lingering contamination.

options.label: D
options.text: A beta emitter with a half-life of fifty years so the signal remains strong for decades after repair.
options.distractorRationale: Beta particles are absorbed by soil/tissue and a 50-year half-life causes persistent environmental or patient dose.

items.stem: A negative kaon ($S = -1$) decays into two pions ($S = 0$): $K^- \to \pi^- + \pi^0$. Which interaction must be responsible for this decay?
items.workedSolution: Here $Q$ and $B$ are conserved, but strangeness changes ($\Delta S = +1$). This must be a weak interaction because strangeness changes. Option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: weak interaction because strangeness changes.

items.stem: Which physical process allows a PET ring scanner to determine the line of response passing through a tumour?
items.workedSolution: An emitted positron annihilates with an electron inside tissue. By momentum and energy conservation, this makes two opposite 511 keV gamma photons detected in coincidence, defining a straight line of response.

markScheme.criterion: States a positron annihilates an electron into two opposite 511 keV gamma photons detected in coincidence.

items.stem: A single UV quantum has frequency $1.00 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$. Use Planck's equation ($E = hf$) to calculate its energy in electron-volts. Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: $E = hf = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 1.00 \times 10^{15} = 6.63 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$. Dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J eV}^{-1}$ gives 4.14 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 4.14 eV.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the quantum energy in joules instead of converting to electron-volts.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a wrong factor of two.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the eV conversion fraction $e / (hf)$.

items.stem: A classroom ceiling light uses a low-pressure mercury fluorescent tube. The inside of the glass tube has a white phosphor coating.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): A high p.d. accelerates free electrons along the tube. They collide with mercury orbital electrons and excite them. Mercury atoms drop back and emit UV photons ($hf = E_1 - E_2$). The phosphor coating absorbs the UV photons and drops in smaller steps to emit visible light.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): High p.d. accelerates free electrons through low-pressure mercury vapour.
L1 (Area 1): Free electrons hit mercury orbital electrons, exciting or ionising the atoms.
L2 (Area 2): Excited mercury electrons rapidly de-excite / fall back to lower discrete energy levels.
L2 (Area 2): Each downward jump emits a photon with hf = E₁ − E₂, mainly in the UV region.
L3 (Area 3): The phosphor coating absorbs UV photons and excites its orbital electrons.
L3 (Area 3): Coating electrons drop in smaller steps, emitting lower-energy visible photons.

parts.prompt: Explain how a fluorescent tube produces visible light when a high p.d. is applied. Include excitation and ionisation of mercury, UV emission, and the role of the phosphor coating.
parts.expectedAnswer: A high p.d. accelerates free electrons along the tube. These electrons collide with orbital electrons in mercury atoms. This excites mercury electrons to higher discrete levels or ionises atoms to free more electrons. Excited mercury electrons fall back to lower levels and emit photons ($hf = E_1 - E_2$), mainly in the UV region. The phosphor coating absorbs these UV photons and excites its own atoms. Phosphor electrons then fall in several smaller steps, emitting lower-energy visible photons.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): High p.d. speeds up free electrons. Collisions excite or ionise mercury atoms.
Area 2 (L2): Mercury electrons fall to lower levels, emitting UV photons with hf = E₁ − E₂.
Area 3 (L3): Phosphor absorbs UV photons and drops in smaller steps to emit visible photons.

items.stem: A single-electron C⁵⁺ ion (Z = 6) has energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The ion starts in level n = 3. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (6)² / (3)² = −54.4 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 54.4 eV. Final answer: 54.4 eV. (b) ΔE = 54.4 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.70 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. f = ΔE / h = 8.70 × 10⁻¹⁸ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz. Final answer: 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (1.31 × 10¹⁶) = 22.9 nm. Final answer: 22.9 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV for the specified Z and n.
Correct answer: 54.4 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Correct answer: 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f and expresses the wavelength in nm to obtain 22.9 nm.

items.stem: A nuclear fusion reaction is: deuteron (A = 2, Z = 1, mass 2.013553 u) + triton (A = 3, Z = 1, mass 3.015501 u) → helium nucleus (A = 4, Z = 2, mass 4.001506 u) + neutron (mass 1.008665 u). Use u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What energy Q, in MeV, is released in one fusion reaction?
items.workedSolution: Mass decrease Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0189 u. Energy released Q = Δm × 931.5 = 17.6 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.0189 u and Q = Δm × 931.5 = 17.6 MeV (A).

items.stem: A student determines the Planck constant $h$ using four LEDs of known wavelengths in a potential-divider circuit ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$). The best-fit graph of threshold voltage $V_0$ against $1/\lambda$ has gradient $1.223 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V m}$, and the red LED has wavelength 640 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 6.52, giving h = 6.52 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s). (b) V₀ = 1.91 V. (c) Viewing through a dark tube blocks room light, so the exact switch-on voltage is judged more accurately.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies gradient = hc/e and rearranges h = e × gradient / c.
Obtains A = 6.52 (h = 6.52 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
Converts wavelength from nm to m and evaluates V₀ = gradient / λ.
Obtains threshold voltage V₀ = 1.91 V.
States room light hides faint initial glow, causing V₀ to be overestimated.
Links the dark tube to lower systematic error when judging the exact switch-on voltage.

items.stem: Light of frequency 1.62 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a clean magnesium surface in a vacuum. The work function of magnesium is Φ = 3.66 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Φ = 3.66 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.86 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f₀ = Φ / h = 5.86 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 8.83 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 8.83 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (b) Photon energy E = hf / e = 6.71 eV. Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 6.71 − 3.66 = 3.05 eV. Final answer: 3.05 eV. (c) Vₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / e = 3.05 V. Final answer: 3.05 V.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Φ from eV to joules and applies f₀ = Φ / h.
Correct answer: 8.83 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Applies Einstein's photoelectric equation Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hf/e − Φ.
Correct answer: 3.05 eV.
Uses eVₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to obtain 3.05 V.

items.stem: Charged pions move at constant speed v = 0.8c along a laboratory tube of proper length L₀ = 18 m. The proper lifetime of a pion in its rest frame is Δt₀ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁸ s.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes β = v/c into γ = 1 / √(1 − β²).
Correct answer: 1.67.
Multiplies proper time interval Δt₀ by γ (Δt = γ Δt₀).
Correct answer: 4.33 × 10⁻⁸ s.
Divides proper length L₀ by γ (L = L₀ / γ).
Correct answer: 10.8 m.

Converts Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to joules and rearranges ½mₑvₘₐₓ² = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ.
Correct answer: 1.74 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, an electron occupies the $n = 2$ stationary orbit of radius $r_2 = 2.12 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$ ($4 r_1$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $L_2 = \frac{2 \times 6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi} = 2.11 × 10⁻³⁴ J s$. (b) $v_2 = \frac{L_2}{m_{\text{e}} r_2} = 1.09 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹$. (c) $E_2 = -13.6/4 = -3.40\text{ eV}$; raising the electron to $E_{\infty} = 0\text{ eV}$ requires 3.40 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes $n = 2$ into $mvr = nh/(2\pi)$.
Correct angular momentum 2.11 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Correct orbital speed 1.09 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
Computes $E_2 = -13.6 / 4 = -3.40\text{ eV}$.
Identifies ionization level as $E_{\infty} = 0\text{ eV}$.
Correct ionization energy 3.40 eV.

parts.prompt: Calculate the orbital angular momentum of the electron in the $n = 2$ state using $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$.
Hence calculate the orbital speed $v_2$ of the electron in the $n = 2$ orbit.
workingSteps: Rearrange $m_{\text{e}} v_2 r_2 = L_2$ to $v_2 = \frac{L_2}{m_{\text{e}} r_2}$.
Substitute $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$ and $r_2 = 2.12 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$ to obtain 1.09 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Using $E = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\text{ eV}$, calculate the minimum photon energy in $\text{eV}$ needed to ionize the hydrogen atom from the $n = 2$ state.
workingSteps: Minimum photon energy required is $E_{\infty} - E_2 = 0 - (-3.40) = 3.40 eV$.

items.stem: A slow electron and positron meet and annihilate. Why are two gamma photons produced instead of one?
items.workedSolution: Total initial momentum is almost zero. Two gamma photons must travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum. Option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

options.label: A
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, a single photon splits into an electron and positron along the same line
options.distractorRationale: Describes pair production rather than annihilation, and still does not balance zero initial momentum.

options.label: B
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, two gamma photons travel in the same direction at half the speed of light
options.distractorRationale: Photons always travel at c in vacuum and parallel photons would carry non-zero net momentum.

options.label: C
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum

options.label: D
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, one photon carries positive charge and the other carries negative charge
options.distractorRationale: Gamma photons are electrically neutral.

items.stem: Required Practical 12 tests the inverse-square law with a gamma source (plus thin aluminium if beta is present). Why is a gamma source used instead of an alpha source?
items.workedSolution: Gamma rays are barely absorbed in air over 0.1–0.6 m, whereas alpha particles stop within a few cm. Always handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs, maximise distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal the systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: States gamma rays are barely absorbed over 0.1–0.6 m in air while alpha stops in a few cm. Notes safe handling and linearised plot against x.

options.text: Because alpha particles travel faster than light and bypass the GM tube dead time.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles are massive, slow, strongly ionising, and stopped by ~5 cm of air.

options.label: B
options.text: Because gamma rays are deflected magnetically into a parallel non-diverging beam.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma rays are uncharged EM photons radiating isotropically (1/r² geometric spreading).

options.label: C
options.text: Gamma rays are negligibly absorbed in air over 0.1–0.6 m whereas alpha range is only a few cm; always handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

options.label: D
options.text: Because sealed gamma sources are harmless outside lead storage boxes.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma radiation is highly penetrating and requires strict ALARA controls (time, distance, shielding, tongs).

items.stem: A bare lithium-7 nucleus ($^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$) is studied in a particle accelerator. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $N = 7 - 3 = 4$. (b) $m = 1.172 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, $Q = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, so $Q/m = 4.10 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. (c) Neutrons add mass without adding charge, lowering $Q/m$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct neutron number $N = 4$.
Calculate total mass $m = 1.17 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$ including both protons and neutrons.
Substitute net charge $Q = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ into $Q/m$.
Obtain specific charge $= 4.10 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$.
State that neutrons contribute mass without adding electric charge.

parts.prompt: State the number of neutrons in the Li nucleus.
Calculate the total mass of the species in kilograms and hence determine the magnitude of its specific charge.
Explain why neutral neutrons affect the specific charge of a nucleus or ion.
parts.expectedAnswer: Neutrons have zero charge, so they add mass without adding electric charge. This increases the denominator and lowers $Q/m$.
workingSteps: Link unchanged charge and larger denominator mass to smaller specific charge.

items.stem: One uranium-235 fission releases about 200 MeV, while one deuterium–tritium fusion releases 17.6 MeV. Using the BE/A curve, why does fusion still release much more energy per kilogram of fuel?
items.workedSolution: D–T fusion releases ~3.5 MeV per nucleon, versus ~0.85 MeV per nucleon for U-235 fission. This gives ~4× more energy per kilogram. The curve rises much more steeply on the low-A fusion side than it falls on the high-A fission side.

markScheme.criterion: States that fusion releases more energy per nucleon and per kilogram because the low-A curve is much steeper than the high-A side.

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion releases more energy per kilogram only because deuterium nuclei are heavier than uranium nuclei.
options.distractorRationale: Uranium-235 is roughly 100 times heavier than deuterium, so 1 kg of fusion fuel contains far more reacting nuclei.

options.label: B
options.text: The high-A side of the curve is much steeper than the low-A side, giving fission a smaller energy jump per reaction.
options.distractorRationale: The low-A fusion side is vastly steeper (~1.1 MeV to 7.1 MeV per nucleon) than the gentle high-A fission slope (~7.6 to 8.5 MeV).

options.label: C
options.text: Comparing the two slopes of the curve, fusion releases much more energy per nucleon and per kilogram than fission because the curve rises far more steeply on the low-A fusion side than it falls on the high-A fission side.

options.label: D
options.text: Fusion violates nucleon conservation by converting whole protons directly into photons.
options.distractorRationale: Nucleon number A is always conserved in fusion. The energy comes from the steep rise in BE/A.

items.stem: High-energy electrons scatter off a thin carbon target, and intensity is plotted against angle θ. Why does the first minimum stay above zero, and why are electrons chosen over alpha particles?
items.workedSolution: Scattering overlays diffraction, so the first dip stays above zero. Electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force, giving nuclear radius directly. Alpha closest approach gives only an energy-dependent upper bound.

markScheme.criterion: States scattering keeps the dip non-zero, and leptonic electrons give direct radius unlike alpha upper bounds.

options.label: A
options.text: The intensity touches zero strictly at θ = 90° because electrons undergo strong-force capture inside the nucleus.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons do not interact via the strong force and the first minimum is non-zero at sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R.

options.label: B
options.text: Electrons are chosen solely because they carry positive charge and match the alpha particle's mass.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are negatively charged leptons ~7300 times lighter than alpha particles.

options.label: C
options.text: Alpha particles give exact nuclear radii while electrons only provide rough upper bounds.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the relative accuracy of the two methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Scattering overlays diffraction so the dip stays above zero, and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

items.stem: An unknown sealed source is tested with a background count rate of 22 counts min⁻¹. The readings are 722 counts min⁻¹ open, 322 counts min⁻¹ with thin paper, 318 counts min⁻¹ with 3 mm aluminium, and 88 counts min⁻¹ with 5 cm lead. Which emissions does the source produce?
items.workedSolution: Thin paper causes a big drop, showing alpha radiation is present. 3 mm aluminium causes almost no further drop, so beta is absent. 5 cm lead cuts the remaining counts, proving gamma radiation. The source emits alpha and gamma radiation.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: alpha and gamma radiation.

items.stem: Newly removed spent fuel rods are stored underwater in deep cooling ponds for several years. Why is this done before vitrification and long-term disposal?
items.workedSolution: Water cools the decay heat and shields intense radiation from high-level fission fragments. The waste is handled remotely, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable rock.

markScheme.criterion: States cooling ponds cool and shield waste before vitrification in glass inside steel canisters and deep stable storage.

options.label: A
options.text: Water dissolves the uranium fuel chemically so all long-lived isotopes turn into stable lead within days.
options.distractorRationale: Water does not change nuclear half-lives; short-lived isotopes decay naturally while long-lived waste still requires vitrification.

options.label: B
options.text: Water freezes the fission fragments below zero kelvin to halt beta-minus decay permanently.
options.distractorRationale: Radioactive decay is spontaneous and completely independent of temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: Water provides both continuous cooling for decay heat and radiation shielding before high-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories

options.label: D
options.text: Water converts high-level waste into low-level waste ready for open-air disposal within one week.
options.distractorRationale: High-level waste remains dangerous for thousands of years and requires deep geologically stable storage.

items.stem: X-ray photons of wavelength $20.0\text{ pm}$ scatter straight back ($180^{\circ}$) from stationary free electrons.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta\lambda = \frac{2h}{m_{\text{e}} c} = 4.85 pm$. (b) $\lambda_{\text{f}} = 24.9 pm$, giving $E_{\text{k}} = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{i}}} - \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{f}}}\right) = 12.1 keV$. (c) Visible wavelengths are about $10^5$ times larger than $2.4\text{ pm}$, so $\Delta\lambda/\lambda$ is tiny. Compton scattering also proves photons carry quantized momentum as well as energy in elastic collisions.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $(1 - \cos 180^{\circ}) = 2$ with $h/(m_{\text{e}}c)$.
Correct wavelength shift 4.85 pm.
Calculates $\lambda_{\text{f}} = \lambda_{\text{i}} + \Delta\lambda$.
Computes $E_{\text{k}} = hc(1/\lambda_{\text{i}} - 1/\lambda_{\text{f}})$ and converts to keV.
Correct recoil kinetic energy 12.1 keV.
Notes $\Delta\lambda / \lambda$ is tiny for visible light because $\lambda_{\text{visible}} \gg 2.4\text{ pm}$.
States Compton scattering proves photons carry quantized momentum and energy in electron collisions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength shift $\Delta\lambda$ of the backscattered photon.
Calculate the kinetic energy gained by the recoil electron in $\text{keV}$.
workingSteps: Find scattered wavelength $\lambda_{\text{f}} = 20.0\text{ pm} + 4.85 pm = 24.9 pm$.
Divide by $1.60 \times 10^{-16}\text{ J keV}^{-1}$ to obtain 12.1 keV.

parts.prompt: Explain why the fractional Compton shift is tiny for visible light. Outline why Compton scattering gives stronger evidence for photons than the photoelectric effect.
parts.expectedAnswer: For visible light ($\lambda \approx 500\text{ nm}$), $\Delta\lambda / \lambda \approx 10^{-5}$, which is far too small to notice. Also, Compton scattering proves photons carry quantized momentum as well as energy in electron collisions.
workingSteps: Compare fixed $\Delta\lambda \sim 2.4\text{ pm}$ with visible wavelength $\sim 5 \times 10^5\text{ pm}$.
Explain that Compton scattering proves photons carry quantized momentum as well as energy.

items.stem: Bertozzi measured electron speed against kinetic energy up to several MeV. How did his results disprove classical mechanics?
items.workedSolution: Speed and calorimeter data matched $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2$. Electron speed approached the speed of light asymptotically as kinetic energy rose, instead of following the classical straight line.

markScheme.criterion: States electron speed approaches light speed asymptotically as kinetic energy rises, unlike the classical straight line.

items.stem: A parent nucleus of Zr has nucleon number A = 95 and proton number Z = 40. It decays by beta-minus decay (d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) to form a daughter nucleus with A = 95 and Z = 42. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Initial neutron number N₀ = 95 − 40 = 55; final neutron number N_f = 95 − 42 = 53. Thus ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −2.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N = A − Z to obtain ΔN = (95 − 42) − (95 − 40) = −2 (A).

options.distractorRationale: Assumes each weak quark transition changes neutron number by 2 instead of 1.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Counts all three valence quarks as converting in each beta decay.

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, an alpha particle (charge +2e) with kinetic energy 4.2 MeV moves head-on toward a fixed tungsten nucleus (Z = 74, A = 184). It scatters back through 180° after stopping at closest distance d. Neglect nuclear recoil and take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 4.2 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.72 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(2e)(74e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2)(74)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 6.72 × 10⁻¹³ = 50.7 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 50.7 fm (B).

items.stem: An unstable nucleus of Ac (A = 227, Z = 89) decays by alpha and beta-minus steps only. The final nuclide has nucleon number A = 211 and proton number Z = 83. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Parent neutron number N₀ = 227 − 89 = 138. Final neutron number N_f = 211 − 83 = 128. Therefore ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −10.

items.stem: The graph shows maximum photoelectron kinetic energy $E_{\text{k(max)}}$ plotted against incident frequency $f$ for two different clean metals A and B. Why are the two straight lines parallel?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi$ shows the gradient equals the Planck constant $h$ for every metal surface. Therefore option B is correct: gradient equals the Planck constant for every metal surface.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: gradient equals the Planck constant for every metal surface.

options.text: The lines have identical slope because the gradient equals the work function of each metal
options.distractorRationale: Work function is the magnitude of the negative vertical intercept (−φ), not the gradient.

options.label: B
options.text: The lines have identical slope because the gradient equals the Planck constant for every metal surface

options.label: C
options.text: The lines have identical slope because the gradient equals the elementary charge divided by Planck constant
options.distractorRationale: Inverts h/e; on an Ek(max)–f graph the gradient is h (and on a Vs–f graph it is h/e).

options.label: D
options.text: The lines have identical slope because both metals share the same threshold frequency
options.distractorRationale: The horizontal intercepts f₀A and f₀B are distinct because the metals have different work functions.

items.stem: Electrons accelerated from rest across 320 V strike a thin nickel foil with atomic spacing d = 2.03 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Diffraction rings appear on a fluorescent screen at distance L = 0.18 m behind the foil. Take sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 6.86 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.338 yields θ = arcsin(0.338) = 19.8 °.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 19.8 ° (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves arcsin(λ / d) in radians while labelling the answer in degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inserts an extra factor of 2 in the denominator despite sin θ = λ / d being specified.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 in p = √(2mₑeV) when computing the electron de Broglie wavelength.

items.stem: A scattering test directs an alpha beam (charge +2e) of energy 5.2 MeV onto a calcium-40 nucleus (Z = 20, A = 40). Assume a uniform spherical nucleus with R = R₀ A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Taking nuclear mass m ≈ A u, what is the nuclear density ρ of the calcium-40 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Since R = R₀ A^(1/3), V = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π R₀³ A. Thus ρ = (A u) / ((4/3)π R₀³ A) = 3u / (4π R₀³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ (C).

items.stem: In a discharge lamp, helium gas has its second excited state at −3.39 eV and another bound level at −4.8 eV. Take zero energy at the ionization level. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−3.39) = 3.39 eV. Final answer: 3.39 eV. (b) ΔE = 3.39 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 5.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (8.18 × 10¹⁴) = 3.67 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 367 nm. Final answer: 367 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 3.39 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Correct answer: 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Correct answer: 367 nm.

items.stem: An STM scans a silicon surface with an initial tunnelling current of 4.50 nA. The current follows $I = I_0 e^{-k\Delta d}$ with $k = 22.0\text{ nm}^{-1}$. The vacuum gap widens by 0.080 nm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 0.774 nA$. (b) Constant-current mode adjusts tip height with piezoelectric feedback. Constant-height mode keeps the tip level and records tunnelling current changes.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes $4.50 \times e^{-22.0 \times 0.080}$.
Correct current 0.774 nA.
Explains constant-current mode uses piezo feedback to maintain gap and record height.

items.stem: The Sun is a class G star with a surface temperature of about $5800\text{ K}$. Its spectrum shows strong lines of ionised and neutral metals. What is the colour of a class G star?
items.workedSolution: Class G stars have surface temperatures of $5000\text{–}6000\text{ K}$ and metal lines. Their colour is yellow-white.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the colour as yellow-white.

options.label: A
options.text: Deep blue-white, matching surface temperatures between 7500 K and 11 000 K.
options.distractorRationale: Blue-white corresponds to spectral class A.

options.label: B
options.text: Pure orange, matching surface temperatures between 3500 K and 5000 K.
options.distractorRationale: Orange corresponds to spectral class K.

options.label: C
options.text: Red, matching surface temperatures below 3500 K.
options.distractorRationale: Red corresponds to spectral class M.

options.label: D

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube measures a background count rate of 26 counts min⁻¹. A source of Bi-214 with half-life 19.9 min is placed in front of the tube. The initial total count rate is 306 counts min⁻¹. The detector is read again after 59.7 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 306 − 26 = 280 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 280 counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 59.7 / 19.9 = 3 half-lives. C_net = 280 / 2^3 = 35.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 35.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 34.99999999999999 + 26 = 61.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 61.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 280 counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 3 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^3.
Correct answer: 35.0 counts min⁻¹.
Adds background count rate back to the remaining net count rate to obtain 61.0 counts min⁻¹.

items.stem: In external radiotherapy, $8$ equal narrow high-energy X-ray beams cross at a deep tumour from different angles. They deliver a total tumour dose of $56.0\text{ Gy}$. The entry paths do not overlap. What dose does healthy tissue along one beam path receive?
items.workedSolution: Splitting $56.0\text{ Gy}$ across $8$ non-overlapping entry paths gives $\frac{56.0}{8} = 7.00 Gy$ per healthy-tissue path.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 7.00 Gy.

items.stem: An alpha emitter has decay constant $\lambda = 2.50 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$. It emits $5.80\text{ MeV}$ $\alpha_1$ particles, or $\alpha_2$ particles followed by a $0.320\text{ MeV}$ gamma photon ($h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $E_{\alpha 2} = 5.48 MeV$, $f = 7.72 × 10¹⁹ Hz$. (b) Alpha particles have discrete kinetic energies matching the gamma photon energies. This proves nuclear energy levels are discrete. (c) $P = 1 - e^{-1.00} = 0.632$. (d) Exact decay probability is one minus e to the minus lambda t. So lambda approximates decay probability per unit time only when lambda times t is much smaller than one.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains E_α2 = 5.48 MeV.
Converts 0.320 MeV to J and applies f = E/h.
Obtains gamma frequency 7.72 × 10¹⁹ Hz.
Notes energy difference between α₁ and α₂ equals emitted γ photon energy.
Links discrete alpha and gamma energies to quantized nuclear energy levels.
Applies P = 1 − exp(−λt) with λt = 1.00.
Obtains exact probability 0.632.
Notes 1 − e^(−λt) ≈ λt only when λt ≪ 1 and fails badly at λt = 1.
Explains exact probability is one minus e to the minus lambda t, so linear approximation needs lambda times t much smaller than one.

parts.prompt: Explain how the observation of sharp alpha-particle kinetic energies and accompanying gamma rays supports the existence of discrete nuclear energy levels.
parts.expectedAnswer: Alpha particles are emitted only with specific discrete kinetic energies. These match fixed nuclear energy gaps and the emitted gamma photon energies. This gives direct evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.
workingSteps: Discrete alpha energies and matching gamma photon energies prove nuclear energy levels are discrete.

parts.prompt: Calculate the exact probability that a given nucleus decays within a $400\text{ s}$ interval.
Using your result from part (c), explain why $\lambda$ approximates the probability of decay per unit time only in the limit $\lambda t \ll 1$.
parts.expectedAnswer: At t = 400 s, the linear rule gives λt = 1.00 (certainty) instead of 0.632. The exact decay probability is one minus e to the minus lambda t. Thus lambda approximates decay probability per unit time only when lambda times t is much smaller than one.
workingSteps: Exact decay probability is one minus e to the minus lambda t. So lambda approximates rate only when lambda times t is much less than one.

items.stem: A hospital compares CT, MRI, and Diagnostic Ultrasound. They need to choose the best scan for trauma, brain soft tissue, and pregnancy.
items.workedSolution: Level 3: CT gives detailed X-ray slices for bone and trauma, but with a high ionising dose. MRI uses strong magnetic fields and Larmor RF pulses on hydrogen protons for high soft-tissue contrast with zero ionising risk. However, MRI is costly and unsafe with metal implants. Ultrasound is safe, cheap, portable, and real-time, but is blocked by bone and air.

markScheme.criterion: Describes CT as rotating X-ray slices giving high bone/trauma detail, but a large ionising dose.
Correctly describes MRI as using strong magnetic fields and RF Larmor resonance of hydrogen protons with zero ionising radiation.
Highlights MRI's superior soft-tissue contrast (e.g. brain/spinal cord) alongside its weakness on dry bone.
Identifies key MRI limitations: high cost, long scan time, and contraindications for ferromagnetic implants or pacemakers.
Describes ultrasound as non-ionising, portable, low-cost, real-time imaging suited to pregnancy.
States ultrasound limits: lower detail and blocked by bone or air due to impedance mismatch.

parts.prompt: Compare CT, MRI, and Ultrasound in how they work, image detail, ionising risk, and clinical limits.
parts.expectedAnswer: CT rotates an X-ray tube and detector ring to build sharp 3D cross-sections of bone and bleeding. However, CT delivers a large ionising X-ray dose, limiting repeat use and pregnancy scans. MRI aligns hydrogen protons in a strong superconducting magnetic field and excites them with RF pulses at the Larmor frequency. It gives top soft-tissue and brain contrast with zero ionising radiation. However, MRI is costly, slow, noisy, poor on dry bone, and unsafe for patients with magnetic metal implants or pacemakers. Ultrasound sends high-frequency sound pulses that reflect at acoustic impedance boundaries. It is non-ionising, cheap, portable, and real-time for pregnancy and heart scans, but has lower resolution and cannot cross bone or air-filled lungs.
workingSteps: Explain CT: rotating X-ray slices, high bone/trauma resolution, significant ionising dose.
Explain MRI: strong B-field + RF Larmor excitation of hydrogen protons, zero ionising risk, superior soft-tissue/brain contrast.
State MRI limitations: expensive, slow, poor dry-bone signal, hazardous with ferromagnetic implants/pacemakers.
Explain Ultrasound: non-ionising acoustic pulse-echo reflection, portable, low-cost, real-time imaging.
State Ultrasound limitations: blocked by bone and air pockets (impedance mismatch), lower spatial detail.
Synthesise clinical selection (e.g. ultrasound for pregnancy, MRI for brain/ligaments, CT for rapid bone/trauma).

items.stem: Ultraviolet radiation of frequency $1.40 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$ falls on a clean zinc plate of work function $4.30\text{ eV}$ in a vacuum photocell.
items.workedSolution: (a) $hf / e = 5.80 eV$. (b) $E_{\text{k(max)}} = 5.80 eV - 4.30\text{ eV} = 1.50 eV$. (c) Einstein showed light travels as discrete photons transferring energy one-to-one to electrons, overturning purely classical wave physics.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $E = hf / e$.
Correct photon energy 5.80 eV.
Correct maximum kinetic energy 1.50 eV.
Explains classical wave failure on threshold frequency or instantaneous emission.
Explains Einstein showed light travels as discrete photons transferring energy one-to-one to electrons.
States significance: light/EM radiation has quantised particle-like nature (wave–particle duality).

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of each incident UV photon in eV.
workingSteps: Divide by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J eV}^{-1}$ to obtain 5.80 eV.

parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons in eV.
workingSteps: Subtract work function: 5.80 eV $- 4.30\text{ eV} = $ 1.50 eV.

parts.prompt: Explain why classical wave theory failed to account for photoelectricity and state the significance of Einstein's explanation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Wave theory predicted any frequency could free electrons over time and intensity would raise maximum kinetic energy. Einstein showed light travels as discrete photons acting one-to-one with electrons, proving wave–particle duality.
workingSteps: Wave theory wrongly predicted no threshold frequency and an intensity-dependent $E_{\text{k(max)}}$ or time delay.
State Einstein showed light travels as discrete photons transferring energy one-to-one to electrons.
Conclude EM radiation shows particle-like photon behaviour as well as wave interference.

items.stem: An atom has $5$ bound energy levels. Electrons can fall from the highest level down to the ground state. All jumps have different energy gaps. How many distinct emission wavelengths can occur?
items.workedSolution: The number of downward pairs among $n = 5$ levels is $n(n - 1)/2 = 5 \times 4 / 2 = 10.0$ distinct lines. Option D (10.0) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Distinct emission lines $= 10$ (10.0, option D).

items.stem: A square flat-panel (FTP) X-ray detector measures $30.0\text{ cm} \times 30.0\text{ cm}$. It uses square photodiode pixels of width $150\text{ }\mu\text{m}$. How many million pixels are in the active detector array?
items.workedSolution: Pixels per side $= \frac{0.300\text{ m}}{150 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}} = 2000$. Total pixels $= 2000^2 = 4.00 million pixels$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 4.00 million pixels.

items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from n = 1 is ΔE = 13.6 × 5² / 1² = 340 eV = 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Finds f = (13.6 Z² / n²)(e / h) = 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz (D).

items.stem: The mass of a sodium-23 nucleus (A = 23, Z = 11) is 22.983733 u. Use mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this sodium-23 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 23 − 11 = 12. Mass defect Δm = 11(1.007276) + 12(1.008665) − 22.983733 = 0.200 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 187 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 187 / 23 = 8.11 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.200 u, B = 187 MeV, and B / A = 8.11 MeV (D).

items.stem: In an evacuated tube, electrons accelerate from rest through a potential difference of 4200 V. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in picometres (pm), of the electrons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 6.72 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 3.50 × 10⁻²³ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 18.9 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 18.9 pm (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: A hospital CT scanner tube accelerates electrons across 110 kV onto a rotating tungsten target embedded in a copper block. Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $E_{\max} = 1.76 × 10⁻¹⁴ J$. (b) $\lambda_{\min} = 11.3 pm$. (c) Higher anode voltage shortens minimum wavelength and raises intensity, while characteristic peaks stay fixed.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $E = eV = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.10 \times 10^5$.
Correct energy 1.76 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
Evaluates $\lambda_{\min} = hc / E_{\max}$.
Correct wavelength 11.3 pm.
States $\lambda_{\min}$ shifts shorter and continuum intensity increases.
States characteristic K-line wavelengths remain unchanged.

options.label: A
options.text: Plotting threshold voltage against wavelength yields a straight line through the origin with gradient hc divided by e.
options.distractorRationale: V₀ is inversely proportional to λ, so plotting V₀ against λ produces a curve rather than a straight line.

options.label: B
options.text: Plotting threshold voltage against reciprocal wavelength gives a gradient equal directly to Planck constant h.
options.distractorRationale: Omits the constants c and e; the gradient is hc/e, so h = (e × gradient)/c.

options.label: C
options.text: Plotting threshold voltage against reciprocal wavelength yields a straight line through the origin with gradient hc divided by e.

options.label: D
options.text: The y-intercept of V₀ against reciprocal wavelength gives the value of h divided by e.
options.distractorRationale: Ideally V₀ = (hc/e)(1/λ) passes through the origin; h is determined from the gradient, not the intercept.

items.stem: In a photocell, light of frequency 2.87 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes a copper plate. The work function of copper is 4.7 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the maximum kinetic energy, in electron-volts (eV), of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.87 × 10¹⁵) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 11.9 eV. Subtracting Φ = 4.7 eV gives Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 7.19 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Converts hf to eV and subtracts Φ = 4.7 eV to obtain 7.19 eV (A).

items.stem: An unstable particle forms at origin O (x = 0, ct = 0) and moves along +x at v = 0.80c in frame S. It decays at Event A (x = 4.0 ls, ct = 5.0 ls).
items.workedSolution: (a) (Δs)² = 9.00 ls². (b) cΔt₀ = 3.00 ls. (c) θ = 38.7°. (d) Inertial observers disagree on separate space and time intervals, but all measure the same invariant spacetime interval. The forty-five degree light worldline bisects both axis pairs, showing invariant c and keeping causal signals inside the light cone.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)².
Obtains (Δs)² = 9.00 ls².
Sets Δx′ = 0 in the particle rest frame so cΔt₀ = √((Δs)²).
Obtains cΔt₀ = 3.00 ls (matching Δt / γ = 5.0 / 1.67).
Applies tan θ = 0.80 to obtain θ = 38.7°.
States (Δs)² has the identical value for all inertial observers.
Notes the 45° light cone bisects both perpendicular and primed axes (invariant speed c).
States massive particles and causal signals remain inside the light cone (v < c).

parts.prompt: Calculate the invariant squared spacetime interval (Δs)² between creation at O and decay at Event A.
Deduce the proper time interval cΔt₀ (in ls) recorded by a clock co-moving with the particle.
workingSteps: In particle rest frame Δx′ = 0, so cΔt₀ = √(Δs)² = √9.0 = 3.00 ls

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, 208 nm UV light strikes a calcium surface. The surface has work function Φ = 2.87 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 9.56 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; work function Φ = 2.87 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.59 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.04 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.04 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A cool monatomic gas produces dark lines in an absorption spectrum. The same hot gas produces bright lines in an emission spectrum. Why do both sets of lines appear at the exact same wavelengths?
items.workedSolution: Photon wavelength follows $\lambda = hc/\Delta E$. Absorption and emission happen between the exact same discrete energy levels. Dark absorption lines and bright emission lines therefore share the same wavelengths.

markScheme.criterion: States absorption and emission lines share wavelengths because both use the same discrete energy levels.

items.stem: In a PET scanner, a positron and an electron annihilate into two gamma photons. Their combined kinetic energy is $0.28\text{ MeV}$. Take rest energy $= 0.511\text{ MeV}$, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, and $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Each photon has $E = 0.651 MeV$, giving $f = 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$. (b) Two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

markScheme.criterion: Each photon energy $= 0.651 MeV$.
Convert photon energy to joules and apply $f = E/h$.
Frequency $= 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$.
Momentum must be conserved (initial momentum ~ 0).
Two gamma photons travel in opposite directions with equal magnitude momentum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of each emitted gamma photon in MeV and its frequency in Hz.
parts.expectedAnswer: Each photon energy $= 0.651 MeV$; frequency $= 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$
workingSteps: Energy of each photon $E = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}E_{\text{k,tot}} = 0.651 MeV$.
Convert to joules and compute $f = E/h = 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$.

parts.prompt: Explain why two photons are emitted in opposite directions during annihilation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Initial momentum is approximately zero, so two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.
workingSteps: State momentum conservation from near-zero initial momentum.
Conclude two identical photons travel in opposite directions (reject 'elimination').

items.stem: In Required Practical 12 with systematic offset $x_0 = 22$ mm, the background-corrected gamma count rate at ruler distance $x_1 = 140$ mm is 123 s⁻¹. Predict the corrected count rate at $x_2 = 420$ mm.
items.workedSolution: Background rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 480/(20\times 60) = 0.400 s⁻¹$. From $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$, gradient $= 1/\sqrt{k} = 0.556$, so $k = 3.24 s⁻¹ m²$, $x_0 = \text{intercept}/\text{grad} = 22$ mm, and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 16.6 s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines cCorr2 $= 16.6 s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A magnesium ion has two fewer orbital electrons than protons in its nucleus. Which statement correctly explains how to determine the specific charge of this ion rather than its bare nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Only the net uncompensated charge (+2e) determines $Q$, while all protons, neutrons (and remaining electrons) contribute to mass $m$. Therefore option C is correct: ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

options.distractorRationale: Commits both classic AQA traps: using nuclear charge Z for a partially ionised atom and ignoring neutron mass.

options.label: B
options.text: For the ion, charge equals the full proton number because neutral neutrons cancel orbital electrons
options.distractorRationale: Neutrons carry zero charge and cannot cancel electron charges; orbital electrons partially cancel protons.

options.label: D
options.text: For the ion, charge is zero because the remaining orbital electrons shield the nucleus completely
options.distractorRationale: Removing two electrons leaves a net positive charge of +2e.

items.stem: Both joining very light nuclei and splitting very heavy nuclei release energy. How does the BE/A against A graph explain this?
items.workedSolution: Both fusion below nucleon number 56 and fission above 56 move products higher up the curve toward iron-56. Higher BE/A means more tightly bound products with less total mass. This mass drop appears as kinetic energy and gamma radiation.

markScheme.criterion: States that fusion (below 56) and fission (above 56) move products toward iron-56, raising total binding energy and releasing energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion increases total binding energy whereas fission decreases total binding energy, releasing the surplus directly as heat.
options.distractorRationale: In any energy-releasing nuclear reaction, total binding energy of the products is greater than that of the reactants.

options.label: B
options.text: Referring to the curve, both fusion of light nuclei below nucleon number 56 and fission of heavy nuclei above 56 move products higher up the curve toward iron-56, increasing total binding energy and releasing energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Products in both reactions have greater total mass than reactants, and the extra mass converts into kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Energy-releasing reactions always have less product mass than reactant mass.

options.label: D
options.text: Heavy nuclei fuse toward A = 240 while light nuclei split toward A = 1 to lower their average binding energy per nucleon.
options.distractorRationale: Moving down the BE/A curve absorbs energy rather than releasing it.

items.stem: Why does high-energy electron diffraction measure nuclear radius more accurately than alpha closest approach?
items.workedSolution: High-energy electrons are leptons and do not feel the strong nuclear force. They diffract to a non-zero first minimum, giving radius directly. Alpha closest approach gives only an energy-dependent upper bound.

markScheme.criterion: States electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong force giving direct radius, while alpha gives only an upper bound.

options.label: A
options.text: Because electrons experience a much stronger strong nuclear force than alpha particles, forcing them to bounce cleanly off the nuclear surface.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons and do NOT feel the strong nuclear force at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Because high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

options.label: C
options.text: Because electron diffraction produces exact zero-intensity dark fringes identical to optical single-slit diffraction.
options.distractorRationale: Nuclear electron diffraction shows a non-zero first minimum superimposed on decreasing scattering intensity.

options.label: D
options.text: Because alpha particles are massless leptons whose closest approach underestimates the true nuclear radius.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles are composite hadrons (helium-4 nuclei) and r_min overestimates (upper bound) the nuclear radius.

items.stem: Alpha and gamma emitters pose very different health risks inside and outside the body. Why do their internal and external hazards differ so much?
items.workedSolution: Inside the body, alpha sources are most dangerous because strongly ionising particles dump all their energy into local living tissue. Outside the body, gamma sources are the main hazard because gamma rays pass through skin into deep organs.

markScheme.criterion: States alpha is most hazardous internally (intense local ionisation) and gamma externally (penetrates skin and organs).

options.label: A
options.text: Gamma sources are harmless externally because they are weakly ionising, whereas alpha sources penetrate clothing and skin from across a room.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles cannot penetrate the outer dead layer of skin or travel far in air, whereas external gamma rays penetrate deep organs.

options.label: B
options.text: Alpha and gamma emitters carry identical internal and external hazards whenever their activities in becquerels are equal.
options.distractorRationale: Equal activities do not mean equal localised dose because ionising power and penetration differ drastically.

options.label: C
options.text: Regarding biological tissue damage, alpha sources are most hazardous if ingested or inhaled because strongly ionising particles deposit all their energy in living tissue, whereas gamma sources pose the greatest external hazard because they penetrate skin and organs.

options.label: D
options.text: Beta emitters are completely safe both internally and externally because electrons are already present inside human atoms.
options.distractorRationale: High-energy beta particles ionise cellular DNA and cause tissue damage both externally on skin/eyes and internally.

items.stem: What is the main role of the graphite or water moderator in a thermal nuclear reactor?
items.workedSolution: The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds by elastic collisions with low-mass nuclei. Thermal neutrons split uranium-235 much more easily, raising uranium-235 fission probability.

markScheme.criterion: States the moderator slows fast neutrons by elastic collisions with low-mass nuclei, raising U-235 fission chance.

options.label: A
options.text: The moderator absorbs excess fast neutrons to shut down the chain reaction safely.
options.distractorRationale: Major AQA mark-scheme trap: control rods absorb neutrons, whereas the moderator must NOT absorb neutrons!

options.label: B
options.text: The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions with low-mass nuclei so uranium-235 fission probability increases

options.label: C
options.text: The moderator accelerates slow neutrons to relativistic speeds so they split uranium-238 nuclei.
options.distractorRationale: Thermal reactors require slowing fast fission neutrons down to thermal speeds for U-235.

options.label: D
options.text: The moderator uses heavy lead nuclei so neutrons bounce off elastically with maximum kinetic energy loss.
options.distractorRationale: Elastic collision energy transfer is maximal when moderator nucleon mass is close to neutron mass (low A), not heavy lead.

items.stem: In Compton scattering, X-ray photons collide elastically with free stationary electrons. Why does the scattered photon always have a longer wavelength for any non-zero angle?
items.workedSolution: Total energy is conserved and $E = hc/\lambda$. The recoil electron gains kinetic energy, so the scattered photon has less energy and a longer wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: States the scattered photon loses energy to the recoil electron, giving a longer wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: By conservation of energy, the scattered photon always has a longer wavelength and lower energy because kinetic energy is transferred to the recoil electron.

options.label: B
options.text: The photon slows down below the speed of light in vacuum after losing energy to the electron.
options.distractorRationale: Photons always travel at speed $c$ in vacuum; losing energy reduces frequency and increases wavelength.

options.label: C
options.text: Classical electromagnetic wave diffraction stretches the wave crest spacing as it bends around the electron.
options.distractorRationale: Classical wave scattering predicts radiation re-emitted at the exact same frequency and wavelength.

options.label: D
options.text: The electron absorbs the incident photon completely and emits two lower-energy photons in opposite directions.
options.distractorRationale: Compton scattering is a one-to-one elastic collision between a single photon and a free electron.

items.stem: A futuristic spacecraft of proper length 240 m cruises past a space station at $0.600c$. An onboard clock ticks through a proper interval of $1.50\,\mu\text{s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $l = 192 m$. (b) $t = 1.88 μs$. (c) Zero fringe shift on ninety degree rotation disproved motion through an ether and supported invariant light speed.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $l = l_0 \sqrt{1 - 0.600^2}$.
Correct contracted length 192 m.
Applies $t = t_0 / \sqrt{1 - 0.600^2}$.
Correct dilated time 1.88 μs.
States zero fringe shift occurred upon $90°$ rotation.

parts.expectedAnswer: Rotating the apparatus by ninety degrees gave zero fringe shift. This disproved absolute motion through an ether and supported invariant light speed.
workingSteps: Rotating the interferometer by $90°$ yielded zero fringe shift despite Earth's orbital motion.
This disproved a stationary ether and confirmed $c$ is identical along every direction.

items.stem: A parent nucleus of iron-52 has nucleon number A = 52 and proton number Z = 26. It decays by beta-plus decay (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) to form a daughter nucleus with A = 52 and Z = 24.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 24 − 26 = −2. Final answer: −2. (b) N₀ = 52 − 26 = 26; N_f = 52 − 24 = 28. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2. Final answer: 2. (c) Accounting for ΔA = 0, charge conservation gives 2 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 2.

Correct answer: 2.

items.stem: An alpha particle (charge +2e) with initial kinetic energy 3.6 MeV is fired head-on at a stationary lead nucleus (Z = 82, A = 208). It comes to rest at distance d before reversing. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 3.6 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 5.76 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(2e)(82e) / Eₖ = 6.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 65.5 fm. Final answer: 65.5 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (208)^(1/3) = 7.11 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 7.11 fm. (c) ρ = (208 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Eₖ to joules, equates Eₖ = k Q₁ Q₂ / d, and converts metres to femtometres.
Correct answer: 65.5 fm.
Applies R = 1.20 × A^(1/3) fm.
Correct answer: 7.11 fm.
Finds ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) in SI units.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A bright visible spotlight shines on the negatively charged clean zinc plate for several minutes. What is observed?
items.workedSolution: Visible photon energy is below zinc's work function ($f < f_0$). No photoelectrons are emitted, so the gold leaf stays deflected. Option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: gold leaf remains deflected because photon frequency is below the threshold frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: Even at very high brightness, the gold leaf eventually falls once surface electrons absorb multiple visible photons together
options.distractorRationale: Photoelectric absorption is a one-to-one photon-electron interaction; electrons do not accumulate energy over time.

options.label: B
options.text: Even at very high brightness, the gold leaf falls immediately at a slower rate than under ultraviolet
options.distractorRationale: No electrons are emitted at all when photon energy hf is below the work function φ.

options.label: C
options.text: Even at very high brightness, the gold leaf rises higher due to radiation pressure
options.distractorRationale: Visible light neither charges the plate nor discharges it below f₀.

options.label: D
options.text: Even at very high brightness, the gold leaf remains deflected because photon frequency is below the threshold frequency

items.stem: Electrons accelerated from rest across 1300 V strike a thin silver foil with atomic spacing d = 2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Diffraction rings appear on a fluorescent screen at distance L = 0.17 m behind the foil. Take sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = √(2mₑeV) = 1.95 × 10⁻²³ N s. λ = h / p = 3.41 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 34.1 pm. Final answer: 34.1 pm. (b) sin θ = λ / d = 3.41 × 10⁻¹¹ / (2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 0.144. θ = 8.30 °. Final answer: 8.30 °. (c) r = L tan θ = 0.17 × tan(8.30°) = 0.0248 m. Final answer: 0.0248 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = h / √(2mₑeV) with SI values and converts to picometres.
Correct answer: 34.1 pm.
Applies sin θ = λ / d and converts to degrees.
Correct answer: 8.30 °.
Finds r = L tan θ using the screen distance L.
Correct answer: 0.0248 m.

items.stem: Alpha particles (Z₁ = 2) of energy 6.5 MeV scatter from a spherical tin-120 target nucleus (Z = 50, A = 120). The nuclear radius is given by R = R₀ A^(1/3). Use R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = 1.20 × (120)^(1/3) = 5.92 fm. Final answer: 5.92 fm. (b) R = 5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Final answer: 5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. (c) m = 120 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; V = (4/3)π(5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵)³. ρ = m / V = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes nucleon number A into R = R₀ A^(1/3).
Correct answer: 5.92 fm.
Multiplies R in fm by 10⁻¹⁵ m fm⁻¹ to obtain 5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Divides nuclear mass A u by spherical volume (4/3)πR³.
Correct answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In nuclear fission physics, what is meant by the critical mass of a fissile isotope such as uranium-235?
items.workedSolution: Critical mass is the smallest mass of fissile uranium-235 needed to keep a chain reaction going. At critical mass, at least one neutron per fission triggers another fission instead of escaping.

markScheme.criterion: Defines critical mass as the minimum mass of uranium-235 so at least one neutron per fission causes another fission.

options.text: Critical mass is the mass defect lost when one mole of uranium-235 undergoes complete induced fission.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses critical mass for sustaining a chain reaction with nuclear mass defect Δm.

options.label: C
options.text: Critical mass is the minimum mass of control-rod boron needed to shut down a thermal reactor immediately.
options.distractorRationale: Control rods absorb neutrons to regulate or halt the reaction; critical mass is the minimum fissile fuel mass needed to sustain it.

options.text: Referring to the chain-reaction diagram, critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile uranium-235 needed to sustain a chain reaction so that on average at least one neutron per fission triggers another fission instead of escaping.

items.stem: Atoms of rubidium vapour have a first excited state at −2.63 eV and a nearby bound level at −4.27 eV. Ionization occurs at zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the lowest photon frequency needed to ionize the atom from the first excited state?
items.workedSolution: Energy needed to reach the continuum is ΔE = 2.63 eV = 4.21 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 4.21 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.35 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f = |E| e / h to obtain 6.35 × 10¹⁴ Hz (D).

items.stem: The blue-green $\text{H}\beta$ Balmer line comes from an electron jump in hydrogen from $n = 2$ ($-3.40\text{ eV}$) to $n = 4$ ($-0.850\text{ eV}$). Calculate the wavelength of this line in nanometres.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta E = -0.850 - (-3.40) = 2.55\text{ eV} = 4.08 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$. Thus $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = 488 nm$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 488 nm.
