items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube measures a background count rate of 18 counts min⁻¹. A technetium-99m source with half-life 6 h is placed in front of the tube at t = 0. The initial total count rate is 118 counts min⁻¹. The detector is read again after 12 h. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 12 h?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 118 − 18 = 100 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 12 / 6 = 2. Remaining net count rate C = 100 / 2^2 = 25 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 25 + 18 = 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (100), divides by 2^2 (25), and adds 18 back to obtain 43.0 counts min⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the uncorrected count rate first and subtracts the background count rate at the end.

items.stem: A sealed source of Ir-192 holds N₀ = 4.3 × 10¹⁵ unstable nuclei with half-life 73.8 d. The source decays for t = 120 d. What is the activity of the sample, in becquerels (Bq), at t = 120 d?
items.workedSolution: T₁/₂ = 73.8 × 86400 = 6.38 × 10⁶ s, so λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 1.09 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 4.67 × 10⁸ Bq. At t = 120 d, A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.51 × 10⁸ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ to seconds, finds A₀ = λN₀, and finds A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.51 × 10⁸ Bq (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Fails to convert half-life from d to seconds (× 86400) when computing A = λN in Bq (s⁻¹).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the initial activity A₀ = λN₀ at t = 0 without multiplying by the exponential decay factor e^(−λt).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ = 1 / T₁/₂ instead of λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ when converting half-life to decay constant.

items.stem: What properties make tracers like $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$, $^{131}\text{I}$, and $^{111}\text{In}$ effective for medical scans?
items.workedSolution: These tracers are gamma emitters (technetium-99m, iodine-131, and indium-111) joined to organ-targeting compounds. Their gamma energy and half-life give clear external counts while keeping patient dose low.

markScheme.criterion: States gamma emitters (technetium-99m, iodine-131, indium-111) are joined to organ-targeting compounds.

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha-emitting isotopes with century-long half-lives are preferred because alpha particles exit the body easily.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles are absorbed within millimetres of tissue, causing severe damage without reaching the gamma camera.

options.label: B
options.text: Suitable gamma emitters like technetium-99m iodine-131 and indium-111 are labelled onto organ-affinity compounds with an appropriate half-life and penetrating gamma energy detectable outside the body.

options.label: C
options.text: Tracers must remain chemically inert so they distribute uniformly everywhere rather than binding to any organ.
options.distractorRationale: Chemically labelling a compound with organ affinity concentrates the tracer in the target organ.

options.label: D
options.text: Tracers are chosen solely for emitting low-frequency radio waves that cannot ionise tissue.
options.distractorRationale: Radionuclide tracers emit penetrating gamma photons (typically $100\text{–}400\text{ keV}$).

items.stem: In the nuclear power plant shown, hot fluid leaves the core and enters a heat exchanger. It does not go straight to the steam turbine. What is the main role of the heat exchanger?
items.workedSolution: The heat exchanger moves thermal energy from the radioactive primary coolant to a separate secondary water loop. This produces clean steam for the turbines without contaminating them.

markScheme.criterion: States the heat exchanger moves heat from radioactive primary coolant to a clean secondary steam loop.

options.label: A
options.text: Heat exchangers transfer thermal energy from the radioactive primary coolant loop to a separate secondary water loop generating steam for turbines without contaminating the turbine circuit.

options.label: B
options.text: Heat exchangers slow down fast fission neutrons into thermal neutrons so uranium-235 can sustain a chain reaction.
options.distractorRationale: Slowing fast neutrons is the role of the moderator inside the reactor core, not the heat exchanger.

options.label: C
options.text: Heat exchangers absorb excess neutrons to shut down the nuclear chain reaction during emergencies.
options.distractorRationale: Absorbing excess neutrons is the role of the boron/cadmium control rods, not the heat exchanger.

options.label: D
options.text: Heat exchangers convert nuclear binding energy directly into alternating electrical current without turbines.
options.distractorRationale: Heat exchangers transfer thermal energy to boil clean secondary water into steam that drives the turbine and generator.

items.stem: Use the particle chart shown. Which statement about baryons is correct?
items.workedSolution: All free baryons decay into a proton. The proton is the only stable free baryon, made of three quarks ($uud$). Option C is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: proton is the only stable free baryon composed of three quarks.

options.label: A
options.text: According to the Standard Model taught at A-Level, the neutron is the only stable free baryon composed of two quarks
options.distractorRationale: Free neutrons beta-decay with a ~10 min half-life, and baryons contain three quarks (qqq), not two.

options.label: B
options.text: According to the Standard Model taught at A-Level, the positive pion is the lightest stable baryon
options.distractorRationale: Pions are mesons (qq̄) with baryon number B = 0, not baryons.

options.label: C
options.text: According to the Standard Model taught at A-Level, the proton is the only stable free baryon composed of three quarks

options.label: D
options.text: According to the Standard Model taught at A-Level, the muon is a heavy baryon that decays into a proton
options.distractorRationale: Muons are fundamental leptons (B = 0) and decay into electrons plus neutrinos.

items.stem: Why was Thomas Young's double-slit experiment (1801) a decisive blow against Newton's corpuscular theory of light?
items.workedSolution: Two beams of classical particles cannot cancel out to make dark bands. Young's double-slit fringes come from wave superposition and path difference, which particles cannot explain.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that Young double-slit fringes arise from wave superposition and path difference impossible for corpuscles.

options.label: A
options.text: Because corpuscles always bend away from the normal when passing through two narrow slits.
options.distractorRationale: Corpuscles travelling straight through two slits would form two bright lines, not alternating dark/bright fringes.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Young measured the exact speed of light in water to be 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options.distractorRationale: Foucault measured the speed of light in water in 1850; Young demonstrated interference fringes.

options.label: C
options.text: Because Young proved that light emits electrons from zinc only above a threshold frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Photoelectricity was investigated by Hertz, Lenard, and Einstein a century later.

options.label: D
options.text: Because Young double-slit fringes arise from wave superposition and path difference impossible for corpuscles, which would only produce two bright patches opposite the slits.

items.stem: Electrons in a diffraction tube accelerate from rest through a p.d. of $4200\text{ V}$. Calculate their de Broglie wavelength in picometres. Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, and $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: $p = \sqrt{2m_{\text{e}}eV} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4200} = 3.50 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹$, giving $\lambda = h/p = 18.9 pm$. Option A (18.9 pm) matches.

markScheme.criterion: de Broglie wavelength $= 18.9 pm$ (18.9 pm, option A).

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing focal spot size improves sharpness while raising tube kV increases soft-tissue contrast.
options.distractorRationale: A larger focal spot worsens geometric penumbra blur, and higher kV penetrates tissues more uniformly, lowering contrast.

options.label: B
options.text: A small focal spot and lead grid improve sharpness while lower tube voltage improves soft-tissue contrast because lower-energy photons are attenuated more differentially across tissues.

options.label: C
options.text: Removing the anti-scatter lead grid sharpens edges while increasing filament current hardens photon energy.
options.distractorRationale: Removing the lead grid allows scattered X-rays to fog the image, and filament current changes intensity, not photon energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Moving the detector far from the patient sharpens edges while removing the aluminium filter improves contrast.
options.distractorRationale: Increasing object–detector distance enlarges penumbra blur, and removing the aluminium filter increases unnecessary skin dose.

items.stem: In a hot gas, a Be³⁺ ion (Z = 4) has quantized energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The electron starts in level n = 5. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (4)² / (5)² = −8.70 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 8.70 eV. Final answer: 8.70 eV. (b) ΔE = 8.70 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. f = ΔE / h = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Final answer: 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.10 × 10¹⁵) = 143 nm. Final answer: 143 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV for the specified Z and n.
Correct answer: 8.70 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Correct answer: 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f and expresses the wavelength in nm to obtain 143 nm.

items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = qV = 5.12 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. v = √(2Eₖ / m) = 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Final answer: 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (b) λ = h / (mv) = 2.17 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 0.0217 nm. Final answer: 0.0217 nm. (c) λ = 21.7 pm. Final answer: 21.7 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV and solves v = √(2qV / m).
Correct answer: 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
Divides Planck's constant h by mv and converts metres to nanometres.
Correct answer: 0.0217 nm.
Multiplies wavelength in nm by 1000 pm nm⁻¹ to obtain 21.7 pm.

items.stem: A radiographer increases the anode p.d. of a tungsten X-ray tube at constant filament current. How does the emitted X-ray spectrum change?
items.workedSolution: Higher anode voltage raises intensity and reduces $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$. Characteristic K-line wavelengths stay fixed because they depend only on tungsten's atomic shells.

markScheme.criterion: States higher anode voltage shortens minimum wavelength and raises intensity, while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing anode voltage shifts both minimum wavelength and tungsten K-line wavelengths shorter.
options.distractorRationale: Characteristic K-line wavelengths depend only on tungsten atomic energy levels, not tube voltage.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing anode voltage keeps minimum wavelength unchanged while raising only the peak height.
options.distractorRationale: Keeping cutoff fixed while raising height occurs when increasing filament current, not anode voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Raising the tube voltage causes increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing anode voltage lengthens minimum wavelength because electrons lose more heat.
options.distractorRationale: Higher anode voltage gives greater maximum photon energy and therefore a shorter cutoff wavelength.

items.stem: In one fission event of plutonium-239, the nuclear equation is: plutonium nucleus (239.0006 u) + 1 thermal neutron (1.008665 u) → tin-134 nucleus (133.8902 u) + Ru-103 nucleus (102.8825 u) + 3 neutrons (each 1.008665 u). Take 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the mass loss Δm, in atomic mass units (u), in one fission reaction?
items.workedSolution: Summing reactant and product rest masses gives Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.211 u.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.211 u (A).

items.stem: A student runs the LED Planck constant practical in a lit room. Why should they look at each LED through a black cardboard tube?
items.workedSolution: Room light hides the faint first glow of an LED, making V₀ readings too high. An opaque dark tube blocks room light so the exact switch-on voltage is judged more accurately.

markScheme.criterion: States the dark tube blocks room light so the exact switch-on voltage is judged more accurately.

options.text: The black tube cools the semiconductor junction so that the emitted wavelength shifts into the ultraviolet.
options.distractorRationale: A cardboard viewing tube shields against stray room light and does not cool the junction.

options.label: B
options.text: The black tube acts as a diffraction grating to separate the LED light into discrete spectral orders.
options.distractorRationale: No diffraction grating is involved; the tube simply darkens the background around the LED.

options.label: C
options.text: The black tube increases the series resistance so that the voltmeter draws larger current.
options.distractorRationale: A cardboard tube is optically shielding the eye and is not electrically connected to the circuit.

options.label: D
options.text: Viewing the LED through an opaque dark tube eliminates ambient light so the exact switch-on threshold voltage is judged more accurately.

items.stem: A beam of light of frequency 2.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz hits a clean zinc plate in a vacuum. The zinc surface has work function 4.33 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Φ = 4.33 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f₀ = Φ / h = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Final answer: 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (b) Photon energy E = hf / e = 10.4 eV. Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 10.4 − 4.33 = 6.03 eV. Final answer: 6.03 eV. (c) Vₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / e = 6.03 V. Final answer: 6.03 V.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Φ from eV to joules and applies f₀ = Φ / h.
Correct answer: 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
Applies Einstein's photoelectric equation Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hf/e − Φ.
Correct answer: 6.03 eV.
Uses eVₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to obtain 6.03 V.

items.stem: A high-speed jet of particles moves at speed v = 0.72c past a gas cloud of proper length L₀ = 2.38 × 10¹⁰ m. In the moving frame, a flare lasts for a proper time Δt₀ = 85.8 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.72²) = 1.44. Final answer: 1.44. (b) Δt = γ Δt₀ = 1.44 × 85.8 = 124 s. Final answer: 124 s. (c) L = L₀ / γ = 2.38 × 10¹⁰ / 1.44 = 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m. Final answer: 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes β = v/c into γ = 1 / √(1 − β²).
Correct answer: 1.44.
Multiplies proper time interval Δt₀ by γ (Δt = γ Δt₀).
Correct answer: 124 s.
Divides proper length L₀ by γ (L = L₀ / γ).
Correct answer: 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m.

options.label: A
options.text: Special relativity rests on the two postulates that Newton's laws hold only in a universal stationary ether frame and the speed of light increases linearly with source speed.
options.distractorRationale: Contradicts both postulates by reintroducing a preferred ether frame and Galilean light-speed addition.

options.label: B
options.text: Special relativity rests on the two postulates that the laws of physics take the same form in all inertial reference frames and the speed of light in vacuum has the same constant value c for all inertial observers regardless of source or observer motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Special relativity rests on the two postulates that time intervals and lengths are absolute across all inertial frames while momentum depends on observer speed.
options.distractorRationale: Time and length are frame-dependent in special relativity; only the spacetime interval and c are invariant.

options.label: D
options.text: Special relativity rests on the two postulates that the laws of physics hold identically in all accelerating frames and gravity travels instantaneously.
options.distractorRationale: Special relativity applies specifically to inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames and limits all signals to speed c.

items.stem: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, an electron occupies the $n = 3$ stationary orbit of radius $r_3 = 4.76 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$. Using $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$, what is the orbital speed $v_3$ of the electron?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging $m_{\text{e}} v_3 r_3 = \frac{3h}{2\pi}$ gives $v_3 = \frac{3 \times 6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi (9.11 \times 10^{-31})(4.76 \times 10^{-10})} = 7.30 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 7.30 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A gamma photon with energy above twice an electron's rest energy creates a pair near a lead nucleus. What happens to the extra photon energy?
items.workedSolution: By mass–energy conservation, energy above $2E_0$ becomes kinetic energy of the created particles. Note that exam answers must say 'kinetic energy', not 'speed'. Option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: kinetic energy of the particles before annihilation or after pair creation.

options.distractorRationale: Rest energy E₀ is an invariant property of each particle species.

items.stem: Why does Required Practical 12 plot $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against ruler distance $x$ instead of $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$? What safety controls are required?
items.workedSolution: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x gives a straight line with negative x-intercept −x₀ despite the unknown offset. Handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs, maximise distance, and limit time outside lead storage. This linear plot against x reveals the systematic offset directly.

markScheme.criterion: States 1/√C_corr vs x stays linear with intercept −x₀ despite unknown offset. Notes tongs, distance, minimal time outside lead storage.

options.text: Plotting C_corr against 1/x² always gives a straight line through the origin even with an unknown internal offset x₀.
options.distractorRationale: Because true distance is x + x₀, C_corr = k/(x + x₀)² curves significantly when plotted against 1/x².

options.label: B
options.text: Simply avoiding touching the source with bare fingers is a sufficient radiological safety protocol.
options.distractorRationale: AQA mark schemes explicitly reject bare 'do not touch'; specify long tongs, maximum distance, minimum exposure time, and lead-lined storage.

options.label: C
options.text: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x eliminates the need to subtract background radiation.
options.distractorRationale: Background count rate MUST be subtracted before taking 1/√C_corr, otherwise the line bends horizontally at large x.

options.label: D
options.text: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x stays linear with negative x-intercept −x₀ despite unknown internal offset; students must handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

items.stem: Calculate the magnitude of the specific charge of a bare $^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ nucleus. Take $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: Net charge magnitude $Q = 26 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 4.16 × 10⁻¹⁸ C$ and mass $m = 9.37 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, giving $Q/m = 4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. Option A (4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Correct specific charge $Q/m = 4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$ (4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹, option A).

items.stem: Measuring nuclear radius by diffraction needs electrons of several hundred MeV (λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m). Why can low-energy keV electrons not be used?
items.workedSolution: Clear diffraction needs λ ~ R (~10⁻¹⁵ m), matching nuclear diameter (~10⁻¹⁵ m). High-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and give radius directly, unlike alpha closest approach.

markScheme.criterion: States diffraction needs λ comparable to nuclear size, and electrons are leptons giving direct radius unlike alpha closest approach.

options.label: A
options.text: Diffraction requires de Broglie wavelength comparable to nuclear diameter (~10⁻¹⁵ m), and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

options.label: B
options.text: Low-energy electrons are hadrons that get absorbed by the strong nuclear force before reaching the detector.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons at all energies and never feel the strong nuclear force.

options.label: C
options.text: High-energy electrons have much longer de Broglie wavelengths so sin θ stays larger than one.
options.distractorRationale: Higher momentum gives a SHORTER de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, and sin θ must be < 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Low-energy electrons move faster than light and bypass the target nuclei completely.
options.distractorRationale: No massive particle exceeds c; low-energy electrons simply have λ >> R, giving no observable nuclear diffraction minimum.

items.stem: Both Compton scattering and the photoelectric effect support the particle model of light. Why is Compton scattering even stronger evidence?
items.workedSolution: The photoelectric effect showed light carries quantized energy $E = hf$. Compton scattering also proves photons carry quantized momentum $p = h/\lambda$ in elastic collisions with electrons.

markScheme.criterion: States Compton scattering proves photons carry quantized momentum as well as energy in electron collisions.

options.label: A
options.text: Compton scattering shows light travels slower than $c$ inside graphite targets, contradicting Maxwell's equations.
options.distractorRationale: Compton scattering concerns photon–electron momentum transfer, not refractive speed reduction.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Compton scattering proves photons carry quantized momentum as well as energy in elastic collisions with electrons, directly confirming billiard-ball-like conservation of linear momentum.

options.label: C
options.text: Compton scattering requires visible red light rather than ultraviolet or X-ray frequencies.
options.distractorRationale: Compton shifts are measurable precisely at short X-ray or gamma wavelengths, not visible light.

options.label: D
options.text: The photoelectric effect can be fully explained by classical wave theory whereas Compton scattering cannot.
options.distractorRationale: Neither effect is explained by classical wave theory, but Compton scattering uniquely proves quantized photon momentum $p = h/\lambda$.

items.stem: A linear particle accelerator tunnel has a proper length of 1500 m in the laboratory frame. What length does this tunnel appear to have in the rest frame of a particle moving through it at $0.800c$?
items.workedSolution: $\sqrt{1 - 0.800^2} = 0.600$, so contracted length is $l = l_0 \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 1500 \times 0.600 = 900 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 900 m.

items.stem: A sodium nucleus (A = 22, Z = 11) decays only by beta-plus decay (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ). The final nucleus has A = 22 and Z = 10. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Initial neutron number N₀ = 22 − 11 = 11; final neutron number N_f = 22 − 10 = 12. Thus ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 1.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N = A − Z to obtain ΔN = (22 − 10) − (22 − 11) = 1 (A).

items.stem: A proton (charge +1e) with initial kinetic energy 5.1 MeV is fired head-on at a stationary Ta nucleus (Z = 73, A = 181). It comes to rest at distance d before reversing. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 5.1 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(1e)(73e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(1)(73)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ = 20.6 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 20.6 fm (D).

items.stem: A nucleus of Cm has nucleon number A = 244 and proton number Z = 96. It decays only by alpha and beta-minus emission. The final nucleus has A = 228 and Z = 90. How many beta-minus particles are emitted in this decay chain?
items.workedSolution: Only alpha decay changes nucleon number A: Nα = (244 − 228) / 4 = 4. Proton balance gives 90 = 96 − 2(4) + Nβ⁻, so Nβ⁻ = 90 − 88 = 2.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Nα = 4 from ΔA / 4 and solves Z_f = Z_0 − 2Nα + Nβ⁻ to obtain Nβ⁻ = 2 (D).

items.stem: Monochromatic light above threshold frequency strikes a photocathode, producing curve Q on the $I\text{–}V$ graph. The light intensity is increased at constant frequency to produce curve P. Which statement describes the resulting changes?
items.workedSolution: Higher intensity brings more photons per second, freeing more electrons per second and raising photocurrent. Since frequency is fixed, $eV_{\text{s}} = hf - \phi$ stays the same. Option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: increasing intensity increases photocurrent while stopping potential remains unchanged.

items.stem: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons accelerate from rest through 4450 V. They pass through a thin gold foil (plane spacing d = 2.35 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) and form bright rings on a screen at distance L = 0.15 m. Use sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the radius r of the first-order bright diffraction ring?
items.workedSolution: λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 1.84 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Then sin θ = λ / d = 0.0783, giving θ = 4.49 ° and ring radius r = L tan θ = 0.15 × tan(4.49°) = 0.0118 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = 1.84 × 10⁻¹¹ m, θ = 4.49°, and r = L tan θ = 0.0118 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full diameter 2r of the diffraction ring instead of its radius r.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mₑeV), overestimating λ and ring radius by √2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the diffraction ratio as d / λ instead of λ / d.

items.stem: Atoms of rubidium vapour have a first excited state at −2.59 eV and a nearby bound level at −4.18 eV. Ionization occurs at zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−2.59) = 2.59 eV. Final answer: 2.59 eV. (b) ΔE = 2.59 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (6.25 × 10¹⁴) = 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 480 nm. Final answer: 480 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 2.59 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Correct answer: 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Correct answer: 480 nm.

items.stem: Both the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) and the Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) use the wave nature of electrons. Both can resolve single atoms, far beyond optical microscopes.
items.workedSolution: Level 3: A TEM uses high voltage to shorten the electron de Broglie wavelength. An STM uses quantum tunnelling across a nanometre gap, where current depends exponentially on gap width. Compare TEM magnetic lenses, thin-sample needs, and lens limits with STM piezo scanning and conducting-surface limits.

markScheme.criterion: Explains TEM uses high voltage for a very short wavelength $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_e e V}$, cutting diffraction.
Describes TEM magnetic lenses (condenser, objective, projector) sending electrons through a thin sample in vacuum.
States TEM limits: sample thickness slows electrons (longer $\lambda$), lens aberrations, or speed spread.
Explains STM uses quantum tunnelling across a nanometre gap, with current decaying exponentially with width.
Describes STM mapping using piezoelectric control in constant-current or constant-height mode.
States STM limits: conducting sample needed, vibration isolation, and surface-only imaging.

parts.prompt: Compare how a TEM and an STM work, how they form images, and their practical limits.
parts.expectedAnswer: Both microscopes use electron wave behaviour in different ways. A TEM uses high voltage to give electrons a very short de Broglie wavelength. An STM uses quantum tunnelling across a tiny gap. In a TEM, an electron gun accelerates electrons through high voltages so $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_e e V}$ is a few picometres. This is much shorter than visible light and cuts diffraction blur. Magnetic condenser, objective, and projector lenses focus the beam through a very thin sample in vacuum onto a screen. Denser parts scatter more electrons and look darker. TEM resolution is limited because thick samples slow electrons and increase $\lambda$. Electrons also have a spread of speeds, and magnetic lenses show aberrations. In an STM, a fine metal tip sits about $1\text{ nm}$ above a conducting sample with a small bias voltage. Electron wavefunctions cross the gap by quantum tunnelling, and current decays exponentially with gap width $d$. Constant-current mode uses piezo feedback to trace surface height, while constant-height mode records current changes. STMs need conducting samples, strong vibration isolation, and only map the surface.
workingSteps: TEM wave principle: high anode p.d. gives picometre wavelength $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_e e V}$, cutting diffraction.
TEM image: magnetic condenser, objective, and projector lenses focus electrons through a thin sample in vacuum.
TEM limits: samples must be very thin (thicker ones slow electrons and raise $\lambda$), lens aberrations, and speed spread.
STM wave principle: electron waves cross a narrow vacuum barrier by quantum tunnelling, sensitive to gap width.
STM scanning: piezo constant-current feedback or constant-height current mapping.
STM limits: needs conducting samples, vibration isolation, and maps only the surface.

items.stem: A star is in spectral class M. It is red and has a surface temperature below $3500\text{ K}$. Which main absorption lines appear in its spectrum?
items.workedSolution: Below $3500\text{ K}$, molecules stay intact. Class M stars therefore show neutral atoms and TiO molecular bands.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies neutral atoms and TiO molecular bands.

options.label: A
options.text: Strong lines from neutral atoms and TiO molecular bands, which survive without dissociating at low stellar temperatures.

options.label: B
options.text: Prominent ionised helium (He⁺) and neutral helium (He) lines with negligible metal lines.
options.distractorRationale: He⁺ and He lines require extreme temperatures of class O (25 000 – 50 000 K).

options.label: C
options.text: The strongest Hydrogen Balmer absorption lines in the entire spectral sequence.
options.distractorRationale: Hydrogen Balmer lines peak in blue-white class A stars (7 500 – 11 000 K).

options.label: D
options.text: Ionised metals only, because all neutral atoms are stripped of electrons below 3500 K.
options.distractorRationale: At < 3500 K thermal energy is too low to ionise most atoms, allowing neutral atoms and TiO molecules to persist.

items.stem: With no source present, a detector records a background count rate of 18 counts min⁻¹. When a source of Ga-68 (half-life 68 min) is placed in front of it at t = 0, the total reading is 418 counts min⁻¹. A second reading is taken after 272 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 418 − 18 = 400 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 400 counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 272 / 68 = 4 half-lives. C_net = 400 / 2^4 = 25.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 25.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 25 + 18 = 43.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 400 counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 4 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^4.
Correct answer: 25.0 counts min⁻¹.
Adds background count rate back to the remaining net count rate to obtain 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Determine the initial corrected count rate from the Ga-68 source at t = 0.
Calculate the corrected count rate from the source alone at t = 272 min.
State the total count rate displayed by the detector at t = 272 min.

Correct answer: 7.77 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

items.stem: Technetium-99m has a short $6\text{ h}$ half-life, ideal for medical scans. This makes long-distance delivery impractical. How does a hospital keep a steady daily supply?
items.workedSolution: Parent $^{99}\text{Mo}$ (molybdenum-99) has a useful $66\text{ h}$ half-life. It decays inside a shielded generator so short-lived technetium-99m can be eluted on site.

markScheme.criterion: States molybdenum-99 decays in a shielded generator so technetium-99m is eluted on site.

options.text: Hospitals run a nuclear fission reactor beneath the ward to fuse technetium directly from lead.
options.distractorRationale: Hospitals do not operate on-site fission reactors; they receive shielded $^{99}\text{Mo}$ elution generators.

options.text: Technetium-99m is frozen in liquid nitrogen to halt radioactive decay until needed.
options.distractorRationale: Radioactive decay is spontaneous and unaffected by temperature.

options.distractorRationale: Linear accelerators deliver radiotherapy X-rays/electrons rather than producing $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$ in vivo.

items.stem: A nuclide has decay constant $\lambda = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Over an interval $t = 600\text{ s}$, the linear product $\lambda t = 1.20$ exceeds unity and fails as a probability. What is the exact probability that a given nucleus decays during this $600\text{ s}$ interval?
items.workedSolution: Survival fraction is $e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-1.20} = 0.301$. Hence exact decay probability is $P = 1 - e^{-\lambda t} = 1 - 0.301 = 0.699$.

items.stem: A negative kaon ($K^-$, quark composition $s\bar{u}$, strangeness $S = -1$) decays into two pions: $K^- \to \pi^- + \pi^0$. Calculate the change in strangeness $\Delta S = S_{\text{after}} - S_{\text{before}}$.
items.workedSolution: Before decay $S = -1$ ($K^-$); after decay $S = 0 + 0 = 0$ ($\pi^-$ and $\pi^0$). Thus $\Delta S = 0 - (-1) = +1.00$. Option A (1.00) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Change in strangeness $\Delta S = +1$ (1.00, option A).

items.stem: How did Max Planck solve the ultraviolet catastrophe in 1900 so theory matched black-body curves?
items.workedSolution: Planck proposed discrete energy quanta E = hf. At short wavelengths, $hf$ is much larger than thermal energy $kT$, preventing high-frequency divergence.

markScheme.criterion: States Planck proposed discrete energy quanta E = hf, preventing high-frequency divergence.

options.label: A
options.text: Planck assumed ultraviolet light is completely absorbed by the luminiferous ether before leaving the cavity.
options.distractorRationale: Planck introduced quantised oscillator energy packets $E = hf$, not ether absorption.

options.label: B
options.text: By breaking with continuous classical energy: Planck proposed discrete energy quanta E = hf preventing high-frequency divergence because high-frequency oscillators rarely receive a full quantum.

options.label: C
options.text: Planck replaced Maxwell's equations with Newton's corpuscular theory of gravity inside the furnace.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity does not control thermal cavity radiation.

options.label: D
options.text: Planck assumed cavity walls could only oscillate at wavelengths longer than 1 mm.
options.distractorRationale: High-frequency modes exist geometrically but are suppressed probabilistically because $hf \gg kT$.

items.stem: Why is the inside of a mercury fluorescent tube coated with white phosphor powder?
items.workedSolution: Excited mercury atoms emit high-energy UV photons. The phosphor coating absorbs these UV photons and de-excites in smaller steps to emit visible light. Option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Option B: phosphor absorbs UV photons and de-excites in smaller steps to emit visible light.

options.label: B
options.text: The coating is needed because the phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and de excites in multiple smaller steps emitting visible light

options.label: C
options.text: The coating is needed because the phosphor speeds up free electrons to higher kinetic energies

items.stem: How does an indirect flat-panel (FTP) X-ray detector form a digital radiograph?
items.workedSolution: In an FTP detector, a scintillator converts X-rays into visible light. Photodiode pixels detect this light and are scanned electronically, giving fast digital images at lower dose.

markScheme.criterion: States a scintillator converts X-rays to light, detected by photodiode pixels and scanned electronically.

options.text: X-ray photons directly darken silver-halide chemical film which must be developed in a darkroom.
options.distractorRationale: That describes conventional photographic film rather than an electronic FTP detector.

options.label: C
options.text: Piezoelectric crystals convert incoming X-rays into standing acoustic waves timed by a computer.
options.distractorRationale: Piezoelectric transducers detect ultrasound echoes, not X-rays.

options.label: D
options.text: A rotating lead disc reflects X-rays into an eyepiece viewed directly by the radiologist.
options.distractorRationale: X-rays are absorbed by lead and cannot be focused with optical eyepieces.

items.stem: A single-electron Be³⁺ ion (Z = 4) has energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The ion starts in level n = 5. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest photon wavelength that can ionize the ion from n = 5?
items.workedSolution: Initial level energy Eₙ = −13.6 × 4² / 5² = −8.70 eV. Ionization requires ΔE = 8.70 eV = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum ionizing wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = 143 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV and λ = hc / ΔE = 143 nm (B).

items.stem: The mass of an iron-56 nucleus (A = 56, Z = 26) is 55.920674 u. Use mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this iron-56 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 56 − 26 = 30. Mass defect Δm = 26(1.007276) + 30(1.008665) − 55.920674 = 0.528 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 492 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 492 / 56 = 8.79 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.528 u, B = 492 MeV, and B / A = 8.79 MeV (A).

items.stem: A beam of protons starts from rest in a vacuum and accelerates through 220 V. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₚ = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in picometres (pm), of the protons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 3.52 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 3.43 × 10⁻²² N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 1.93 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 1.93 pm (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.workedSolution: (a) $\mu_m = 0.220 m² kg⁻¹$. (b) Transmitted $= 2.35\%$. (c) $x = 0.921 mm$.

Correct transmitted percentage 2.35%.
Correct tenth-value thickness 0.921 mm.

items.stem: Consider this nuclear fusion reaction of deuterium and helium-3: deuteron (2.013553 u) + helium-3 nucleus (3.014932 u) → alpha particle (4.001506 u) + proton (1.007276 u). Take u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0197 u. Final answer: 0.0197 u. (b) Q = 0.0197 × 931.5 = 18.4 MeV. Final answer: 18.4 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 5. Final answer: 5.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Correct answer: 0.0197 u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.
Correct answer: 18.4 MeV.

items.stem: Light of frequency 6.16 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on a clean caesium surface in a vacuum. The work function of caesium is 1.95 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What stopping potential Vₛ reduces the photocurrent to zero?
items.workedSolution: Photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.16 × 10¹⁴) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.55 eV. Maximum kinetic energy Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = E − Φ = 2.55 − 1.95 = 0.603 eV. Hence stopping potential Vₛ = 0.603 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds eVₛ = hf − Φ to obtain Vₛ = 0.603 V (D).

items.stem: A spacecraft travels at constant speed v = 0.84c between two space stations a proper distance L₀ = 5.04 × 10⁹ m apart. A clock on the spacecraft measures a proper time interval Δt₀ = 19.6 s. What contracted length L of the path L₀ is measured in the moving frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.84²) = 1.84. Contracted length L = L₀ / γ = 5.04 × 10⁹ / 1.84 = 2.73 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds γ = 1.84 and L = L₀ / γ = 2.73 × 10⁹ m (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies classical Galilean subtraction u′ = u − v without the relativistic denominator (1 − uv/c²).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds velocities instead of subtracting when both motions share the +x direction.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses a plus sign in the denominator (1 + uv/c²) instead of (1 − uv/c²).

items.stem: UV light of wavelength 148 nm falls on a clean lithium plate in a vacuum. The work function of lithium is 2.93 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 1.34 × 10⁻¹⁸ J; work function Φ = 2.93 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.69 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 8.75 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.39 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.39 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (A).

options.distractorRationale: Adds the work function Φ to hc/λ instead of subtracting Φ before solving ½mₑv² = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 in vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ), evaluating √(Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Equates ½mₑv² directly to the incident photon energy hc/λ without subtracting the work function.

items.stem: The figure shows the dark-line absorption spectrum of a cool gas cloud. It also shows the emission spectra of three elements: P, Q, and R. Which element is present in the gas cloud?
items.workedSolution: Compare the line positions vertically down the figure. Every dark absorption line lines up with an emission line of Element Q. Element Q is therefore present.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies Element Q because every dark absorption line matches an emission line of Element Q.

items.stem: A $1.64\text{ MeV}$ gamma photon creates an electron–positron pair near a heavy nucleus. Each particle has rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the pair.
items.workedSolution: $E_{\text{k,tot}} = E_\gamma - 2E_0 = 1.64 - 2(0.511) = 0.618 MeV$. Option C (0.618 MeV) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Total kinetic energy $= 0.618 MeV$ (0.618 MeV, option C).

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student plots $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against ruler distance $x$ (in m). The straight line has gradient 0.500 s^{1/2} m⁻¹ and y-intercept 9.00 × 10⁻³ s^{1/2}. Calculate the hidden offset distance $x_0$ inside the source and GM tube (in mm).
items.workedSolution: Background rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 540/(20\times 60) = 0.450 s⁻¹$. From $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$, gradient $= 1/\sqrt{k} = 0.500$, so $k = 4.00 s⁻¹ m²$, $x_0 = \text{intercept}/\text{grad} = 18$ mm, and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 18.3 s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines sourceOffsetX0Mm $= 18.0 mm$.

items.stem: Removing 3 electrons forms an $^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ ion. Calculate the magnitude of its specific charge. Take $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: Net charge magnitude $Q = 3 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ and mass $m = 4.52 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, giving $Q/m = 1.06 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. Option B (1.06 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Correct specific charge $Q/m = 1.06 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$ (1.06 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹, option B).

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines the binding energy of an atomic nucleus?
items.workedSolution: A nucleus has less mass (mass defect Δm) than its separate nucleons. Binding energy Δm c² is the work needed to split a nucleus completely into separate protons and neutrons.

markScheme.criterion: Defines binding energy as the work needed to split a nucleus into individual protons and neutrons.

options.label: A
options.text: Binding energy is the kinetic energy released when a nucleus absorbs a thermal neutron and splits into two equal fragments.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses binding energy of a nucleus with the Q-value of induced fission.

options.label: B
options.text: Binding energy is the electrostatic energy required to remove all orbital electrons from a neutral atom.
options.distractorRationale: Describes total atomic ionisation energy rather than nuclear binding energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Binding energy is the energy stored inside a nucleus that can be extracted by pulling its nucleons apart.
options.distractorRationale: Work must be supplied to separate a bound nucleus into free nucleons; energy is released during assembly, not separation.

options.label: D
options.text: By definition, binding energy is the work required to completely separate a nucleus into its individual constituent protons and neutrons.

items.stem: A beam of 250 MeV electrons (λ ≈ hc / E) scatters off iron-56 nuclei, producing a non-zero first diffraction minimum at θ_min = 43.3° (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). Using sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R, calculate the nuclear radius R of iron-56 in femtometres.
items.workedSolution: λ = hc / E = 4.97 fm. Rearranging sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R gives R = 0.61 λ / sin(43.3°) = 4.40 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates nuclear radius R = 4.40 fm.

items.stem: In a diffraction experiment, electrons pass through a thin foil and form circular rings. The first intensity minimum is at angle $\theta_1$. What happens to $\theta_1$ when the accelerating p.d. $V$ is increased?
items.workedSolution: From $\lambda = h / \sqrt{2m_{\text{e}} e V}$, raising $V$ shortens the de Broglie wavelength. Since $\theta_1 \approx \lambda / b$, the first minimum moves to a smaller angle.

markScheme.criterion: States higher accelerating p.d. shortens de Broglie wavelength and moves the minimum to a smaller angle.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing accelerating potential lengthens the de Broglie wavelength and expands the diffraction minimum outward.
options.distractorRationale: Since $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_{\text{e}} e V}$, raising $V$ decreases $\lambda$ and shrinks the diffraction angle.

options.label: B
options.text: The diffraction minimum angle remains fixed because it depends solely on the atomic spacing of the target.
options.distractorRationale: Minimum location scales with $\lambda/b$, so changing electron momentum changes $\theta_1$.

options.label: C
options.text: The rings disappear completely at higher voltage because fast electrons stop displaying wave properties.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons retain wave behaviour; the rings simply contract to smaller angles as $\lambda$ decreases.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher kinetic energy means greater momentum, so increasing accelerating potential shortens the de Broglie wavelength and shifts the diffraction minimum to a smaller angle toward the centre of the screen.

items.stem: In a Bertozzi-type experiment, electrons reach a speed of $0.9165c$. Their rest energy is $m_0 c^2 = 0.511\text{ MeV}$. Calculate the relativistic kinetic energy $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2$ in MeV.
items.workedSolution: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.9165^2}} = 2.50$. Using the electron rest energy $m_0 c^2 = 0.511\text{ MeV}$ ($0.510999\text{ MeV}$ on the AQA Data Sheet), $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2 = 0.769 MeV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 0.769 MeV.

items.stem: A parent nucleus of barium-141 has nucleon number A = 141 and proton number Z = 56. It decays by beta-minus decay (d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) to form a daughter nucleus with A = 141 and Z = 59. How many d → u quark changes occur in this decay chain?
items.workedSolution: Each weak beta step flips exactly one quark inside a nucleon, changing Z by +1 while keeping A constant. Accounting for ΔA = 0 gives 3 weak quark transitions.

markScheme.criterion: Balances A and Z to identify 3 single-quark weak beta transitions (D).

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, an alpha particle (charge +2e) of kinetic energy 4.5 MeV approaches a fixed palladium nucleus (Z = 46, A = 106) head-on. Electrostatic repulsion stops it at a closest distance d. Neglect recoil and take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 4.5 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 7.20 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(2e)(46e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2)(46)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 7.20 × 10⁻¹³ = 29.4 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 29.4 fm (D).

items.stem: An unstable radium nucleus (A = 226, Z = 88) decays by alpha and beta-minus steps only. The final nuclide has nucleon number A = 206 and proton number Z = 80. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Parent neutron number N₀ = 226 − 88 = 138. Final neutron number N_f = 206 − 80 = 126. Therefore ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −12.

items.stem: Which statement is the exact AQA definition of the work function $\phi$ of a metal?
items.workedSolution: AQA requires both 'minimum energy' and 'metal surface': minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface. Therefore option C is correct: minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface.

items.stem: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons accelerate from rest through 980 V. They pass through a thin gold foil (plane spacing d = 2.35 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) and form bright rings on a screen at distance L = 0.15 m. Use sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 3.92 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.167 yields θ = arcsin(0.167) = 9.61 °.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 9.61 ° (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves arcsin(λ / d) in radians while labelling the answer in degrees.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inserts an extra factor of 2 in the denominator despite sin θ = λ / d being specified.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 in p = √(2mₑeV) when computing the electron de Broglie wavelength.

items.stem: The carbon-14 decay curve shown (T₁/₂ = 5730 yr) is used to date old wooden objects. Which statement gives a key assumption and the upper age limit of radiocarbon dating?
items.workedSolution: Radiocarbon dating assumes the atmospheric ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 stayed constant while the organism lived. After ~10 half-lives (~57 000 yr), activity falls below 0.1% of A₀, blending into background counts.

markScheme.criterion: States dating assumes constant atmospheric carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio, and fails beyond roughly ten half-lives near background.

options.text: Radiocarbon dating works accurately on billion-year-old granite rocks because carbon-14 is locked inside silicate crystals.
options.distractorRationale: Radiocarbon dating applies only to once-living organic matter younger than ~50 000–60 000 years.

options.label: B
options.text: Carbon-14 continues to be absorbed at the same rate after the tree dies, so the ratio of C-14 to C-12 stays constant.
options.distractorRationale: Carbon uptake stops at death, so C-14 activity then decays exponentially.

options.label: C
options.text: When interpreting a radiocarbon age, radiocarbon dating assumes the atmospheric ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 was constant while the organism lived and becomes unreliable beyond roughly ten half-lives because the sample count rate falls close to background.

options.label: D
options.text: Radiocarbon dating fails for samples younger than 10 000 years because the activity is too high for GM detectors.
options.distractorRationale: Living carbon activity is tiny (~15 counts min⁻¹ per gram); the problem occurs in *very old* samples where activity blends into background.

items.stem: In a discharge lamp, barium vapour has its second excited state at −2.34 eV and another bound level at −3.55 eV. Take zero energy at the ionization level. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What energy, in electron-volts (eV), is needed to ionize an atom from the second excited state?
items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from the second excited state to the continuum is ΔE = 0 − (−2.34) = 2.34 eV.

items.stem: The Feynman diagram shows $\beta^-$ decay of a free neutron into a proton, electron, and electron antineutrino. Which exchange particle should replace the question mark?
items.workedSolution: Charge conservation at the $n \to p + W^-$ vertex requires a $W^-$ boson (reject bare 'W' or 'W meson'). Therefore option B is correct: W minus boson.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: W minus boson.

options.text: The interaction is mediated by a W plus boson
options.distractorRationale: At the n → p vertex charge goes 0 → +1, so the emitted boson must carry −1 charge (W⁻), not +1.

options.label: B
options.text: The interaction is mediated by a W minus boson

options.label: C
options.text: The interaction is mediated by a virtual photon
options.distractorRationale: Photons mediate electromagnetic interactions and cannot change quark flavour.

options.label: D
options.text: The interaction is mediated by a neutral pion meson
options.distractorRationale: Pions mediate the strong nuclear force, whereas beta decay is a weak interaction; never call W a meson.

items.stem: In a Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM), a sharp metal tip sits about one nanometre above a conducting sample. The small bias voltage is far below the work function. How does a current still cross the empty vacuum gap?
items.workedSolution: An electron's wavefunction penetrates the narrow vacuum barrier. Electrons cross by quantum tunnelling, and the current decays exponentially as gap width increases.

markScheme.criterion: States electrons cross the vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling, with current decaying exponentially with gap width.

options.text: Electrons boil out of the sample by thermionic emission at room temperature.
options.distractorRationale: STMs run at room or very low temperatures, where thermionic emission is negligible.

options.label: B
options.text: Visible light from a laser ionises air molecules between tip and sample to form a spark.
options.distractorRationale: STM imaging operates across a vacuum gap via quantum tunnelling, not gas ionisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Due to wave-particle duality, electrons cross the narrow vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling with current decaying exponentially as gap width increases.

options.label: D
options.text: Classical electrostatic force accelerates electrons linearly with gap width.
options.distractorRationale: Classically electrons lack energy to cross the barrier; quantum tunnelling probability decays exponentially with gap width.

items.stem: A hot blue class O star has a surface temperature of $35\,000\text{ K}$ and lots of hydrogen. Why are its hydrogen Balmer absorption lines very weak?
items.workedSolution: At $35\,000\text{ K}$, high-energy collisions strip electrons from hydrogen atoms. Most hydrogen is ionised, so very few electrons occupy n=2.

markScheme.criterion: States that in very hot O stars most hydrogen is ionised, so few electrons occupy n=2.

options.text: Because class O stars are too cool to excite hydrogen electrons out of the n = 1 ground state.
options.distractorRationale: That explains weak Balmer lines in cool class M stars, not hot class O stars.

options.label: B
options.text: Because hydrogen molecules fuse into titanium oxide bands at 35 000 K.
options.distractorRationale: Molecules like TiO dissociate completely above ~4000 K.

options.label: C
options.text: Because in very hot O stars most hydrogen is ionised so few electrons occupy n=2 to absorb visible Balmer photons.

options.label: D
options.text: Because class O stars emit zero visible continuum light for hydrogen to absorb.
options.distractorRationale: A 35 000 K black body emits strongly across UV and visible wavelengths.

items.stem: With no source present, a detector records a background count rate of 46 counts min⁻¹. When an iodine-123 source (half-life 13.2 h) is placed in front of it, the total reading is 286 counts min⁻¹. A second reading is taken after 26.4 h. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 26.4 h?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 286 − 46 = 240 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 26.4 / 13.2 = 2. Remaining net count rate C = 240 / 2^2 = 60 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 60 + 46 = 106 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (240), divides by 2^2 (60), and adds 46 back to obtain 106 counts min⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the uncorrected count rate first and subtracts the background count rate at the end.

items.stem: A radioactive sample of Lu-177 contains 8.6 × 10¹³ undecayed nuclei. Its half-life is T₁/₂ = 6.65 d. The sample is left to decay for 9.11 d. What is the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Converting half-life to SI seconds: T₁/₂ = 6.65 × 86400 = 5.75 × 10⁵ s. Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 1.21 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 1.04 × 10⁸ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = ln 2 / (6.65 × 86400) and A₀ = λN₀ = 1.04 × 10⁸ Bq (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves T₁/₂ in d instead of converting to seconds when evaluating A₀ = (ln 2 / T₁/₂) N₀ in Bq.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor ln 2 ≈ 0.693 in λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Finds the decayed activity at elapsed time t instead of A₀ at t = 0.

items.stem: Doctors treat local tumours such as prostate or eye cancer using internal radiotherapy. Why are sealed beta-emitting implants often chosen over gamma sources?
items.workedSolution: Gamma rays penetrate far and expose healthy organs away from the site. Beta-emitting implants give short-range ionisation inside the tumour, sparing nearby healthy cells.

markScheme.criterion: States beta implants deliver short-range ionisation inside the tumour while sparing nearby healthy cells.

options.text: Beta particles pass cleanly through the entire torso so external detectors can focus them onto the tumour.
options.distractorRationale: Beta particles have a short range of only a few millimetres in tissue—that is precisely why they spare distant organs.

options.label: B
options.text: Beta particles are non-ionising and destroy cancer cells purely by heating the implant capsule.
options.distractorRationale: Beta radiation kills tumour DNA via intense ionisation within its short tissue range.

options.label: C
options.text: Beta emitters cannot be sealed inside capsules and must circulate freely through the bloodstream.
options.distractorRationale: Brachytherapy implants are sealed seeds or wires placed directly in or adjacent to the tumour.

options.label: D
options.text: Because beta-emitting radioactive implants deliver short-range ionisation inside a tumour sparing surrounding healthy cells outside the immediate tumour volume.

items.stem: Beta particles from a source have a continuous range of kinetic energies. Alpha particles from one nuclide have only sharp kinetic energies, with matching gamma photons. What does this prove?
items.workedSolution: Alpha particles are emitted at sharp kinetic energies that match the nuclear transition and gamma photon energies. This gives direct evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.

markScheme.criterion: States discrete alpha and gamma energies give direct evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.

options.text: Alpha particles share kinetic energy continuously with emitted neutrinos so nuclear energy levels form a smooth continuum.
options.distractorRationale: No neutrino is emitted in alpha decay; two-body recoil plus quantized nuclear levels yields sharp discrete alpha energies.

options.label: B
options.text: Atomic electrons alone determine alpha-particle energies while the nucleus itself has no quantized energy states.
options.distractorRationale: MeV alpha and gamma transitions arise from discrete energy states inside the nucleus, far larger than eV atomic transitions.

options.label: C
options.text: Every alpha particle from any element always carries the exact same kinetic energy regardless of the parent nuclide.
options.distractorRationale: Each nuclide has its own characteristic set of discrete nuclear energy levels and alpha line energies.

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha particles are emitted with discrete kinetic energies matching specific nuclear transitions and associated gamma photon energies providing direct evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.

items.stem: What is the main difference between hadrons and leptons in the particle chart?
items.workedSolution: Leptons are fundamental particles and do not feel the strong nuclear force. Hadrons are made of quarks and do feel the strong force. Option D is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: leptons are fundamental particles that do not experience the strong nuclear force.

items.stem: A fluorine-18 FDG tracer injected for a PET scan has a physical half-life of 1.83 h and a biological half-life of 7.32 h. Calculate its effective half-life inside the body.
items.workedSolution: $T_E = \frac{T_P T_B}{T_P + T_B} = \frac{1.83 \times 7.32}{1.83 + 7.32} = 1.46 h$. Note that $T_E$ is always shorter than both $T_P$ and $T_B$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 1.46 h.

items.stem: Newton's particle theory of light was preferred over Huygens' wave theory for over a century. Why did scientists favour Newton's model?
items.workedSolution: Newton had great authority, and sharp straight-line shadows hid light's tiny diffraction. Wave theory waited for Young (1801) and Foucault (1850).

markScheme.criterion: States Newton's authority and sharp shadows hiding tiny-wavelength diffraction.

options.text: Because Foucault had already measured light travelling faster in glass than in air in 1690.
options.distractorRationale: Foucault's 1850 measurement actually showed light travels SLOWER in water, refuting Newton.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Huygens' wave theory could not explain straight-line reflection off plane mirrors.
options.distractorRationale: Huygens' wavelet principle explained both reflection and refraction cleanly.

options.label: C
options.text: Because Newton had immense authority and sharp rectilinear shadows hid tiny-wavelength diffraction, and no experiment could yet measure the speed of light inside glass or water.

options.label: D
options.text: Because Young's double-slit fringes directly confirmed Newton's corpuscles in 1704.
options.distractorRationale: Young's 1801 double-slit experiment contradicted corpuscles and supported waves.

items.stem: An excited mercury orbital electron drops from the $-5.5\text{ eV}$ level to the $-10.4\text{ eV}$ ground state. Using $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, calculate the wavelength of the emitted UV photon in nanometres.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta E = (-5.5) - (-10.4) = 4.90\text{ eV} = 7.84 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, so $\lambda = hc/\Delta E = 254 nm$. Option C (254 nm) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Emitted UV wavelength $= 254 nm$ (254 nm, option C).

items.stem: Barium meals are used to image the digestive tract. Why is barium used, and why is an image intensifier needed for real-time fluoroscopy?
items.workedSolution: Soft organs have similar $\mu$, so high-Z barium or iodine absorbs X-rays strongly to create contrast. Image intensification brightens faint signals for low-dose real-time fluoroscopy.

markScheme.criterion: States barium or iodine absorbs X-rays strongly, and image intensification enables low-dose real-time fluoroscopy.

options.text: Barium emits beta particles that light up the stomach while fluoroscopy converts X-rays into MRI radio signals.
options.distractorRationale: Barium sulfate is non-radioactive and attenuates external X-rays strongly via its high Z.

options.label: B
options.text: Barium lowers soft-tissue density so more X-rays pass through, while image intensifiers increase tube kV.
options.distractorRationale: Barium increases attenuation strongly; image intensifiers amplify faint X-ray signals electronically.

options.label: C
options.text: High atomic number barium or iodine absorbs X-rays strongly and image intensification enables low-dose real-time fluoroscopy without giving a dangerously high continuous X-ray dose.

options.label: D
options.text: Barium is used strictly for bone fractures while fluoroscopy records only static photographic stills.
options.distractorRationale: Bone already has high natural contrast; fluoroscopy provides continuous moving X-ray images.

items.stem: In a hot gas, a N⁶⁺ ion (Z = 7) has quantized energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. The electron starts in level n = 5. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the lowest photon frequency needed to ionize the ion from n = 5?
items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from n = 5 is ΔE = 13.6 × 7² / 5² = 26.7 eV = 4.26 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 6.43 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Finds f = (13.6 Z² / n²)(e / h) = 6.43 × 10¹⁵ Hz (D).

items.stem: A sulfur-32 nucleus has nucleon number A = 32 and proton number Z = 16. Its nuclear mass is 31.963294 u. Take mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this sulfur-32 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 32 − 16 = 16. Mass defect Δm = 16(1.007276) + 16(1.008665) − 31.963294 = 0.292 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 272 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 272 / 32 = 8.49 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.292 u, B = 272 MeV, and B / A = 8.49 MeV (B).

items.stem: Electrons initially at rest are accelerated across a potential difference of 160 V in a vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the electrons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 2.56 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 6.83 × 10⁻²⁴ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 0.0971 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 0.0971 nm (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: Before an abdominal X-ray radiograph of the digestive tract, a patient swallows a barium sulfate suspension. Why does this greatly improve image contrast?
items.workedSolution: Photoelectric absorption rises strongly with atomic number ($\propto Z^3$). High-Z barium therefore increases absorption sharply, creating clear contrast with soft tissue.

markScheme.criterion: States high-atomic-number barium increases photoelectric absorption, giving sharp contrast with soft tissue.

items.stem: In Co-60 decay to the 2.50 MeV Ni-60 level, beta-minus particles have kinetic energies from zero up to 0.32 MeV. How did this continuous energy range lead to the neutrino hypothesis?
items.workedSolution: A two-body decay gives fixed particle energies, like α decay. A continuous β⁻ spectrum needs a third particle. The transition energy is shared with an electron antineutrino, conserving energy and lepton number.

markScheme.criterion: States beta-minus transition energy is shared with an electron antineutrino, conserving energy and lepton number.

options.label: A
options.text: Beta particles always lose variable random fractions of their kinetic energy by colliding with orbital electrons before leaving the nucleus.
options.distractorRationale: Atomic electron scattering does not account for the missing energy observed in vacuum beta-decay calorimetry.

options.label: B
options.text: To uphold conservation of energy, in beta-minus decay the available transition energy is shared continuously between the beta particle and an electron antineutrino, conserving energy and lepton number.

options.label: C
options.text: The parent Co-60 nucleus occupies a continuous band of unstable energies rather than a single discrete ground state.
options.distractorRationale: Nuclear ground states have sharply defined rest energies; a third unseen particle carries away the missing energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Conservation of energy holds only on average across large samples of beta decays, not for individual nuclear events.
options.distractorRationale: Pauli proposed the neutrino so energy, momentum, and lepton number are always conserved in every decay.

items.stem: In one fusion event of deuterium and helium-3, the nuclear equation is: deuteron (2.013553 u) + helium-3 nucleus (3.014932 u) → alpha particle (4.001506 u) + proton (1.007276 u). Take 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the mass loss Δm, in atomic mass units (u), in one fusion reaction?
items.workedSolution: Summing reactant and product rest masses gives Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0197 u.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0197 u (D).

items.stem: A beam of light of frequency 1.59 × 10¹⁵ Hz hits a clean nickel plate in a vacuum. The nickel surface has work function 5.04 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the threshold frequency f₀ of the nickel surface?
items.workedSolution: Work function Φ = 5.04 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f₀ = Φ / h = 8.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.22 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Finds f₀ = Φ / h = 1.22 × 10¹⁵ Hz (C).

items.stem: Cosmic-ray muons travel at constant speed v = 0.98c through Earth's atmosphere over a proper distance L₀ = 9940 m. The mean lifetime of a muon in its rest frame is Δt₀ = 2.38 × 10⁻⁶ s. What contracted length L of the path L₀ is measured in the moving frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.98²) = 5.03. Contracted length L = L₀ / γ = 9940 / 5.03 = 1.98 × 10³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds γ = 5.03 and L = L₀ / γ = 1.98 × 10³ m (A).

items.stem: Photons of wavelength 173 nm hit a clean barium surface in a vacuum. The work function of barium is 2.52 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the threshold wavelength λ₀ for this barium surface?
items.workedSolution: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc / Φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.52 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 493 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ₀ = hc / Φ = 493 nm (A).

items.stem: An atom drops between two energy levels separated by $\Delta E = 1.89\text{ eV}$. It emits one visible photon. Calculate the wavelength of this photon in nanometres.
items.workedSolution: Convert $\Delta E = 1.89 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.02 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$. Then $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^8)}{3.02 \times 10^{-19}} = 658 nm$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 658 nm.

items.stem: An electron and a positron each have rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$. Using $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ and $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, calculate the minimum frequency of a gamma photon required for electron–positron pair production.
items.workedSolution: $E_{\min} = 2 \times 0.511\text{ MeV} = 1.022\text{ MeV} = 1.635 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, so $f_{\min} = E_{\min}/h = 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$. Option B (2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Minimum photon frequency $= 2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz$ (2.47 × 10²⁰ Hz, option B).

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, the $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ graph has a negative x-intercept $-x_0$. What physically causes this offset $x_0$?
items.workedSolution: The offset comes from the depth of the radioactive pellet inside its capsule plus the sensitive depth behind the GM tube window. Handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs, maximise distance, and limit time outside lead storage. Plotting one over square root corrected count rate against x reveals this systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies hidden depth inside the source capsule and behind the GM tube window. Notes safe handling and linearised plot against x.

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Background subtraction error bends the curve at large x rather than producing a clean geometric shift x₀.

items.stem: A proton-rich sodium nucleus emits a positron ($\beta^+$ decay) to form a neon nucleus. How does the specific charge of the daughter nucleus compare with the parent nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Positron emission lowers nuclear charge from $Z e$ to $(Z-1)e$ with constant $A$, so specific charge decreases. Therefore option B is correct: specific charge decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: specific charge decreases.

items.stem: The Compton shift is given by $\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_{\text{e}} c}(1 - \cos\theta)$. What determines the maximum wavelength shift $\Delta\lambda_{\max}$?
items.workedSolution: The factor $(1 - \cos\theta)$ reaches its peak of $2$ at $\theta = 180^{\circ}$ (180 degrees). Since $\frac{h}{m_{\text{e}} c}$ does not contain $\lambda_{\text{i}}$, the maximum shift does not depend on incident wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: States the maximum shift occurs at 180 degrees and does not depend on incident wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Maximum wavelength shift occurs at ninety degrees and increases proportionally with the incident wavelength.
options.distractorRationale: At $90^{\circ}$, $(1 - \cos\theta) = 1$, which is only half the maximum at $180^{\circ}$, and $\Delta\lambda$ does not depend on $\lambda_{\text{i}}$.

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum wavelength shift occurs in the forward zero-degree direction where the electron receives maximum impulse.
options.distractorRationale: At $\theta = 0^{\circ}$, $1 - \cos 0^{\circ} = 0$, giving zero shift and no deflection.

options.label: C
options.text: The maximum wavelength shift occurs at backscattering of 180 degrees and is independent of the incident photon wavelength.

options.label: D
options.text: Maximum wavelength shift decreases to zero as incident photon energy increases into the gamma-ray region.
options.distractorRationale: $\Delta\lambda_{\max} = 2h/(m_{\text{e}}c)$ is fixed by universal physical constants regardless of incident wavelength.

items.stem: Cosmic-ray muons form high in the atmosphere and travel toward Earth at $0.960c$. A muon at rest has a mean proper lifetime of $t_0 = 2.20\,\mu\text{s}$. What mean lifetime is measured by an observer on Earth?
items.workedSolution: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.960^2}} = \frac{1}{0.280} = 3.57$. Time dilation gives $t = \gamma t_0 = 3.57 \times 2.20 = 7.86 μs$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 7.86 μs.

items.stem: A strontium-82 nucleus (A = 82, Z = 38) decays only by beta-plus decay (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ). The final nucleus has A = 82 and Z = 36. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Initial neutron number N₀ = 82 − 38 = 44; final neutron number N_f = 82 − 36 = 46. Thus ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N = A − Z to obtain ΔN = (82 − 36) − (82 − 38) = 2 (D).

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, an alpha particle (charge +2e) with kinetic energy 6.9 MeV moves head-on toward a fixed gold nucleus (Z = 79, A = 197). It scatters back through 180° after stopping at closest distance d. Neglect nuclear recoil and take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 6.9 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.10 × 10⁻¹² J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(2e)(79e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2)(79)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 1.10 × 10⁻¹² = 32.9 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 32.9 fm (A).

items.stem: A radioactive decay chain starts from a uranium nucleus (A = 238, Z = 92). It emits only alpha and beta-minus particles. The daughter nucleus has A = 222 and Z = 86. What is the change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent?
items.workedSolution: Parent neutron number N₀ = 238 − 92 = 146. Final neutron number N_f = 222 − 86 = 136. Therefore ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −10.
