items.stem: A clean, negatively charged zinc plate sits on a gold-leaf electroscope. UV light above the threshold frequency shines on the plate. What happens and why?
items.workedSolution: Since $f > f_0$, UV photons free photoelectrons from the negatively charged zinc plate. As negative charge leaves, the gold leaf falls quickly. Option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: gold leaf falls rapidly as photoelectrons are emitted from the negatively charged zinc plate.

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately upon illumination, the gold leaf rises further as ultraviolet photons donate negative charge to the gold leaf
options.distractorRationale: Photons are uncharged; UV releases electrons from the zinc plate, reducing negative charge.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately upon illumination, the gold leaf falls rapidly as photoelectrons are emitted from the negatively charged zinc plate

options.label: C
options.text: Immediately upon illumination, the gold leaf falls because electrons are ejected directly from the gold leaf inside the case
options.distractorRationale: AQA explicitly rejects electrons emitted 'from the gold leaf'; emission occurs from the zinc plate.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately upon illumination, the gold leaf waits several minutes to accumulate wave energy before falling
options.distractorRationale: Photoelectric emission is instantaneous above threshold frequency, contradicting the classical wave model.

items.stem: A beam of electrons is accelerated from rest through 2900 V onto a thin silicon film (spacing d = 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). A screen at distance L = 0.2 m shows bright diffraction rings. Use sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 2.28 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.0726 yields θ = arcsin(0.0726) = 4.16 °.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 4.16 ° (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves arcsin(λ / d) in radians while labelling the answer in degrees.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inserts an extra factor of 2 in the denominator despite sin θ = λ / d being specified.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 in p = √(2mₑeV) when computing the electron de Broglie wavelength.

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, alpha particles (Z₁ = 2) of energy 5.7 MeV hit a titanium-48 nucleus (Z = 22, A = 48). Model the nucleus as a uniform sphere with radius R = R₀ A^(1/3). Take R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. What is the nuclear radius R, in femtometres (fm), of the titanium-48 nucleus?

items.stem: The diagram shows energy levels of krypton gas. The ground level is at −14.12 eV, and a nearby bound level is at −4.15 eV. A free electron has zero energy. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest wavelength of light that can ionize an atom from the ground level?
items.workedSolution: Ionization from the ground level requires ΔE = 0 − (−14.12) = 14.1 eV = 2.26 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.26 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 88.0 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Converts ΔE = 14.1 eV to joules and applies λ = hc / ΔE to obtain 88.0 nm (B).

items.stem: Two electrons approach and deflect away from one another as shown in the Feynman diagram. Which exchange particle mediates this interaction?
items.workedSolution: Electromagnetic forces between charged particles are mediated by a virtual photon. Therefore option C is correct: virtual photon.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: virtual photon.

items.stem: How do constant-current and constant-height modes in an STM map an atomic surface?
items.workedSolution: Constant-current mode uses piezoelectric feedback to move the tip up and down. Constant-height mode keeps the tip level and measures changes in tunnelling current.

markScheme.criterion: States constant-current mode adjusts tip height with piezo feedback, while constant-height mode records current changes.

items.stem: Nearly all stars are made mostly of hydrogen. Yet visible hydrogen Balmer lines are strongest in class A stars ($7500\text{–}11\,000\text{ K}$). Why are these lines strongest in this temperature range?
items.workedSolution: Visible hydrogen Balmer absorption needs electrons in the n=2 level. In class A stars, thermal energy excites many atoms to $n = 2$ without ionising most of them.

markScheme.criterion: States that Balmer absorption needs electrons in n=2, which peaks in class A stars.

options.label: A
options.text: Class A stars contain ten times more hydrogen by mass than class O or class M stars.
options.distractorRationale: Most normal stars have similar hydrogen levels. Surface temperature controls line strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Because hydrogen Balmer absorption requires electrons in the n=2 level which peaks in class A stars, where thermal collisions excite many atoms to $n = 2$ without ionising most of them.

options.label: C
options.text: Visible Balmer absorption occurs only when ground-state electrons jump directly from n = 1 to n = 2.
options.distractorRationale: The $n = 1 \to n = 2$ jump is an ultraviolet Lyman transition; Balmer lines originate from $n = 2$.

options.label: D
options.text: Class A stars are the hottest stars on the HR diagram so their Balmer photons undergo no absorption.
options.distractorRationale: Classes O and B are hotter than class A, and absorption lines require atoms in $n = 2$ to absorb photons.

items.stem: With no source present, a detector records a background count rate of 26 counts min⁻¹. When a technetium-99m source (half-life 6 h) is placed in front of it, the total reading is 1146 counts min⁻¹. A second reading is taken after 30 h. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 30 h?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 1146 − 26 = 1120 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 30 / 6 = 5. Remaining net count rate C = 1120 / 2^5 = 35.000000000000014 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 35.000000000000014 + 26 = 61.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (1120), divides by 2^5 (35.000000000000014), and adds 26 back to obtain 61.0 counts min⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides the net count rate by 2n instead of 2ⁿ.

items.stem: A sealed source of iodine-131 holds 2.4 × 10¹³ unstable nuclei with half-life 8.02 d. The source decays for t = 7.3 d. What is the activity of the sample, in becquerels (Bq), at t = 7.3 d?
items.workedSolution: T₁/₂ = 8.02 × 86400 = 6.93 × 10⁵ s, so λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 2.40 × 10⁷ Bq. At t = 7.3 d, A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.28 × 10⁷ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ to seconds, finds A₀ = λN₀, and finds A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.28 × 10⁷ Bq (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Fails to convert half-life from d to seconds (× 86400) when computing A = λN in Bq (s⁻¹).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the initial activity A₀ = λN₀ at t = 0 without multiplying by the exponential decay factor e^(−λt).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ = 1 / T₁/₂ instead of λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ when converting half-life to decay constant.

items.stem: Inside a gamma camera, a faint flash of light enters a photomultiplier tube (PMT). How does this become a measurable voltage pulse?
items.workedSolution: A light photon frees a photoelectron from the photocathode by the photoelectric effect. The photoelectron accelerates through increasingly positive dynodes, releasing a cascade of secondary electrons to the anode.

markScheme.criterion: States photoelectrons accelerate across increasingly positive dynodes, producing a secondary electron cascade at the anode.

options.label: A
options.text: Gamma photons directly heat a tungsten filament until thermionic electrons boil across to the collimator.
options.distractorRationale: PMTs rely on the photoelectric effect at a cold photocathode followed by secondary emission at positive dynodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Scintillation light undergoes nuclear fission inside each dynode to double the photon frequency.
options.distractorRationale: No nuclear reactions occur inside a PMT; electrons multiply via kinetic impact on dynodes.

options.label: C
options.text: Light strikes the photocathode and each photoelectron accelerates across increasingly positive dynodes releasing a secondary electron cascade to the anode, producing a detectable voltage pulse.

options.label: D
options.text: Dynodes are kept at progressively more negative potentials to repel electrons back to the crystal.
options.distractorRationale: Each successive dynode must be MORE positive to accelerate negatively charged electrons onward.

items.stem: Fluorine-18 and fluorine-19 are isotopes, and fluorine-18 is radioactive. Which statement defines isotopes and spontaneous, random radioactive decay?
items.workedSolution: Isotopes have the same proton number Z but different neutron numbers N. Decay is spontaneous because external conditions cannot change it. It is random because we cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay.

markScheme.criterion: States isotopes share proton number with different neutron numbers, and decay is unaffected by outside conditions and unpredictable.

options.text: Isotopes have the same neutron number and different proton numbers, and heating a sample speeds up its radioactive decay.
options.distractorRationale: Isotopes share proton number Z (not neutron number), and spontaneous decay is unaffected by temperature or pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers and radioactive decay is spontaneous and random because external conditions cannot alter it and individual decay times cannot be predicted.

options.label: C
options.text: Isotopes have identical nucleon numbers, and random decay means the exact decay instant of every nucleus is predetermined by age.
options.distractorRationale: Isotopes differ in nucleon number A, and random decay means any undecayed nucleus has the same probability of decaying regardless of age.

options.label: D
options.text: Spontaneous decay requires bombardment by thermal neutrons while random decay means half-life changes unpredictably every hour.
options.distractorRationale: Spontaneous decay occurs without external triggering, and the half-life of a given nuclide is a fixed constant.

items.stem: In the strong interaction $\pi^- + p \to X + \Lambda^0$, the $\Lambda^0$ baryon has strangeness $S = -1$. Using the conservation ledger, identify particle $X$.
items.workedSolution: With $\pi^-$ ($Q=-1, B=0, S=0$) + $p$ ($Q=+1, B=+1, S=0$) and $\Lambda^0$ ($Q=0, B=+1, S=-1$), $X$ requires $Q=0, B=0, S=+1$, which is a neutral kaon ($K^0$). Therefore option B is correct: neutral kaon.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: neutral kaon.

items.stem: A patient receives a Tc-99m radioactive tracer with initial activity 640 MBq. Both its physical half-life and biological half-life are 6.00 h. What activity remains in the patient after 9.00 h?
items.workedSolution: $\frac{1}{T_E} = \frac{1}{6.00} + \frac{1}{6.00} \Rightarrow T_E = 3.00\text{ h}$. After $9.00\text{ h}$ ($3$ effective half-lives), $A = 640 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 80.0 MBq$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 80.0 MBq.

items.stem: In the late nineteenth century, what was the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' that challenged classical wave physics?
items.workedSolution: Equipartition of continuous classical wave energy gave $I \propto \lambda^{-4}$, meaning classical theory predicted infinite radiated intensity at short ultraviolet wavelengths.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that classical theory predicted infinite radiated intensity at short ultraviolet wavelengths.

options.label: A
options.text: The failure in which classical theory predicted infinite radiated intensity at short ultraviolet wavelengths, contradicting experimental black-body curves that fall to zero at short wavelengths.

options.label: B
options.text: The prediction that hot objects could emit only radio waves and never emit visible or ultraviolet light.
options.distractorRationale: Classical theory predicted too MUCH (infinite) UV radiation, not zero UV radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: The observation that ultraviolet light travels slower in a vacuum than red light.
options.distractorRationale: All electromagnetic waves travel at $c$ in free space.

options.label: D
options.text: The disappearance of interference fringes whenever ultraviolet light passed through Young's double slits.
options.distractorRationale: Ultraviolet waves still diffract and interfere normally.

items.stem: Fast electrons pass through a thin graphite film. Why do they form circular rings on the screen instead of one spot?
items.workedSolution: The electron de Broglie wavelength matches the atomic spacing in graphite. The electrons diffract like waves and form rings. Option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Option A: electron diffraction shows wave behaviour when de Broglie wavelength matches atomic spacing.

items.stem: The spacetime diagram shows frame S′ moving at velocity v = 0.68c relative to laboratory frame S. In frame S, a deuteron beam travels along the same axis at velocity u = −0.58c. What is the angle θ, in degrees, between the ct′ axis of frame S′ and the ct axis of frame S?
items.workedSolution: On a Minkowski diagram with axes x and ct, tan θ = |v| / c = 0.68, so θ = arctan(0.68) = 34.2 °.

markScheme.criterion: Uses tan θ = v / c to obtain θ = 34.2 ° (D).

items.workedSolution: A rotating X-ray tube sends a narrow monochromatic beam onto a detector array. A computer reconstructs attenuation slices, which stack into a 3D view as the couch moves.

markScheme.criterion: States a rotating X-ray tube emits a narrow monochromatic beam onto detectors for computer slice reconstruction.

items.stem: For a one-electron C⁵⁺ ion (Z = 6), the bound energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. An electron is in state n = 3. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest photon wavelength that can ionize the ion from n = 3?
items.workedSolution: Initial level energy Eₙ = −13.6 × 6² / 3² = −54.4 eV. Ionization requires ΔE = 54.4 eV = 8.70 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum ionizing wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = 22.9 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV and λ = hc / ΔE = 22.9 nm (C).

items.stem: A bare aluminium-27 nucleus (Z = 13, A = 27) has a rest mass of 26.974395 u. Take mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this aluminium-27 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 27 − 13 = 14. Mass defect Δm = 13(1.007276) + 14(1.008665) − 26.974395 = 0.242 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 225 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 225 / 27 = 8.33 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.242 u, B = 225 MeV, and B / A = 8.33 MeV (B).

items.stem: Electrons initially at rest are accelerated across a potential difference of 900 V in a vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the electrons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 1.62 × 10⁻²³ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 0.0409 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds p and λ = h / p to obtain 0.0409 nm (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves out the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: Why is a thin sheet of aluminium placed directly across the exit window of a clinical diagnostic X-ray tube?
items.workedSolution: The aluminium filter absorbs low-energy soft X-rays that would add patient skin dose without reaching the detector.

markScheme.criterion: States the aluminium filter absorbs soft X-rays that raise skin dose without reaching the detector.

options.label: A
options.text: The aluminium filter eliminates high-energy hard X-rays so bones appear transparent.
options.distractorRationale: Hard X-rays penetrate the body to expose the detector; soft low-energy photons are filtered out.

options.label: B
options.text: The aluminium filter absorbs low energy soft X-rays that would raise patient skin dose without reaching the detector.

options.label: C
options.text: The aluminium filter accelerates electrons further to shorten the minimum wavelength.
options.distractorRationale: Aluminium sits outside the evacuated tube and interacts only with emitted X-ray photons.

options.label: D
options.text: The aluminium filter shifts tungsten characteristic K-lines into the visible spectrum.
options.distractorRationale: Filtering attenuates low-energy photons without changing photon wavelengths.

items.stem: An excited daughter nucleus drops down the vertical gamma arrows on the right of the decay chart. How do its proton number Z and nucleon number A change?
items.workedSolution: Gamma photons carry energy only, with zero charge and zero baryon number. Gamma de-excitation therefore leaves both proton number Z and nucleon number A unchanged.

markScheme.criterion: States gamma de-excitation releases excess energy as a photon while leaving proton number Z and nucleon number A unchanged.

options.text: Proton number Z decreases by 1 and nucleon number A stays constant because a proton converts into a neutron.
options.distractorRationale: Describes beta-plus decay or electron capture, not gamma de-excitation.

options.label: B
options.text: Both proton number Z and nucleon number A decrease by 2 as a neutral pair of nucleons leaves the nucleus.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma rays are massless, uncharged electromagnetic photons carrying energy only.

options.label: C
options.text: During the vertical transition, gamma de-excitation releases excess nuclear excitation energy as a high-energy photon while leaving both the proton number Z and nucleon number A unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Nucleon number A decreases by 1 because the emitted gamma photon removes one atomic mass unit of energy.
options.distractorRationale: Nuclear mass decreases slightly by ΔE/c², but the integer count of protons and neutrons does not change.

items.stem: Consider this nuclear fusion reaction of deuterium and ³He: deuteron (2.013553 u) + helium-3 nucleus (3.014932 u) → alpha particle (4.001506 u) + proton (1.007276 u). Take u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What energy Q, in MeV, is released in one fusion reaction?
items.workedSolution: Mass decrease Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0197 u. Energy released Q = Δm × 931.5 = 18.4 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Δm = 0.0197 u and Q = Δm × 931.5 = 18.4 MeV (A).

items.stem: In an LED practical, a student plots threshold voltage $V_0$ against $1/\lambda$. The straight line through the origin has gradient $1.215 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V m}$. Use $eV_0 = hc/\lambda$ with $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ and $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to write $h = A \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$. What is the value of $A$?

items.stem: In a photocell, light of frequency 1.09 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes a potassium plate. The work function of potassium is Φ = 2.29 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the maximum kinetic energy, in electron-volts (eV), of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.09 × 10¹⁵) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 4.52 eV. Subtracting Φ = 2.29 eV gives Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 2.23 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Converts hf to eV and subtracts Φ = 2.29 eV to obtain 2.23 eV (D).

items.stem: Fast beryllium-11 nuclei travel at speed v = 0.76c along a laboratory vacuum tube of proper length L₀ = 294 m. In the rest frame of the nuclei, a proper time interval is Δt₀ = 1.19 × 10⁻⁶ s. What contracted length L of the path L₀ is measured in the moving frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.76²) = 1.54. Contracted length L = L₀ / γ = 294 / 1.54 = 191 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds γ = 1.54 and L = L₀ / γ = 191 m (A).

items.stem: In frame S, Event A and Event B happen at the same time ct = 4.0 ls. Event B has a larger positive x-coordinate than Event A. Frame S′ moves along +x at v = 0.60c. Which event happens first in frame S′?
items.workedSolution: Lines of equal t′ run parallel to the tilted x′ axis (slope +v/c). The line through Event B (larger x) cuts the ct′ axis lower than Event A. Event B therefore happens before Event A in frame S′.

markScheme.criterion: States Event B happens before Event A in S′ because its line parallel to x′ cuts ct′ lower than Event A.

options.label: A
options.text: Reading along the dashed simultaneity lines parallel to x′, event B occurs before event A in frame S prime because its line of simultaneity parallel to the tilted x prime axis intersects the ct prime axis lower than event A.

options.label: B
options.text: Reading along the dashed simultaneity lines parallel to x′, events A and B remain strictly simultaneous in frame S′ because they share the same horizontal line.
options.distractorRationale: Horizontal lines represent simultaneity only in frame S; simultaneity lines in S′ are tilted parallel to x′.

options.label: C
options.text: Reading along the dashed simultaneity lines parallel to x′, event A occurs before event B in frame S′ because lines parallel to ct′ reach the x-axis further left.
options.distractorRationale: Projecting parallel to ct′ finds x′ (position), not ct′ (time); time ordering comes from projecting parallel to x′ onto ct′.

options.label: D
options.text: Reading along the dashed simultaneity lines parallel to x′, event A occurs before event B in frame S′ because both events lie outside the light cone.
options.distractorRationale: For v > 0 and x_B > x_A at equal t, t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) is smaller for Event B, so Event B occurs first in S′.

items.stem: Photons of wavelength 207 nm hit a clean magnesium surface in a vacuum. The work function of magnesium is 3.66 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the threshold wavelength λ₀ for this magnesium surface?
items.workedSolution: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc / Φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (3.66 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 340 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ₀ = hc / Φ = 340 nm (A).

items.stem: A nuclide of uranium is represented in standard nuclear notation as ${}^{235}_{92}\text{U}$. How many neutrons are contained inside one nucleus of this isotope?
items.workedSolution: The nucleon number is $A = 235$ (protons plus neutrons) and proton number is $Z = 92$. Therefore neutron number $N = A - Z = 235 - 92 = 143$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value: 143.
